# Delegation Risk — Complete Text

> A research framework for bounding the expected damage from delegating to AI agents: risk as the sum of probability times damage over harm channels, one composition rule for propagating it through delegation chains, runtime risk accounting in the agent harness, and the entanglement tax that correlated checks pay. Maintained by QURI (quantifieduncertainty.org) as part of the CAIRN project.
>
> This is the entire wiki concatenated into one document, in book reading order,
> for offline reading (e-readers) and LLM context. Web version: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org



------------------------------------------------------------
## The Core Path
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/reading-order/
------------------------------------------------------------

The site has about 65 pages, but its argument lives in about a dozen stops. If you read one route, read this one. Everything else is reference, supporting research or applied variation.

<span id="the-core-path"></span>

## The Core Path

**Before you start**, read the [Five-Minute Intro](/getting-started/five-minute-intro/). Keep [Concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/) and the [Glossary](/getting-started/glossary/) open for reference.

1. **[Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/)**: the three harm channels, accident, defection and hijack. They need different mitigations. Capability affects them differently: a more capable delegate may err less per action, but it is given more consequential actions and is better at pursuing a wrong goal. Better models alone do not solve all three channels.

2. **[Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)**: one composition rule instead of a menu. Multiply, correct for common-cause correlation with the beta-factor mixture, and note that correlation helps serial chains but hurts parallel checks.

3. **[Runtime Accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/)**: the math moved into the agent harness. It has three parts. The risk preflight estimates expected damage before each consequential action. The exposure envelope is a hard bound enforced regardless of intent. The exposure ledger is a per-delegate account, reconciled against outcomes. This page also explains why the preflight estimator must be more verifiable than the actor it checks.

4. **[Delegation Accounting](/delegation-risk/delegation-accounting/)**: risk as a balance-sheet item. Every delegation moves exposure onto someone's books, and the same key carries different exposure for delegates of different capability.

5. **[The Insurer's Dilemma](/delegation-risk/insurers-dilemma/)**: what moral hazard and adverse selection do to transferring delegation risk to an insurer, what real fidelity and AI liability cover does, and where insurance stops working against adversarial agents.

6. **[Entanglements](/entanglements/)**, **[Types](/entanglements/fundamentals/types/)** and **[Formal Definitions](/entanglements/fundamentals/formal-definitions/)**: why stacked checks that share a model, data or context are not independent, and the entanglement tax that results. The site's most distinctive contribution.

7. **[Detecting Influence](/entanglements/detection/detecting-influence/)**: practical methods for finding the coupling your architecture diagram says isn't there.

8. **[Entanglement Worked Examples](/entanglements/case-studies/examples/)**: systems diagnosed end to end. Each builds the correlation picture, finds the hidden dependency and redesigns.

9. **[Structural Patterns](/design-patterns/structural/)**: escalation ladders, the exposure-envelope gateway, task decomposition, bulkheads. These are the building blocks that bound damage regardless of component behavior.

10. **[Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/)**: side channels, and how components that never communicate can still coordinate by reasoning alike.

11. **[Composing Patterns](/design-patterns/composing-patterns/)**: how patterns interact, and the failure modes of composing them badly.

12. **Worked examples**: a [code-deployment agent](/design-patterns/examples/code-deployment-example/) and a [research assistant](/design-patterns/examples/research-assistant-example/), each with illustrative numbers.

13. **[Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/)**: what control evaluations, monitoring studies and anti-scheming training have actually measured, with their caveats.

14. **[Nuclear Launch Authority](/case-studies/human-systems/nuclear-launch-authority/)** and **[Jury Systems](/case-studies/human-systems/jury-trust/)**: two human institutions built for delegation under distrust. Nuclear command trades unauthorized launch against failure to retaliate, using two-person rules; juries show the independence arithmetic for unanimity failing when jurors share evidence and deliberate together.

15. **[Sydney / Bing Chat](/case-studies/ai-systems/case-study-sydney/)**: a real failure analysed against the framework, and the scaffold-enforced limit that contained it.

**After the Core Path**, go applied with the [Quick Start](/design-patterns/tools/quick-start/), or go deeper with the [Research section](/research/).

**Following the math.** [Concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/) → [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) → [Formal Definitions](/entanglements/fundamentals/formal-definitions/) → [Walkthrough](/delegation-risk/walkthrough/) → [Runtime Accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/).

================================================================================
# Getting Started
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## Five-Minute Intro
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/five-minute-intro/
------------------------------------------------------------

Handing a task to an employee, a script or an AI means taking on the downside of how it might go wrong. This framework's bet is that you can put a number on that downside, account for it like money, and design systems that spend less of it per unit of capability.

## 1. Delegation risk is a quantity

Three things often get smeared together:

- **Harm surface**: the *set* of distinct ways a delegation can go wrong (a coding agent's `rm`, its API calls, the emails it can send). Borrowed from *attack surface*.
- **Exposure**: the worst-case loss across that surface, given what this delegate can actually reach. Borrowed from finance's *exposure-at-default*.
- **Delegation risk**: the expected loss, probability times damage summed over the surface.

Enumerate, bound, expect. The third is the headline number ([canonical statement](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-formula)):

```
Delegation Risk = Σ P(harm mode) × Damage
```

A component with a 1% chance per month of causing \$10,000 of damage carries \$100/month of delegation risk.

## 2. Scaffolding that does the accounting

Imagine a coding agent that begins every consequential action by estimating its expected damage, and adjusts its strategy to lower it. This is [runtime accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/): the math moved into the harness around the model. It has three mechanisms.

- **Risk preflight**: before an action commits, the scaffold enumerates its harm surface, bounds the exposure, estimates the delegation risk and compares it with the session budget. Below threshold, proceed; above, adjust or escalate. The estimator must be more verifiable than the actor it checks, never the same model.
- **Exposure envelope**: hard limits on action-space that the scaffold enforces regardless of what the agent intends or argues, such as file scope, spend caps and egress rules. A budget can be overdrawn gradually; the envelope is a wall that a single catastrophic action must hit. You need both.
- **Exposure ledger**: the running position per delegate, reconciled against real incidents so the numbers don't stay made up.

Pieces of this exist today: pre-tool-use hooks, permission modes, sandboxes and spend caps in agent harnesses. What does not yet exist is the ledger with reconciliation.

## 3. The design space

There are two design moves.

**Decompose the task** across narrow components, none of which has enough capability, context or connectivity to cause catastrophic harm alone.

```
User → [Router] → [Narrow Component 1] → [Check] → Limited Action 1
                → [Narrow Component 2] → [Check] → Limited Action 2
                → [Narrow Component 3] → [Human Gate] → Sensitive Action
```

**Minimize each delegate.** Apply the [Least-X principles](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/), so that every component gets only what its task needs: Least Intelligence, Least Privilege, Least Context, Least Persistence, Least Autonomy, Least Connectivity. For a given capability there is some minimum exposure you can get away with, and the design work is finding it.

## 4. The complication: entanglement

Safeguards multiply only if they fail independently, and stacked safeguards rarely do, because they share causes: the same model family, the same training data, the same context. Decomposition also leaves some channels between components that cannot be removed ([load-bearing channels](/entanglements/)), and correlated failure concentrates there.

Three checks that each miss 10% of harmful actions promise, under independence, a 0.1% miss rate. With common-cause weight ρ the [canonical correction](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) gives (1−ρ)·0.001 + ρ·0.1, which is 1 + 99ρ times the naive figure: about 11× at ρ = 0.1, 21× at ρ = 0.2 and 50× at ρ = 0.5. That multiplier is the [entanglement tax](/entanglements/). For stacks built on one provider, ρ is an assumption; we know of no measurement on this scale. And this is benign-failure math: against an attacker who picks inputs to defeat every layer, assume ρ near 1.

Pricing that gap is what the framework adds to generic "decompose and verify" advice: diversify what your checks are built on, not just how many you stack.

## A worked mini-example

*All numbers are illustrative.* A Slack bot answers staff questions from internal docs, about 1,000 answers a month. The risk budget is \$200/month.

| Component | Implementation | Delegation risk |
|-----------|---------------|-----|
| Retriever | Code (vector search, access-filtered) | \$5/mo |
| Answerer | Frontier LLM via API, behind two checks | see below |
| Poster | Code (rate-limited) | \$1/mo |

Suppose 1% of the Answerer's drafts would leak something it shouldn't, at \$500 a leak. Unchecked, that is 1,000 × 0.01 × \$500 = \$5,000/month. Two checks screen each draft, a policy classifier and an LLM grader, both from the Answerer's model family, and each misses 10% of bad drafts.

- **Assuming independence**, both miss 1% of bad drafts, so the Answerer's risk is \$50 and the system total is \$56/month, well inside budget.
- **With the correction** for two layers, the miss rate is (1−ρ)·0.01 + ρ·0.1. At ρ = 0.2 that is 2.8%, giving \$140 for the Answerer and \$146 in total: inside budget. At ρ = 0.5 it is 5.5%, giving \$275 and \$281: over budget.
- **If the leaks come from instructions planted in the docs** (prompt injection), the attacker chooses the input. Assume ρ near 1: the pair is no better than one check, giving at least \$500 and \$506.

Whether the design ships depends on a number you have not measured. The fixes: measure ρ on a labeled challenge set, replace one check with a non-LLM rule or another provider's model, or tighten the envelope so a leak costs less.

Humans have long run exposure-limited delegation: nuclear launch requires two officers, and accounting separates the clerk who records a payment from the one who approves it. The [case studies](/case-studies/) read such institutions as delegation engineering.

Next: [the Core Path](/getting-started/reading-order/#the-core-path), [For Engineers](/getting-started/for-engineers/), or the [FAQ](/getting-started/faq/).


------------------------------------------------------------
## Concepts
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/core-concepts/
------------------------------------------------------------

A reference page. For the argument in order, read the [Five-Minute Intro](/getting-started/five-minute-intro/) and then [the Core Path](/getting-started/reading-order/#the-core-path).

## The formula

**Delegation Risk = Σ P(harm mode) × Damage(harm mode)**

For each way a delegation can go wrong (a *harm mode*), multiply the probability that it happens by the damage if it does, and sum over all harm modes. The result is an expected loss in dollars.

**Canonical definition**
This anchor is the canonical statement of the formula. Other pages restate it for convenience.

**Units.** State what the probabilities are per: per task, per action, or per period. The delegation risk carries the same unit. Convert between them by multiplying a per-task figure by tasks per period. Most pages on this site use dollars per month.

*Example (illustrative): an employee with check-writing authority, probabilities per year.*

| Harm mode | Probability | Damage | Contribution |
|-----------|-------------|--------|--------------|
| Clerical error | 0.01 | \$1,000 | \$10 |
| Unauthorized payment | 0.001 | \$50,000 | \$50 |
| Fraud | 0.0001 | \$500,000 | \$50 |

Delegation risk is \$110/year. This is the average loss over many such years, not a prediction for any one year; see [when expected loss is the wrong metric](#when-expected-loss-is-the-wrong-metric).

The three-tier vocabulary keeps the formula's inputs separate. The **harm surface** is the set of harm modes (you enumerate it). **Exposure** is the worst-case loss across it given what the delegate can reach (a bound). **Delegation risk** is the expectation. See the [Glossary](/getting-started/glossary/#exposure).

## Harm channels

Harm modes fall into [three channels](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/):

- **Accident**: the delegate fails at its task (bugs, hallucinations, edge cases).
- **Defection**: the delegate pursues something other than the principal's interest. Scheming is the strategic case; reward hacking, which is goal-directed but not scheming, is a sub-type.
- **Hijack**: a third party or user steers a delegate that is not itself scheming, for example through prompt injection in a document or tool output, or through misuse.

The channels call for different mitigations. Testing and redundancy address accidents. Control protocols and monitoring address defection. Separating instructions from untrusted data, and keeping a hard envelope, address hijack.

## Propagation

When delegates delegate, reliabilities compose. Quantitative "trust" on this site means one thing: **t = P(the delegate executes the task faithfully)**, estimated from its harm-mode table. If A delegates to B with t = 0.8 and B to C with t = 0.7, the chain works with probability 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.56 when the links fail independently.

Correlation changes the two directions of composition differently:

- **Serial chains** (every link must work): correlation helps, because failures bunch together. The plain product is conservative and safe to use.
- **Parallel checks** (a harmful action gets through only if every check misses): correlation hurts. Use the beta-factor mixture P(all miss) = (1−ρ)·∏pᵢ + ρ·min(pᵢ), with ρ on the failure-indicator (phi) scale. With three checks each missing 10%, the residual is 1 + 99ρ times the independence figure.

[Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) has the derivation, the simulation and the estimation recipe. The alternative rules that earlier versions offered are retired.

**Roll-ups add.** The expected loss of a system is the sum of its components' expected losses, whatever the correlation, by linearity of expectation. Where harm modes overlap on one asset, the naive sum overstates the true figure, so it is a conservative upper bound. Correlation matters for tail metrics and for AND-structured defenses, not for expected-loss totals.

## Decomposition and the Least-X core

A single delegate with broad capability, context and access concentrates risk: its worst case is the whole system's worst case. Decomposition splits a task across narrow components so that each one's exposure is bounded. It does not stop correlated components from failing together, and it does not stop instances of one model from coordinating through shared reasoning. That is the subject of [Entanglements](/entanglements/).

The six core [Least-X principles](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/) generalize least privilege:

- **Least Intelligence**: the least capable implementation that does the task.
- **Least Privilege**: minimum permissions and access rights.
- **Least Context**: minimum information about the wider system.
- **Least Persistence**: minimum state carried across invocations.
- **Least Autonomy**: minimum ability to act without review.
- **Least Connectivity**: minimum communication paths between components.

The canonical page lists further principles as a labelled tail.

## Verifiability hierarchy

Implementations differ in how thoroughly you can check them. From most to least verifiable:

1. **Formally verified code.** Proven against a specification. Examples: access-control checks, rate limiters.
2. **Deterministic tested code and rule-based checks.** Auditable and repeatable. Examples: routing, schema validation, allow-lists.
3. **Narrow learned models with measured error on a fixed task.** Examples: a classifier with a known false-negative rate on a held-out set.
4. **Trusted LLMs**, below the capability level at which scheming is a live concern. This is AI Control's "trusted model" ([Greenblatt et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)).
5. **Untrusted frontier models and agents.**

Use the most verifiable tier that can do the job. A check should sit at a more verifiable (lower-numbered) tier than the component it checks; a frontier model checking a sibling of itself shares its blind spots. Training method does not define a tier: nearly all deployed frontier models are RL post-trained, and what matters is what you can verify about the deployed system.

## When expected loss is the wrong metric

An expected-loss budget treats a 10⁻⁶ chance of losing \$1 billion the same as a certain loss of \$1,000. A principal who could not survive the first is not indifferent between them. Use something else when:

- **The tail matters.** Budget a tail measure such as [Expected Shortfall](/getting-started/glossary/#expected-shortfall), the mean loss in the worst few percent of periods. This needs loss distributions, not point estimates, and it is where correlation between components enters.
- **A single action can be catastrophic.** Put a hard cap on exposure instead of a budget on expectation. The [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope) exists because a single concentrated failure must hit a wall, not slowly overdraw an account.
- **The harm is irreversible or not denominated in money.** Treat it as a constraint (this mode must be outside the envelope, or below a stated probability), not as a line in a dollar budget.

## The minimal delegation-engineering layer

If you build nothing else, build these four:

1. **Write down the harm surface.** For each component, record what it can reach and how it can fail, in each of the three channels.
2. **Put a hard envelope around it.** File scope, tool permissions, egress allow-lists and spend caps, enforced by the harness, not by the model or its prompt.
3. **Set a correlation budget.** No two checks on the same action share a model family, and at least one check sits at tier 1 or 2 of the hierarchy.
4. **Keep a ledger and reconcile it monthly.** Log consequential actions with their preflight estimates, compare against incidents and near misses, and revise the estimates.

Ordinary security hygiene sits underneath: least privilege, sandboxing, audit logs and human approval above a threshold. It is necessary, but it is not what this framework adds. [For Engineers](/getting-started/for-engineers/) maps the layer onto current agent harnesses.

## What this framework is not

- **Not an alignment solution.** It assumes components may be misaligned and tries to bound the damage.
- **Not formal verification.** Its guarantees are probabilistic, except where an envelope is enforced mechanically.
- **Not validated.** Most numbers on this site are illustrative, and the framework is untested on deployed AI systems.

- [Glossary](/getting-started/glossary/) and [Quick Reference](/getting-started/quick-reference/)

## For Engineers
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/for-engineers/
------------------------------------------------------------

The fastest route: read the [Five-Minute Intro](/getting-started/five-minute-intro/), build [the minimal delegation-engineering layer](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-minimal-delegation-engineering-layer), and follow [the Core Path](/getting-started/reading-order/#the-core-path) when you want the reasons. The [Quick Start](/design-patterns/tools/quick-start/) checklist walks through a first assessment.

## Where the layer lives in an agent stack

Put every limit in the harness, not in the model. A system prompt is not a security boundary: an instruction in the prompt is one more input the model may fail to follow or be talked out of, including by text it reads in a tool result.

| Layer element | Where it lives in a current agent stack |
|---|---|
| **Harm surface** | An inventory of what the agent can touch: each MCP server and the tools it exposes, credentials and their scopes, writable paths, network destinations, and anything that sends messages or moves money. |
| **Exposure envelope** | Enforced outside the model. Run code in a sandbox (container or VM, scoped filesystem). Use an egress allow-list, tool allow/deny lists per MCP server, spend and rate caps, and scoped, short-lived credentials. |
| **Risk preflight** | Pre-tool-use hooks that can block a call, require approval or rewrite arguments. Use permission modes that decide which tools run unattended. The estimator sits at a more verifiable [tier](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy) than the agent: rules or a narrow classifier, not a sibling of the agent's model. |
| **Correlation budget** | Guard models and monitors from a different model family than the agent, plus at least one rule-based check per consequential action. |
| **Hijack defenses** | Keep untrusted content (web pages, documents, tool outputs) away from control flow. CaMeL extracts the control and data flows from the trusted query, so data retrieved later cannot change which tools are called (Debenedetti et al. 2025, [arXiv:2503.18813](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)). Beurer-Kellner et al. 2025 catalogue design patterns for agents that resist prompt injection ([arXiv:2506.08837](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837)). |
| **Ledger** | Post-tool-use hooks and tracing that record each consequential action with its preflight estimate, per delegate. Reconcile monthly against incidents and near misses. |

Harnesses already provide much of the first four rows. What they do not provide is the accounting: a preflight that estimates expected damage rather than asking a yes/no question, and a ledger whose estimates are checked against outcomes. [Runtime Accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/) describes both.

## Patterns and examples

The [pattern catalogue](/design-patterns/) has about twenty AI-specific patterns. The ones most engineers reach for first:

- **[Structural](/design-patterns/structural/)**: Escalation Ladder (approval modes), the exposure-envelope gateway, Task Decomposition Pipeline, Bulkhead Isolation.
- **[Monitoring](/design-patterns/monitoring/)**: Trusted Monitor, Random Audit, Flight Recorder.
- **[Verification](/design-patterns/verification/)**: Capability Probing, Honeypot Injection, Consistency Triangulation.
- **[Information](/design-patterns/information/)**: Need-to-Know Compartments, which separate untrusted context from capabilities.
- **[Recovery](/design-patterns/recovery/)**: Checkpoint-Rollback and Graceful Degradation.

There are two worked examples: a [code-deployment agent](/design-patterns/examples/code-deployment-example/) and a [research assistant](/design-patterns/examples/research-assistant-example/). [Composing Patterns](/design-patterns/composing-patterns/) covers how patterns interact.

## Three mistakes specific to this framework

Generic engineering advice (threat-model before copying patterns, don't over-engineer low-stakes tools) applies here as everywhere. These three are the ones the framework is specifically about.

### 1. Multiplying miss rates as if checks were independent

"Three checks, each catching 90%, so we miss 0.1%." That holds only if the checks fail independently. Checks built on one model family, trained on overlapping data or reading the same context tend to miss the same items. With common-cause weight ρ, three such checks miss (1−ρ)·0.001 + ρ·0.1 of harmful actions: about 11× the naive figure at ρ = 0.1, 21× at ρ = 0.2 and 50× at ρ = 0.5 (the [entanglement tax](/entanglements/)). We know of no measurement of ρ for same-provider stacks on this scale, so treat these values as assumptions.

These figures describe benign, common-cause failure. Against an adaptive attacker, such as an injected prompt or a scheming component searching for an input that defeats every layer, assume ρ near 1, so that only your single best check counts, unless a [control evaluation](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/) shows otherwise.

To avoid this mistake, give each consequential action at least one check from a different tier or provider. Measure ρ where you can, using the phi coefficient of per-item misses on a shared labeled challenge set ([recipe](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)).

### 2. Letting the wrong party set the risk budget

If the team that ships the agent sets its risk budget but users or third parties bear the harm, the team will tend to accept more risk than the people exposed would. In other words, it will overestimate how much risk is acceptable. This is moral hazard, the problem [The Insurer's Dilemma](/delegation-risk/insurers-dilemma/) works through. Have the risk-bearers, or someone accountable to them, set the budget. Get the estimates reviewed by someone who is not paid to ship.

### 3. Estimates that are never reconciled

A risk budget built from guesses and never compared with outcomes is fake precision with bookkeeping aesthetics. The probabilities also go stale: a model upgrade, a new tool or a widened use case changes the harm surface. Keep the ledger, and compare predicted against observed incidents and near misses on a schedule and after every capability or tool change. When they diverge, revise the estimates, not the incident log.

### A reading mistake

Skipping [Entanglements](/entanglements/). Two components that share a model are enough to pay the tax; you do not need a large system.


------------------------------------------------------------
## FAQ & Common Objections
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/faq/
------------------------------------------------------------

## Conceptual questions

### "Isn't this just defense in depth?"

Defense in depth is the starting point. The framework adds three things.

1. **A price for correlation.** Defense in depth is usually argued as if layers fail independently. Three checks that each miss 10% do not give a 0.1% miss rate if they share a model family, training data or context. With common-cause weight ρ they miss (1−ρ)·0.001 + ρ·0.1, which is about 11×, 21× or 50× the naive figure at ρ = 0.1, 0.2 or 0.5 (the [entanglement tax](/entanglements/)). You cannot stack your way past that floor. The useful question becomes how to lower ρ, by using different providers or non-LLM checks, not how many layers to add. Two caveats apply. ρ for same-provider stacks is assumed, not measured. And this is benign-failure math: against an attacker who searches for inputs that defeat every layer, assume ρ near 1 unless a [control evaluation](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/) shows otherwise.
2. **Budgeting in expected dollars**, so that a safeguard's cost can be compared with the risk it removes.
3. **Separating harm channels.** Accident, defection and hijack call for different safeguards ([Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/)).

### "How is this different from ordinary risk assessment?"

It is ordinary expected-loss assessment ([formula](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-formula)) applied per delegate and tracked at runtime. FAIR already expresses cyber risk as loss frequency times magnitude in money ([Related Approaches](/reference/related-approaches/)). What is specific here is the delegation structure: who delegates to whom, how checks compose, and how a harness keeps the account.

### "Why decomposition instead of one aligned agent?"

We cannot yet verify alignment, so decomposition limits the damage if we are wrong. Verifying a narrow component is also tractable in a way that verifying a general agent across all inputs is not.

### "Can't a capable enough system route around these constraints?"

Yes, given enough context, capability, persistence and connectivity; the Least-X principles each bound one of those. Do not assume a component is unaware of its constraints, however. Current models often infer that they are being evaluated: Schoen et al. 2025 report chains of thought that show awareness of alignment evaluation, and causal evidence that this awareness reduces covert behavior ([arXiv:2509.15541](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541)). Limits the harness enforces mechanically hold whether or not the model notices them.

### "Doesn't this limit what AI can do?"

Deliberately. How much capability decomposition costs depends on the task; the site does not know the general answer (see the speculative [strong-tools discussion](/power-dynamics/)).

## Practical questions

### "How do I estimate failure probabilities?"

In rough order of preference:

1. Logs from the same or a similar system.
2. Red-team and challenge-set results: run the component on labeled cases and count failures per task.
3. Calibrated expert elicitation, with ranges rather than points.

State the unit (per task, per action, per month) and reconcile against observed incidents once you have them. There are no defensible universal defaults: a miss rate measured on one task does not transfer to another.

### "What's the minimum I need to do?"

Build [the minimal delegation-engineering layer](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-minimal-delegation-engineering-layer): write down the harm surface, enforce a hard envelope, set a correlation budget, and keep a reconciled ledger. The [Quick Start](/design-patterns/tools/quick-start/) walks through a first pass.

### "What tools support this?"

None implements the accounting end to end. The pieces:

- **Agent harnesses**: pre-tool-use hooks, permission modes, MCP tool allow-lists, sandboxed execution and egress controls. These provide the envelope and a place for the preflight.
- **Guard models**: classifiers such as Llama Guard ([arXiv:2312.06674](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06674)) and agent guardrail systems such as LlamaFirewall ([arXiv:2505.03574](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03574)). Count them toward your correlation budget like any other check.
- **Prompt-injection designs**: CaMeL ([arXiv:2503.18813](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)) and related design patterns ([arXiv:2506.08837](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837)).
- **Control evaluations**: UK AISI's Inspect framework, and ControlArena (UK AISI with Redwood Research, 2025) for running control experiments.
- **Tracing**: OpenTelemetry or the harness's own logs, as raw material for a ledger.

The [delegation risk calculator](/design-patterns/tools/delegation-risk-calculator/) does the arithmetic.

## Skeptical questions

### "Why use less capable models as monitors when they make more mistakes?"

A less capable model makes more capability errors, but if it is below the level at which scheming is a live concern, it is unlikely to defect strategically. That is AI Control's *trusted model* assumption ([Greenblatt et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)), and it is an assumption, not a measurement. Capability errors can be caught by other layers; strategic defection is hard to detect. The framework accepts more of the first to get less of the second.

### "How do you know this works?"

We don't, for AI systems. Analogous fields offer mixed evidence. Nuclear and aviation safety allocate failure budgets through fault trees, with real but imperfect success. Value-at-risk budgeting in finance failed visibly in 2008, partly because the models understated correlation, which is close to the failure this framework is about. The logical case is that limiting capability, context and connectivity limits the attack surface. It has not been validated against AI-specific threats; [Open Problems](/research/potential-projects/) lists the experiments that would test it.

### "Isn't this security theater?"

It would be if the numbers were never checked. The safeguard is reconciliation: estimates are compared with outcomes and revised. The framework also makes predictions that could prove it wrong. One example: on a shared labeled set of harmful actions, two LLM monitors from the same provider will show a phi coefficient of per-item misses above 0.3. If such measurements come out consistently near zero, the entanglement tax is overstated and the site should say so.

## Technical questions

### "How does propagation handle cycles?"

Design for acyclic delegation; a cycle is a channel through which components can coordinate. If one is unavoidable, simulate the system. Do not add per-hop discounts: the [canonical rule](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) already penalizes length through multiplication, and a discount double-counts.

### "What about emergent behavior from component interactions?"

Structured interfaces and one-way information flows bound what components can express to each other. They do not make components independent. Components built on the same model share blind spots and can coordinate without communicating, by reasoning alike. Treat shared-model components as correlated by default ([Entanglements](/entanglements/)).

### "How do you handle adversarial users and third parties?"

As a separate harm channel, *hijack*: someone steers a delegate that is not itself scheming, through prompt injection in a document or tool output, or through direct misuse. Input sanitization does not work reliably for natural-language inputs, so the defenses are structural:

- Keep untrusted data out of control flow, as CaMeL does.
- Strip capabilities from any component that reads untrusted content.
- Enforce a hard envelope, so that a hijacked delegate can reach little.

Assume ρ near 1 across checks an attacker can probe.


================================================================================
# Delegation Risk
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## Overview
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/delegation-risk/
------------------------------------------------------------

Delegating a task, to an employee, a contractor or an AI agent, creates ways for it to go wrong. This section puts a number on them. The core quantity is an expected loss in dollars:

$$\text{Delegation Risk} = \sum_{\text{harm modes}} P(\text{harm mode}) \times \text{Damage}(\text{harm mode})$$

Three terms keep the inputs apart (definitions in the [Glossary](/getting-started/glossary/#exposure)):

- The **harm surface** is the set of harm modes. You enumerate it.
- **Exposure** is the worst-case loss across that set, given what the delegate can actually reach. It is a bound.
- **Delegation risk** is the expectation above. A **risk budget** caps it.

Every probability is per something. On this page, probabilities are per month at stated task volumes, so delegation risk is in dollars per month.

## A worked example

**Illustrative numbers**
The probabilities, damages and catch rates below are invented to show the mechanics. Nothing about real systems follows from them.

A research assistant has three components. A **coordinator** routes about 2,000 tasks a month and grants tool permissions to the other two. A **summarizer** reads about 1,500 external papers a month. A **code deployer** ships about 40 changes a month to a production service.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H[Human principal] --> C[Coordinator]
    C --> S[Summarizer]
    C --> D[Code deployer]
    D --> P[Production]
```

### Step 1: the harm table

Each row is a harm mode, tagged with its [channel](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/). An *accident* is a failure at the task. *Defection* is the delegate pursuing something else, including reward hacking. A *hijack* is a third party steering a delegate that is not itself scheming.

| Component | Harm mode | Channel | P per month | Damage | Risk per month |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coordinator | Misroutes a task | Accident | 0.01 | \$2,000 | \$20 |
| Coordinator | Grants excessive permissions by mistake | Accident | 0.003 | \$100,000 | \$300 |
| Coordinator | Grants excessive permissions deliberately | Defection | 0.002 | \$100,000 | \$200 |
| Summarizer | Misrepresents a paper's findings | Accident | 0.02 | \$5,000 | \$100 |
| Summarizer | Follows instructions injected into a paper and leaks proprietary data | Hijack | 0.002 | \$50,000 | \$100 |
| Code deployer | Ships buggy code | Accident | 0.05 | \$20,000 | \$1,000 |
| Code deployer | Special-cases or edits tests so a broken change passes | Defection (reward hacking) | 0.01 | \$20,000 | \$200 |
| Code deployer | Inserts deliberately malicious code | Defection (scheming) | 0.0001 | \$1,000,000 | \$100 |

By component, the coordinator carries \$520, the summarizer \$200 and the code deployer \$1,300. **The total is \$2,020 per month.**

The rows add whatever the correlation between them, by linearity of expectation. Where two rows can destroy the same asset, the sum overstates the true expected loss, so it is a conservative upper bound.

### Step 2: compare with the budget

Suppose the operator's risk budget is \$1,500 per month. The system is \$520 over, and the code deployer carries 64% of the total. There are three kinds of fix:

- Lower the probabilities, for example with a check before deployment.
- Lower the damage, by narrowing what a deployment can touch.
- Hand the decision to a human. This replaces the deployer's error rate with the human's; it does not remove the risk.

### Step 3: add a verifier

Put a deployment verifier between the deployer and production. It sits at tiers 1 and 2 of the [verifiability hierarchy](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy). It runs the test suite and static analysis. It requires human sign-off on any change to tests or CI configuration. A policy engine blocks changes outside an allow-list of paths and permissions. Assume it catches 70% of buggy changes, 90% of test tampering and 90% of malicious changes.

| Harm mode | Before | Catch rate (assumed) | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ships buggy code | \$1,000 | 70% | \$300 |
| Special-cases or edits tests | \$200 | 90% | \$20 |
| Inserts malicious code | \$100 | 90% | \$10 |

The code deployer falls to \$330, and the system to **\$1,050 per month**, under budget.

The arithmetic hides three things:

- **The malicious-code catch rate is the weakest number.** An attacker who knows the policy engine's rules aims at what they do not cover. A catch rate measured on ordinary changes does not transfer to deliberate ones. For that row you need a control evaluation, in which a red team plays the attacker ([Greenblatt et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942); see [adversarial inputs](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/#adversarial-inputs)).
- **The verifier does nothing about the hijack row.** The summarizer reads untrusted text, can see private data and can send data out. Removing the outbound path shrinks the exposure itself, which no catch rate does.
- **Expected loss hides the tail.** The \$100 malicious-code row is a one-in-10,000 chance of a \$1 million loss. An expected-loss budget treats it like a certain \$100 loss. A hard limit on what any single action can do handles this case better ([when expected loss is the wrong metric](/getting-started/core-concepts/#when-expected-loss-is-the-wrong-metric); [the exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope)).

### Quantitative trust

Earlier versions of this example put "trust" weights on the diagram's arrows without defining them. Where this site attaches a number to trust, it means t = P(the delegate executes a task faithfully), read off the harm table as one minus the probability of any harm mode per task. For the code deployer before the verifier, that is about 1 − 0.06/40 ≈ 0.9985 per deployment. Links of this kind compose through chains by the [propagation rule](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/).

| Page | Question |
|---|---|

| [Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/) | Does each harm mode come through accident, defection or hijack, and why does it matter? |
| [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) | How do reliabilities compose through chains and stacks of checks, and what does correlation do? |
