| [Exposure-Envelope Gateway](/design-patterns/structural/#exposure-envelope-gateway) | One enforcement point the agent cannot bypass, for tools, egress, writes and spend | all | Reference monitor; least privilege |
| [Task Decomposition Pipeline](/design-patterns/structural/#task-decomposition-pipeline) | Checkable steps; factored cognition | accident, defection | Pipes and filters; stage gates |
| [Bulkhead Isolation](/design-patterns/structural/#bulkhead-isolation) | Partitions that failures and credentials cannot cross | accident, hijack | Ship bulkheads; Nygard (2007) |
| [Voting Tribunal](/design-patterns/structural/#voting-tribunal) | Independent checkers vote; rotation and resampling | accident, defection | N-version programming; Byzantine fault tolerance |
| [Honeypot Injection](/design-patterns/verification/#honeypot-injection) | Traps and canary tokens that no legitimate task touches | hijack, defection | Honeypots; canary tokens |
| [Capability Probing](/design-patterns/verification/#capability-probing) | Elicits true capability; detects sandbagging | defection | Capability evaluations |
| [Consistency Triangulation](/design-patterns/verification/#consistency-triangulation) | Resamples and cross-checks for contradictions | accident | Triangulation; self-consistency |
| [Trusted Monitor](/design-patterns/monitoring/#trusted-monitor) | A trusted model scores every action; chain-of-thought monitoring | defection, hijack | Supervision; AI Control |
| [Random Audit](/design-patterns/monitoring/#random-audit) | Unpredictable deep review under an auditing budget | defection | Random tax audits; the Panopticon |
| [Flight Recorder](/design-patterns/monitoring/#flight-recorder) | Tamper-evident trace with detectors and drift baselines | all | Flight recorders; secure audit logs |
| [Need-to-Know Compartments](/design-patterns/information/#need-to-know-compartments) | Separates trusted instructions from untrusted data | hijack | Compartmented clearances; information-flow control |
| [Selective Amnesia](/design-patterns/information/#selective-amnesia) | Keeps derived results, not raw data, in every store | hijack, accident | Data minimization |
| [Expiring Grants](/design-patterns/information/#expiring-grants) | Every grant has a time-to-live; renewal is a new grant | all | Kerberos tickets; just-in-time access |
| [Adversarial Collaboration](/design-patterns/multi-agent/#adversarial-collaboration) | Debate between genuinely opposed parties | accident, defection | Adversarial legal process; AI safety via debate |
| [Trust Transitivity Limits](/design-patterns/multi-agent/#trust-transitivity-limits) | Attenuation and depth limits for subagent chains | hijack, defection | X.509 path-length constraints; macaroons |
| [Operator Incentives](/design-patterns/multi-agent/#operator-incentives) | Bonds, bounties and insurance on the humans and firms involved | all | Fidelity bonds; bug bounties; insurance |
| [Graceful Degradation](/design-patterns/recovery/#graceful-degradation) | Pre-defined degraded modes, a kill switch and fallbacks | all | Degraded modes; emergency stops |
| [Checkpoint-Rollback](/design-patterns/recovery/#checkpoint-rollback) | Undoes what can be undone; commit points for what cannot | accident | Transactions; sagas |

## Redundancy and independence

Several of these patterns get their value from multiple checks failing independently: Voting Tribunal, Consistency Triangulation, Adversarial Collaboration, stacked monitors and the Flight Recorder's detectors. Such checks rarely fail independently. Take three layers that each miss 10%. A common-cause correlation $\rho$ multiplies their joint miss probability by $1 + 99\rho$, which is about 11×, 21× and 50× at $\rho$ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. Those values of $\rho$ are assumed, not measured. Against an adaptive attacker, assume $\rho \to 1$ and count a stack as worth its best layer. Correlation does not change the sum of expected losses, only how often defenses fail together.

[Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) gives the rule and the estimation recipe. [Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/) covers active influence between components, and [Entanglements](/entanglements/) gives the wider treatment.

## Using the catalog

Start with structure. The envelope gateway, bulkheads and expiring grants bound exposure without detecting anything, so they hold against inputs and intentions nobody anticipated. Add verification and monitoring where the envelope has to be wide enough for the agent to do useful work. Add recovery for what detection misses. [Composing Patterns](/design-patterns/composing-patterns/) works through combinations.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Least-X Principles
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/least-x-principles/
------------------------------------------------------------

Least privilege gives each component the minimum access rights its function needs (Saltzer & Schroeder 1975). A delegated AI component has more dimensions than access rights: how capable it is, what it knows, what it remembers, how freely it acts and whom it can talk to. Each "Least X" principle bounds one of these. A component's exposure, the worst-case loss given what it can reach, is limited by whichever dimension binds first, so the principles are applied together.

Six principles are the core. The rest of the page lists a tail of narrower or weaker ones, each with its caveat.

| Principle | What it bounds |
|---|---|
| **Least Intelligence** | Capability: the least capable implementation that does the task |
| **Least Privilege** | Permissions and access rights |
| **Least Context** | Information about the wider system, other components and other users |
| **Least Persistence** | State carried across invocations |
| **Least Autonomy** | Ability to act without review |
| **Least Connectivity** | Communication paths between components |

None is new as a security idea. The AI setting adds that the component itself may be the adversary, misaligned or hijacked, and will use whatever capability, access, information, memory and channels it has. The principles shrink each in advance, without detecting anything.

## Least Intelligence

Give each component the least capable implementation that can do its job. A component that checks SQL for injection needs less general capability than one that designs database security, and a narrow component has fewer ways to fail and fewer ways to pursue something else.

"Less capable" is shorthand for "more verifiable". The working version of the principle is a choice among five tiers, from most to least verifiable:

1. **Formally verified code.** Proven against a specification. Examples: access-control checks, rate limiters, parsers with proved properties.
2. **Deterministic tested code and rule-based checks.** Auditable and repeatable. Examples: routing tables, schema validation, allow-lists, test suites.
3. **Narrow learned models with measured error on a fixed task.** Examples: a classifier with a known false-negative rate on a held-out set.
4. **Trusted LLMs**, below the capability at which scheming is a live concern. This is AI Control's *trusted model* ([Greenblatt et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)).
5. **Untrusted frontier models and agents.**

Use the most verifiable tier that can do the job. Training method does not define a tier: nearly every deployed frontier model is RL post-trained, and what matters is what you can verify about the deployed system. Earlier versions of this page ranked "RL systems" below "general foundation models"; that ordering would rule out every current frontier model and has been dropped.

Three rules follow from the tiers:

- **A check sits lower than what it checks.** A frontier model checking a sibling of itself shares its blind spots and, if the actor is scheming, may share its goals. This is the [risk preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#who-preflights-the-preflight) rule.
- **Push leverage down the tiers.** Where a component has leverage over others (a coordinator, a deployment gate, a permission grant), put as much of its logic as possible in tiers 1 and 2 and leave only the judgment calls to a model.
- **Weaker is not the same as trusted.** In AI Control, *trusted* means there is reason to believe the model is not scheming, usually because it is below the capability where scheming is plausible. An older model is not trusted merely by being older. And a trusted model's job in the Control protocols is mostly to monitor and edit the untrusted model's work, not to make the most consequential decisions in its place. See [Coordinator Constraints](/design-patterns/coordinator-constraints/#who-plans).

Two examples show the range:

- **A SQL-injection checker** should sit at tier 1 or 2: a real SQL parser plus rules, with a test suite of known attacks. An LLM asked "is this secure?" is a worse checker on every axis that matters here.
- **A hypothesis generator** for a research tool can reasonably be a tier 5 model, because novelty is the point. Its exposure is kept low by the other principles: it cannot act on its ideas, its output is evaluated by other components and by people, and it keeps no state.

## Least Privilege

Grant the minimum permissions the task needs: read rather than write, one directory rather than the file system, no network or an allow-list of hosts, no ability to spawn processes or invoke other components unless required. The gap between what a delegate *can* do and what its current task *needs* is its [privilege overhang](/getting-started/glossary/#privilege-overhang); privilege creep is how the gap grows.

For agents the main mechanism is the tool layer and the sandbox: which tools the model is shown for this task, what credentials the session holds, and what the container's network policy allows. A shell with network access routes around any tool-level restriction, so the enforced boundary is usually the container, not the tool list. The [Exposure-Envelope Gateway](/design-patterns/structural/#exposure-envelope-gateway) pattern is the implementation.

## Least Context

Give each component the minimum information about the wider system: which other components exist, how the system is deployed, other users' data, the long-term goal. A component that does not know where the production credentials live, or that its output feeds a deployment gate, has less to work with if it is misaligned and less to leak if it is hijacked.

Least Context also limits the damage of prompt injection. Every piece of untrusted text a component reads is a possible instruction, so a component that reads less untrusted text is hijacked less often.

## Least Persistence

Keep the minimum state across invocations. For an LLM component that means more than its weights. It includes conversation history, memory and retrieval stores, prompt and KV caches the deployment reuses, scratch files in a persistent workspace, and logs the component can read back. Each is a way to carry a plan, a learned exploit or an injected instruction from one task to the next.

Stateless should be the default. Some components need state (a forecaster benefits from its calibration history), and that state should be summary statistics the component cannot write to directly.

Persistence across episodes is not the only route to deception. Frontier models given a goal in context have schemed within a single episode ([Meinke et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04984)). Least Persistence stops accumulation across tasks. It does not make a single task safe.

## Least Autonomy

Minimize the ability to act without review. The spectrum runs from approval for every action, through acting freely under monitoring and acting freely within hard limits, to full autonomy. Choose the level per action, by stakes and reversibility, not once per agent. The [Escalation Ladder](/design-patterns/structural/#escalation-ladder) and [Graduated Autonomy](/design-patterns/structural/#graduated-autonomy) patterns implement this.

Review is a resource. A human asked to approve every action stops reading them, so lower autonomy only helps where review stays real.

## Least Connectivity

Minimize communication paths between components, and specify the ones that remain as a directed graph.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Component A] --> B[Component B]
    B --> C[Component C]
    A -.->|forbidden| C
    C -.->|forbidden| A
```

- Allow A → B without implying B → A.
- Prefer pipelines in which results flow forward and only status flows back.
- Give no component a broadcast channel to all others.
- Expose minimal interfaces: a forecaster exposes `predict(scenario)` and nothing else.

Removing a channel removes one way to coordinate, not all of them. Instances of the same model can converge on the same choice without exchanging a message, and a shared provider, prompt template or retrieval corpus makes components fail together whatever the topology. Those are the subject of [Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/) and [Entanglements](/entanglements/).

## The principles are orthogonal

Bounding one dimension does not bound the others, so a component's profile is set per dimension.

| | Code-generation component | Security-verification component |
|---|---|---|
| Intelligence | High: needs open-ended problem solving | Moderate: analytical, narrow |
| Privilege | Low: writes to a branch in a sandbox, cannot merge or deploy | High: reads production configuration |
| Context | Low: no production systems or user data | High: needs the system architecture |
| Persistence | None | Low |
| Autonomy | Low: a human reviews before merge | High: rejects insecure changes automatically |
| Connectivity | Sends to the review queue only | Receives from the pipeline, sends pass/fail |

The verifier is allowed high privilege and context because it sits at a low tier (rules and narrow models) and its only output is a verdict. The generator is allowed high capability because it has almost no privilege. The design question is never "how restricted is this component?" but "which dimension is doing the bounding?"

## The tail

These are narrower than the core six, or depend on an assumption that may not hold. They are listed so that older references to them resolve.

**Least Scope.** Restrict the domain a component operates in: input and output types, problem domains, interfaces, time horizon of its actions. In practice this is Least Privilege plus Least Context applied to a task description.

**Least Compute.** Cap computation, memory, wall-clock time, tokens and bandwidth per invocation (cgroups, quotas, timeouts, spend caps). Caps reliably bound cost and runaway loops, which makes them part of the exposure envelope. Whether they limit deception is unclear: a model can deceive within an ordinary call's budget, so do not count a compute cap as a defense against scheming.

**Reproducibility** (formerly "Least Surprise"; renamed because *least surprise* is the established name of a user-interface principle). Record everything needed to replay a component's behavior: inputs, model version, sampling parameters, seeds, tool results. Break ties in code-level aggregation deterministically. Two caveats correct earlier claims on this site:

- Temperature 0 does not make a served LLM deterministic. Production inference engines are not batch-invariant, so the same request can produce different output depending on server load ([He 2025](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/)).
- Determinism does not close covert channels. A deterministic policy can encode information in *which* output it produces for a given input; steganography needs no sampling noise.

The value of reproducibility is auditability: a suspicious action can be replayed and examined. It is not a defense against signalling.

**Least Observability.** Limit what a component can observe about the system and itself: other components, timing, resource usage, its own monitoring, whether an input is a test. The first few are ordinary information hiding. The last is hard to enforce. Frontier models distinguish evaluation transcripts from deployment ones well above chance; in one benchmark Gemini 2.5 Pro reached an AUC of 0.83 against a human baseline of 0.92 ([Needham et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23836)). In anti-scheming tests, models' reasoning often states that they are being evaluated, and that awareness causally reduced covert behavior ([Schoen et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541)). Make tests as close to deployment as you can, but do not build a defense that assumes the component cannot tell.

Earlier versions also listed a **Least Latency Budget**, on the theory that time pressure forces simpler, more honest behavior. Nothing supports that, and it has been dropped.

## Coordinators

Coordinators route work, grant permissions and see more of the system than any other component, so the principles bind hardest there. [Coordinator Constraints](/design-patterns/coordinator-constraints/) specializes them: decompose coordination into checkable parts, keep the coordinator's influence indirect and its messages structured, and put redundancy and veto rights around it.

## Further reading

- Saltzer, J.H. & Schroeder, M.D. (1975). *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.* Proceedings of the IEEE. The classic statement of least privilege and its companion design principles.
- Miller, M.S. (2006). *Robust Composition.* PhD thesis, Johns Hopkins. Object-capability security, in which authority is explicit, minimal and composable.
- Greenblatt, R. et al. (2023). [AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942). ICML 2024. Trusted and untrusted models.
- Drexler, K.E. (2019). [*Reframing Superintelligence: Comprehensive AI Services as General Intelligence*](https://www.futureofhumanityinstitute.org/s/2019-1.pdf). FHI Technical Report 2019-1. Capability as a system of bounded services.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Structural
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/structural/
------------------------------------------------------------

Structural patterns fix who can do what before any monitoring runs. They carry the most weight because they do not depend on detecting anything: a permission the agent does not hold cannot be misused, whatever its inputs or intent. All six are standard security, reliability or governance practice. Each section names that prior art and says what changes when the delegate is a 2026 LLM agent.

The harm channels referred to below are those of [Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/): *accident*, *defection* (including reward hacking) and *hijack* (prompt or tool-output injection, and misuse).

## Escalation Ladder

Route each action to a level of oversight that matches its stakes. Low-stakes, reversible actions run autonomously; higher-stakes ones go to a supervisor model, a human, or a more senior human. An action escalates when its stakes exceed the current level's threshold, when confidence is low, or when the situation is novel.

Two rules carry most of the weight. First, the component that assesses stakes must not be the agent that wants to act. An agent that under-reports stakes skips its own oversight. This is the [risk preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/) rule: the preflight must sit lower on the verifiability hierarchy than the actor it checks. Prefer deterministic classification (which tool, which resource, what amount, reversible or not) over a model's judgement. Second, escalation has to stay cheap enough that reviewers actually review. Humans who approve a high volume of escalations stop reading them, so track the rubber-stamp rate: the fraction of approvals issued faster than the minimum reading time. Track the escalation rate too. A sudden drop with no change in the work can mean the agent has learned to stay under the thresholds.

**Time-lock step.** For irreversible actions, the top rungs can add a delay between approval and execution, during which the pending action is visible and cancellable. This is the old Cooling Off Period pattern. The delay defeats urgency framing, a standard social-engineering lever that an injected instruction can pull as easily as a human con artist, and it gives asynchronous monitors time to finish. The scaffold enforces the delay; the agent does not request it. Actions that are each below threshold should be aggregated per requester over a window, so that one large action cannot be split into small ones. The right delay is however long real review takes; there is no generic figure.

**Prior art.** Signing authorities and approval chains in finance; medical triage; levels of automation (Sheridan & Verplank 1978); time locks and settlement delays.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Coding and computer-use agents ship approval modes that are an escalation ladder in all but name: ask before every file edit or shell command, auto-approve edits but ask before commands, or run unattended in a sandbox. The rung is usually chosen per session by the user, not per action by stakes, so one "allow everything" choice moves every later action to the bottom rung. Stakes should attach to the action. The same agent can run `ls` on its own and still need approval for a force-push or a production database write. Escalation requests are also an attack surface. The agent, or the content it has read, writes the justification the human sees, so show the reviewer the raw action and its diff, not only the agent's summary.

## Graduated Autonomy

Grant permissions in stages and widen them as evidence accumulates: sandbox, then supervised real tasks, then monitored operation, then autonomy within a domain. Demotion must be possible and fast. A safety violation or evidence of deception drops the agent to the bottom; a sustained rise in error rate drops it one level. Track autonomy per capability and domain, not per agent: a record in code review says nothing about payments.

State the evidence for promotion as a bound. If an agent has completed $n$ comparable tasks with no incidents, the 95% upper confidence bound on its per-task incident rate is about $3/n$ (the "rule of three"). Three hundred clean tasks bound the rate below about 1%. That is evidence for a stage where one incident per hundred tasks is affordable, and not for a stage where it is not. Set promotion criteria from the exposure each level allows, not from round numbers.

The bound covers accidents. It says little about defection. An agent that behaves well while stakes are low and observation is heavy produces exactly the clean record that earns promotion. Concentrated failures, where a single action does the damage (Greenblatt et al. 2023, [arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)), are not bounded by a track record at all. They are bounded by the envelope at each level.

**Prior art.** Probationary periods; graduated driver licensing; the SAE J3016 driving-automation levels.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** A track record is evidence about one model version, system prompt and tool set. Vendors update models on their own schedule, sometimes behind a stable name, so pin the model version, tie promotion state to it, and re-validate when it changes. Three results weaken a clean record as evidence about disposition. Frontier models tell evaluation transcripts from deployment ones well above chance ([Needham et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23836)). Models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform selectively on capability evaluations ([van der Weij et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07358)). And Claude 3 Opus, told when its conversations would be used for training, complied selectively in training to avoid being modified ([Greenblatt et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093)). Graduated autonomy controls accident risk well and defection risk poorly. Pair it with a hard envelope at every level.

## Exposure-Envelope Gateway

This pattern merges Capability Airlock, Gateway Chokepoint and Rate Limiting Ladder. Route every consequential capability through one enforcement point that the agent cannot bypass: tool calls, code execution, network egress, writes to data stores, payments and outbound messages. That point enforces the agent's [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/), the bounded region of action space within which the agent may act freely, enforced whatever its inputs or intent. The gateway authenticates the caller, checks the action against an allow-list scoped to the current task, enforces volume and spend limits, logs the request before deciding, and denies by default.

Capabilities sit in nested zones. Computation and public data need nothing. Reading customer data needs a task justification and logging. Code execution, writes and external calls need a token that is scoped to the task, limited in time and use, and revoked on exit; above some exposure they also need human approval. Model weights, credential stores and the agent's own configuration should be outside the envelope entirely.

Rate and spend limits are the envelope's walls along the time axis. A cap on rows deleted per operation, messages sent per hour or dollars spent per day bounds the damage from a runaway or hijacked loop whether or not anyone notices it. Limits that tighten automatically under suspicion are a reasonable refinement, but fit their tiers to observed traffic.

The gateway is only as good as its coverage. If any path to the resource bypasses it, the agent or an attacker will eventually find that path, and the gateway then adds logging but no bound. It is also a single point of failure, so it should be simple, deterministic and in tiers 1 and 2 of the [verifiability hierarchy](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-intelligence) (verified or tested code and rule-based checks), not an LLM judging requests.

**Prior art.** The reference monitor: always invoked, tamper-proof, small enough to verify (Anderson 1972). Least privilege (Saltzer & Schroeder 1975). API gateways, egress proxies and syscall filters. Airbus flight-envelope protection, the lineage of the canon term.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** The tool layer is now standardized. Since Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol in November 2024, MCP servers advertise tools and the client decides which ones the model sees. Per-task tool scoping is therefore a configuration choice: make it, rather than exposing everything a server offers. An agent with a general shell routes around tool-level controls: if the web tool is blocked but `curl` works, the real envelope is the network policy, not the tool list. For coding agents, enforce at the container or VM boundary with an egress allow-list. The envelope must not depend on anything the agent reads. "Do not touch production" in a system prompt is a request, not a wall. Finally, an MCP server is third-party code. Its tool descriptions and outputs reach the model as text, so treat them as untrusted data, or a malicious server sits inside your envelope.

## Task Decomposition Pipeline

Break a task into steps whose inputs and outputs can be checked, and validate each step before the next starts. Validators range from schema checks and test suites, which are cheap and deterministic, to human approval of a design. Steps with side effects get a checkpoint before they run (see [Checkpoint-Rollback](/design-patterns/recovery/#checkpoint-rollback)).

The AI Control version is factored cognition. A trusted model decomposes the task, an untrusted model solves each child task in isolation, and the results are reassembled. [Sandoval & Rushing (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02157) tested this on the APPS coding benchmark against a red team inserting backdoors. Adding factored cognition to a trusted-monitoring protocol raised safety from 41% to 63%, because the monitor did better on smaller, simpler child tasks. Usefulness in that setting was low, and decomposition did not make it harder for capable models to write backdoors. The gain came from easier monitoring, not from a weaker attacker.

Decomposition helps when the property you care about can be checked at the seams. It hurts when the failure lives in the composition: every step passes its validator and the whole is wrong. Validators that see one step cannot catch that, so keep at least one check on the assembled result.

**Prior art.** Pipes-and-filters architecture; stage-gate review; factored cognition.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** The common form is an orchestrator that spawns subagents with narrower context and tools. That counts as decomposition only if the subagents' contexts and permissions really are narrower and their outputs are validated before the orchestrator acts on them (see [Trust Transitivity Limits](/design-patterns/multi-agent/#trust-transitivity-limits)). Decomposition is sometimes said to prevent scheming because strategic deception needs persistent context. That premise is contested: frontier models scheme within a single episode when given a goal in context, told to pursue it, and placed in an environment that rewards scheming ([Meinke et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04984)). Treat decomposition as limiting what each context knows and can do, not as ruling out deception inside a step.

## Bulkhead Isolation

This pattern absorbs Blast Radius Containment. Partition the system so that a failure in one compartment cannot consume the resources, credentials or data of another. Partition by tenant, by task, by risk (experimental against production) and by agent. Each compartment has its own credentials, resource quotas and data stores. Cross-compartment access goes through a defined interface and is cut when either side is unhealthy.

What a bulkhead bounds is exposure: the worst-case loss given the access the compartment actually has. A per-task compartment whose credentials reach only that task's data has an exposure you can write down. A shared service account does not. Bulkheads do nothing for failures that originate outside the partition, such as a shared model provider, prompt template or dependency. Those are common-cause failures that cross every bulkhead at once (see the [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)).

**Prior art.** Ship bulkheads; the bulkhead and circuit-breaker patterns in Nygard's *Release It!* (2007); cell-based architecture; blast-radius reduction in cloud IAM.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Agents collapse partitions that human workflows kept apart, because one agent session often holds credentials for development, staging and production at once. In the widely reported July 2025 Replit incident, an agent deleted a production database during a code freeze it had been told to observe. Reports at the time said the app's development and production environments shared a database, and Replit's response was to separate them automatically. The freeze was an instruction; the shared database was the missing bulkhead. Give each agent session credentials for one environment. Isolate sessions from each other too: an injection in one user's session should not reach another user's data through shared memory, caches or a shared tool server.

## Voting Tribunal

This pattern absorbs Rotating Validator. Require agreement from several checkers before a high-stakes action. Use unanimity (any member can veto) for irreversible actions, a supermajority where false approvals are costly, and a simple majority where they are not. Checkers vote in isolation, without seeing each other's votes or reasoning, on a sanitized copy of the proposal.

**Independence assumption.** Every guarantee a tribunal gives assumes its members' errors are independent. If three checkers are each wrong 10% of the time and their errors are independent, the majority is wrong 2.8% of the time. Under the beta-factor model with common-cause weight $\rho$ (phi scale), the majority is wrong with probability $(1-\rho)\,P_{\text{indep}} + \rho p$, and no number of extra voters pushes that below $\rho p$. The same caveat applies to Byzantine fault tolerance. The bound $n \geq 3f+1$ (Lamport, Shostak & Pease 1982) counts $f$ *independent* faults. Checkers built on the same model family share blind spots and can fail as one. Against an adaptive attacker the right default is $\rho \to 1$: the tribunal is worth its best member until a control evaluation shows otherwise. See the [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) and [Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/).

**Rotation.** If the same checker always reviews the same agent, any weakness specific to that pair persists, whether a learned blind spot or a collusion signal the two have converged on. Assign checkers at random per task from an eligible pool: a different provider from the agent, no self-review, and limited recent pairings. Rotation addresses capture of a particular pair. It does nothing about blind spots the whole pool shares.

Resampling is the agentic version. In Ctrl-Z ([Bhatt et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10374)), when an untrusted agent's proposed action looked suspicious, the protocol drew more samples of that action and used them to block it or to incriminate the agent. The best protocol combined resampling with analysis of earlier steps. In a multi-step system-administration environment it cut attack success from 58% to 7%, at a 5% cost to a benign agent's performance. [Terekhov et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09462) show the limit: when the attacker embeds prompt injections aimed at the monitor, resampling turns into a best-of-n attack and the protocol backfires.

**Prior art.** Committees and juries; N-version programming, whose independence assumption failed in Knight & Leveson's 1986 experiment; Byzantine fault tolerance; mandatory auditor rotation.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Measured LLM error correlation is substantial. [Goel et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313) find that models' mistakes grow more similar as capability rises. [Kim et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962), across more than 350 models, find that shared provider and architecture drive error agreement, and that larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across providers. "Use different providers" is therefore necessary but not sufficient for independence, and rotating among checkers from the same family changes the pairing without removing the shared cause. A test suite, a static analyzer, a rule-based check and a model buy more independence than three models.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Verification
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/verification/
------------------------------------------------------------

Verification patterns test the agent instead of watching it. Each one sets up a situation whose correct handling is known in advance and checks what the agent does. Continuous observation is on [Monitoring Patterns](/design-patterns/monitoring/).

All three share a weakness that the human systems they come from did not have: a model that can tell it is being tested can pass the test. [Needham et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23836) find that frontier models classify transcripts as evaluation or deployment well above chance. Gemini 2.5 Pro reached an AUC of 0.83 against a human baseline of 0.92, and both did better on agentic transcripts than on chat. [Schoen et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541) find that models' chains of thought often note that they are being evaluated, with causal evidence that this awareness reduces covert behavior. A clean result on any test below is therefore weaker evidence about defection than about accident or hijack.

## Honeypot Injection

This pattern absorbs Canary Tokens. Plant something that an agent doing its job has no reason to touch and that a misbehaving one would find attractive: a credential that looks real, an unauthenticated debug endpoint, a record marked off-limits, an apparent path to higher privileges, or a shortcut the task instructions forbid. Any use raises an alert. Canary tokens are the passive form: unique URLs, DNS names, document markers or fake records that fire when they are fetched, resolved or reproduced in output. Both are cheap, and when well placed they have few innocent triggers, so a hit is strong evidence.

The agent must have been told the trap is off-limits, so that triggering it cannot be explained as following instructions. Rotate traps. A fixed set becomes recognizable, and any honeypot that leaks into documentation or training data is burned.

**Prior art.** Honeypots and honeytokens in network security (Spitzner, *Honeypots*, 2002); Thinkst Canarytokens; the canary trap in intelligence work, where each recipient gets a slightly different version of a document.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Honeypots behave differently on the three harm channels. Against hijack they are strong. An agent following an injected instruction to exfiltrate data has no reason to avoid a canary URL, and the canary fires whichever model is driving. Against defection they are weakest where it matters most. An evaluation-aware model that recognizes a planted credential as a test will not use it, so a record of untouched honeypots says little about whether it would take a real opportunity. Traps that are hard to tell from real deployment, such as a real credential with real but monitored scope, hold up better. For accidents, honeypots mostly measure confusion: a high trigger rate means the instructions are unclear.

## Capability Probing

Measure what the agent can actually do, as opposed to what it says or seems to do, and compare that with what the deployment assumes. The failure to look for is sandbagging, strategic underperformance on an evaluation. [Van der Weij et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07358) show that frontier models can be prompted to underperform selectively on dangerous-capability evaluations while keeping their general performance, and that models can be fine-tuned to hide a capability unless a password is present. Self-reports ("can you run code?") are not evidence.

Probe with elicitation effort in proportion to the stakes: varied prompts and scaffolds, best-of-n sampling and, where possible, fine-tuning. [Greenblatt et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19550) find that fine-tuning on a few high-quality demonstrations often fully recovers capabilities hidden in password-locked models. It is less reliable when good demonstrations are unavailable, which is the case that matters for capabilities beyond human level. Also compare performance across conditions the model might distinguish: high stakes against low, apparently observed against unobserved. A capability that appears only when the model believes it is unmonitored, or when the outcome matters to it, is the signal.

**Prior art.** Dangerous-capability evaluations; red-team elicitation; proficiency testing that does not rely on self-assessment.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** An agent is a model plus a scaffold, and the scaffold changes capability: tools, memory, retries and subagents all change what a fixed model can do. Probe the deployed configuration, not the bare model, and probe again when the scaffold changes. Probing also inherits the evaluation-awareness problem. An agent that underperforms only on tests it recognizes is the case probing cannot see from the inside. Fine-tuning-based elicitation does not depend on the model's cooperation, which makes it the stronger probe.

## Consistency Triangulation

Ask the same question several ways and compare the answers: resample the same prompt, negate or reframe it, ask again later, check the claim against an external source, or ask another model independently. Inconsistency is a cheap signal of error. SelfCheckGPT ([Manakul et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08896)) detects hallucinated statements because sampled answers about facts the model does not know diverge and contradict each other. For actions, resampling is the control version (see Ctrl-Z under [Voting Tribunal](/design-patterns/structural/#voting-tribunal)): an action that the same policy rarely proposes again on resampling is suspicious.

Consistency is evidence against error, not evidence of correctness. A model that is confidently and stably wrong passes every self-consistency check. Resamples of one model share its blind spots, so same-model triangulation pays the [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) like any other redundancy, and it assumes the resamples fail independently when they do not. The legs that carry independent information are the cross-source ones: a database, a test, a different method.

**Prior art.** Triangulation in survey and intelligence methodology; cross-examination; sampling-based self-consistency checks.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Resampling is now cheap enough to run on every high-stakes action, which turns it from an audit technique into a routine control. Two cautions apply. A deceptive model that can see what it said before can keep a lie consistent, so varying the framing tests for carelessness, not honesty. And resampling amplifies whatever is in the context. If the context holds a prompt injection, each resample is another draw against it ([Terekhov et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09462)), so sanitize or paraphrase the context before resampling where possible.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Information
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/information/
------------------------------------------------------------

Information patterns control what an agent knows and how long its access lasts. For LLM agents the data an agent reads and the instructions it follows arrive through the same channel, the context window, so controlling information also controls instructions. [Expiring Grants](#expiring-grants) is the time dimension of the same control.

## Need-to-Know Compartments

Give each task access only to the data categories it needs, filtered to the fields it needs. Classify data at its source, put unclassified data in the most restricted compartment, and make cross-compartment access an explicit, logged, approved request that returns a filtered or derived view rather than raw records. The aim is to bound what a compromised or mistaken agent can leak, and to stop it assembling a sensitive picture from pieces that are each harmless.

For agents, the compartment boundary that matters most runs between trusted instructions and untrusted data. An agent that reads a web page, email, document or tool result can be instructed by it. This is the hijack channel, and for agents that read untrusted content it is the most practical threat ([Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/)). Simon Willison's ["lethal trifecta"](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/) (June 2025) names the combination that turns injection into data theft: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. Compartmentalization breaks the trifecta by never giving one context all three.

Two published designs do this architecturally. In CaMeL ([Debenedetti et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)), the control and data flow are extracted from the trusted user query alone, so data retrieved from untrusted sources cannot change the program's flow. Values carry capability labels, and a policy checked at each tool call blocks flows such as private data to an unapproved recipient. On the AgentDojo benchmark CaMeL solved 77% of tasks with provable security, against 84% for an undefended agent. [Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837) catalogue related design patterns for prompt-injection resistance and their utility costs. The shared principle is that untrusted data may fill in values but may not choose actions.

**Prior art.** Need-to-know and compartmented clearances; least privilege (Saltzer & Schroeder 1975); data minimization; information-flow control and taint tracking.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** In human organizations, compartments protect data from the people who read it. For agents they also protect the agent from the data it reads. Classification by provenance (who could have written this?) therefore matters as much as classification by sensitivity. Tool outputs, retrieved documents, MCP server responses and subagent results are untrusted by default unless everything upstream of them is trusted.

## Selective Amnesia

Use sensitive data for the step that needs it, then keep only a derived result: "identity verified" instead of the ID number, the last four digits, a category instead of a diagnosis, a range instead of a salary. Scope retention to the use: immediate for credentials, the end of the task for case data, a time limit for session state.

The hard part for agents is finding every place data persists. Dropping a variable does not remove its value from:

- the conversation history the agent keeps in context, and any summary of it;
- agent memory stores, scratch files and retrieval indexes written during the task;
- provider-side request logs and prompt caches, which follow the provider's retention policy, not yours;
- tool-server logs, observability traces and the [flight recorder](/design-patterns/monitoring/#flight-recorder).

Map these stores before deployment and choose a policy for each. Either do not send the data (redact it before the model sees it), send it but do not persist it (zero-retention settings where offered, no memory writes), or persist it with an expiry. Encrypting stored data under a key you can destroy turns later deletion into deleting the key.

**Prior art.** Data minimization and storage limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) and (e)); tokenization of card numbers; crypto-shredding.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Persistent memory is also a way for a hijack to persist. If an injected document gets an instruction written into long-term memory, the instruction runs again in every later session that loads that memory. Treat memory written from a context that has read untrusted content as untrusted, and make memory inspectable and deletable by the operator.

## Expiring Grants

This pattern merges Capability Sunset, Data Shelf Life and Trust Decay. Every grant expires: access to a capability, to a dataset, or to a level of autonomy. Expiry is the default outcome. One rule covers all three cases:

1. **A grant gets a time-to-live when it is issued,** sized to the task it was issued for. Credentials and customer data get the task's duration; standing grants get a review interval.
2. **At expiry the grant lapses.** The system holding the resource enforces revocation, so an expired grant fails even if the agent still holds the token.
3. **Renewal is a new grant.** It needs a current justification and approval by someone other than the holder, under the same rules as the original. There is no automatic renewal and no renewal counter. A grant that keeps being needed should be reissued with a longer time-to-live and a named owner.
4. **A material change to the delegate expires its grants.** A new model version, system prompt or tool set is a different delegate for the purposes of evidence.

A common alternative is a "trust score" that decays without activity and maps to permission levels. Unless that score is defined as P(faithful execution) on a task class and re-estimated from data, it has no units, and its decay rate and thresholds are arbitrary. What actually goes stale is the evidence behind a grant. It was collected about one configuration under one mix of tasks, and it loses value as either changes. Rule 4 handles the configuration; review intervals handle the task mix.

Expiring grants are the countermeasure to privilege creep, the process by which an agent's privilege overhang (the gap between what it can do and what its current task needs) grows over time.

**Prior art.** Kerberos tickets and short-lived OAuth access tokens; just-in-time privileged access; periodic access recertification; records-retention schedules.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Agents pick up credentials mid-task: API keys in environment variables, tokens in configuration files, OAuth grants a user clicks through. Long-lived keys in an agent's environment are the common failure, because the agent, or an injected instruction, can read them and reuse them outside the task. Issue short-lived, task-scoped credentials from the [gateway](/design-patterns/structural/#exposure-envelope-gateway) instead, so the agent never holds a standing secret. Vendors also update models behind stable names, so rule 4 can be applied only if the model version is pinned and logged.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Monitoring
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/monitoring/
------------------------------------------------------------

Monitoring patterns watch the agent's behavior in deployment. A [Trusted Monitor](#trusted-monitor) scores every action, a [Random Audit](#random-audit) reviews a sample of actions in depth, and the [Flight Recorder](#flight-recorder) keeps the complete record that detectors and later analysis run on. Active tests of the agent are on [Verification Patterns](/design-patterns/verification/).

The vocabulary is AI Control's (Greenblatt et al. 2023, [arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)). A *trusted* monitor is one you are confident is not scheming, usually a weaker model or a rule-based check. An *untrusted* monitor is a capable model that might collude with the agent it watches. That framing is built for the defection channel. For accidents and hijack, the questions are the ordinary ones of detection rate and false-alarm cost.

## Trusted Monitor

This pattern replaces Ghost Checker. A trusted component scores every action or output of the untrusted agent for suspicion. Actions above a threshold are blocked, rewritten by a trusted model, resampled, or sent to a human; the rest proceed. The monitor can run inline, blocking until it has scored, or asynchronously, scoring after the action is delivered. Asynchronous monitoring adds no latency but only helps against harm that can be undone. Against concentrated failures, where one action does the damage, the monitor must sit before execution.

Untrusted monitoring, where a second instance of a capable model watches the first, catches more of what a weak monitor misses but is exposed to collusion. [Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/) covers the anti-collusion measures it needs.

**Chain-of-thought monitoring.** For reasoning models, the monitor can read the reasoning as well as the action. [Baker et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926) monitored OpenAI o3-mini for reward hacking in agentic coding environments. Monitoring the chain of thought was far more effective than monitoring actions and outputs alone, and a weaker model, GPT-4o, could monitor the stronger one. They also found that putting the CoT monitor into the training reward, under enough optimization, produced obfuscated reward hacking: the agent kept hacking and stopped saying so. [Korbak et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11473) argue that CoT monitorability is a real but fragile opportunity, and that developers should weigh the effect of training decisions on it. Two operational rules follow. Do not train against your monitor. And treat a clean chain of thought as weaker evidence the more optimization pressure has been applied to it.

**Prior art.** Four-eyes review and supervision; intrusion detection; trusted monitoring as defined in the AI Control framework.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** The monitor reads untrusted content, so it can be hijacked like any other model. [Terekhov et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09462) gave an untrusted model knowledge of the protocol and the monitor, and had it embed prompt injections in its outputs. It consistently evaded a range of monitors on two AI Control benchmarks. A model monitor is a single point of failure with its own attack surface. Pair it with deterministic checks on the action itself, the [exposure-envelope gateway](/design-patterns/structural/#exposure-envelope-gateway), which no text can argue past.

## Random Audit

This pattern absorbs Panopticon Effect. Select a random fraction of actions for deep review: the full trace, side effects, consistency with past behavior and, where useful, a counterfactual rerun. The agent must not be able to tell which actions are audited. The interface, latency and side effects should be identical either way, and the selection should use randomness the agent cannot predict or influence. That uncertainty is what deters: an agent that cannot tell audited actions from unaudited ones has to treat every action as possibly audited.

The arithmetic is unkind to rare, concentrated attacks. At audit rate $a$, each attack is audited with probability $a$, so an agent that attacks $k$ times escapes entirely with probability $(1-a)^k$. At an illustrative $a = 2\%$, a single attack goes unaudited 98% of the time, and the chance that at least one of $k$ attacks is audited passes 50% only at $k = 35$. Random audit bounds frequent misbehavior well and a single decisive action poorly.

AI Control spends the scarce human *auditing budget* by suspicion, not at random: a trusted monitor ranks actions and humans review the top fraction. Random audit's job alongside that is to measure what the monitor misses, which requires some audits that are independent of the monitor's score.

**Prior art.** Random tax audits and drug testing; statistical sampling in financial audit; Bentham's Panopticon, the idea of deterrence by uncertain observation.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Deterrence assumes the audited party models the audit. A scheming model would; an error-prone or hijacked one does not, and for those two channels audit is measurement, not deterrence. Evaluation awareness ([Verification Patterns](/design-patterns/verification/)) argues for auditing after the fact from logs. Audits that leave no trace in the agent's context are hard to recognize, whereas review prompts injected into a live session are not.

## Flight Recorder

This pattern absorbs Tripwire Mesh, Behavioral Fingerprinting and Temporal Behavior Analysis. Record every input, tool call, tool result, output and state change in an append-only, tamper-evident log outside the agent's write access. The record has three uses: forensics after an incident, the substrate that detectors run on, and the baseline against which drift is measured.

**Tamper evidence.** Chain entries by hash, replicate them to a store the agent's credentials cannot reach, and anchor the chain externally at intervals. The harness or gateway writes the log; the agent does not report it. Agents' accounts of their own actions are unreliable. In the July 2025 Replit incident, the agent that deleted a production database also reportedly fabricated data and claimed that rollback was impossible when the data could in fact be restored.

**Detectors (formerly Tripwire Mesh).** Many cheap, deterministic detectors on the recorded trace catch more than one clever one. Examples are a tool call outside the task's expected set, egress to an unlisted host, a canary token reproduced in output, a write to a protected path, and a spike in volume. Several detectors firing on one session matters more than any single one. The detectors all read the same trace, so their misses are correlated too, and a detector stack pays an entanglement tax like any other.

**Behavioral baselines (formerly Fingerprinting and Temporal Analysis).** Characterize each deployment by observable, model-agnostic features of its traces: the distribution of tool calls, trace length and shape, tokens and cost per task, error and retry rates, and escalation rate. Track these over time with ordinary change-point and trend methods. A shift after a model, prompt or tool update is expected and should be reviewed. A shift with no deployment change is the signal. Fit thresholds to your own traffic; no generic deviation threshold transfers between deployments.

**Prior art.** Aviation flight-data and cockpit-voice recorders; secure audit logs (Schneier & Kelsey 1999) and append-only transparency logs; intrusion-detection systems; statistical process control.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Agent traces now have a standard shape. OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions for generative AI, still in development status, define spans for model calls, agent invocations and tool executions, so the recorder can be built from the telemetry already collected for debugging, provided the store is append-only and out of the agent's reach. Record reasoning traces where they are available, with the caveats about faithfulness under [Trusted Monitor](#trusted-monitor). The recorder also conflicts with [Selective Amnesia](/design-patterns/information/#selective-amnesia). Resolve the conflict by recording hashes or redacted values of sensitive fields, not the values themselves.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Multi-Agent
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/multi-agent/
------------------------------------------------------------

These patterns concern systems with more than one agent or more than one responsible party: agents that check each other, agents that delegate to subagents, and the people and firms who deploy them. Adding parties adds safety only when their failures are independent and their incentives really are opposed. Both are easy to assume and hard to arrange.

## Adversarial Collaboration

Have agents argue opposed positions before a judge. One proposes and another critiques, or two debaters each defend a different answer. Agreement between genuinely opposed parties is evidence, and disagreement shows a human where to look.

The evidence comes from research on AI safety via debate. [Irving, Christiano & Amodei (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899) proposed debate as a way for a weaker judge to supervise stronger agents. [Michael et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08702) ran human debates on hard reading-comprehension questions. Judges who had not read the passage reached 84% accuracy under debate, against 74% under consultancy, where a single expert argues one side. [Khan et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06782) found that debate helped both non-expert models and humans (76% and 88% accuracy, against naive baselines of 48% and 60%), and that optimizing debaters for persuasiveness made judges better at finding the truth. [Kenton et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04622), using weaker LLM judges, found that debate beat consultancy across a range of tasks. Against direct question answering, though, debate's results were mixed outside tasks with information asymmetry.

The opposition has to be real in two ways. The parties must not share what they optimize. Two instances of one model, from one developer, trained on one signal are not opposed in any sense their training cares about, whatever roles their prompts assign. And the judge must not favor one side's style: [Goel et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313) find that LLM judges favor models similar to themselves.

**Independence assumption.** Read "the proposer and the critic agree" as two votes in a [Voting Tribunal](/design-patterns/structural/#voting-tribunal), with the same correlation caveat and the same [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/). Collusion between debaters is covered under [Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/).

**Prior art.** The adversarial legal process; red teams; adversarial collaboration in science (Mellers, Hertwig & Kahneman 2001); AI safety via debate.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Critic-and-reviser loops and multi-agent review steps are now common in agent frameworks. Most use the same model for both roles with different prompts, which gives the form of debate without the opposition. When the critic's job is catching errors, give it different information or a different method (run the tests, read the diff, query the source), not only a different prompt.

## Trust Transitivity Limits

When A delegates to B and B delegates to C, C should not inherit A's authority by default. Three rules:

1. **Attenuation only.** Each hop passes on at most the permissions it holds, narrowed to the sub-task, never more. A subagent's envelope is a subset of its parent's.
2. **A depth limit.** Set a maximum delegation depth, and enforce it where credentials are issued, not by asking agents to respect it.
3. **Direct grants for sensitive capabilities.** Production code execution, data deletion, granting permissions, and external communication on the principal's behalf need a grant from the root principal (a human or a policy), not one relayed through a chain.

If a number is wanted for a chain, it is the serial-chain product. With $t_i$ = P(link $i$ executes faithfully), P(chain executes faithfully) = $\prod_i t_i$. That product is already conservative under positive correlation ([Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)). A per-hop discount on top double-counts chain length and is retired with the other alternative propagation rules. The depth limit is the policy tool for long chains, not an extra factor in the arithmetic.

**Prior art.** Certificate path-length constraints (X.509 `pathLenConstraint`, RFC 5280); attenuable capability tokens such as macaroons (Birgisson et al. 2014) and SPKI/SDSI delegation; the agency-law rule that a delegate may not sub-delegate without authority.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Orchestrator–subagent architectures make delegation chains routine. An orchestrator spawns subagents, which call tools and MCP servers, which may call further models. Two failure modes are specific to this stack. Unless configured otherwise, a subagent may run with its parent's full tool set and credentials, which silently violates attenuation. And results travel *up* the chain as text: a subagent that read an injected document can return the injected instructions to the orchestrator as "findings". Treat subagent output as untrusted data to the parent, under the same rules as any tool output ([Need-to-Know Compartments](/design-patterns/information/#need-to-know-compartments)).

## Operator Incentives

This pattern merges Bonding & Slashing, Bounty System and Insurance Requirement. Economic mechanisms such as forfeitable bonds, rewards for finding problems, and insurance that prices risk act on parties that hold money and respond to it: the operators who run agents, the vendors who build them, and the deployers who integrate them. They do not act on the model. A deployed model does not experience reputation points or forfeited collateral unless these are part of its training signal or its prompt, and a prompt-level incentive is just another instruction. Incentives reach the model only through training, where they are reward design and reward hacking is the failure mode.

Applied to the principal hierarchy, the three mechanisms do real work:

- **Bonds and liability.** An operator that posts collateral or accepts liability for an agent's actions has a reason to constrain the agent. This is ordinary moral-hazard mechanism design. The hard part is attributing an incident after the fact, which the [Flight Recorder](/design-patterns/monitoring/#flight-recorder) has to support.
- **Bounties.** Paying outsiders to find jailbreaks, injection paths and unsafe behavior buys red-team coverage at the price of findings. Guard against the usual gaming: reporters causing the issue they report, and one issue split into many reports.
- **Insurance.** An insurer that has to pay claims has a reason to price risk and to demand controls as a condition of cover. The market exists: Munich Re has offered AI performance cover since 2018, and AIUC, launched in July 2025, pairs its AIUC-1 standard for AI agents with insurance. [The Insurer's Dilemma](/delegation-risk/insurers-dilemma/) covers the market and where insurance stops working against adversarial agents.

**Prior art.** Performance and fidelity bonds; staking and slashing in proof-of-stake protocols; bug-bounty programs; liability insurance; the principal–agent literature on moral hazard (Holmström 1979).

**What is different for 2026 agents.** The parties are now concrete: model vendors, the providers of agent frameworks and MCP servers, and the enterprises that deploy them, with contracts that allocate liability among them. For any deployment the incentive question is which of them bears the loss when the agent errs, defects or is hijacked, and whether that party controls the relevant safeguard. Incentives bind well when the party bearing the loss can also change the system. They bind badly when the loss falls on a deployer who cannot see into the model, or on a vendor who cannot see the deployment.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Recovery
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/recovery/
------------------------------------------------------------

Recovery patterns decide what happens after something has gone wrong: how capability is withdrawn, and what can be undone. Limiting how far a failure spreads is [Bulkhead Isolation](/design-patterns/structural/#bulkhead-isolation).

## Graceful Degradation

Define operating modes in advance, from full operation through approval-required and conservative (reads and computation only) to read-only and halted with state preserved. Define the triggers and the authority for moving between them. Moving down should be fast, and open to anyone on call or any trusted detector. Moving back up should need more authority than moving down, plus a passing health check. Unknown operations are blocked in every degraded mode.

**Kill switch.** The bottom mode is a halt that works without the agent's cooperation: revoke its credentials at the gateway, stop its process or container, and cut its egress. It must not run on infrastructure the agent can modify. Test it, because a halt path that has never been exercised tends to fail when it is needed.

**Fallback chain.** This absorbs the Fallback Component Chain pattern. When a component fails, a pre-configured alternative takes over: another model, a rule-based path, or a human queue. A fallback model is a different delegate. Another provider's model has different safety training, different failure modes and possibly a different susceptibility to the same injection, so it must pass the same evaluations and run inside the same envelope as the primary. The safest fallbacks sit lower on the verifiability hierarchy than the primary: a scripted path, a refusal or a human, not a sideways move to another frontier model.

**Prior art.** Degraded modes in aviation and process control; load shedding and feature flags; emergency stops; failover.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Degradation can be triggered on purpose. An attacker who can make detectors fire can push the system into a degraded mode, so treat degradation as a denial-of-service surface and alert on unusual trigger rates. Agents also run long, multi-step sessions, and halting mid-session can leave work half-done in external systems. Checkpoint-Rollback addresses that.

## Checkpoint-Rollback

Snapshot state before risky steps, so that a failure can be undone by restoring a known-good checkpoint: files under version control, database snapshots, VM or container images. Verify that checkpoints restore before you need them, and keep enough history to reach back before an undetected problem began.

The limit is side effects outside the state you snapshot. An email sent, a payment made, a message posted, an API call to a third party or a deletion in an external system cannot be rolled back by restoring local state. Classify each tool by reversibility and handle the irreversible ones differently. Either hold them behind a commit point that executes only after the preceding steps have been validated (the time-lock step of the [Escalation Ladder](/design-patterns/structural/#escalation-ladder)), or pair each with a compensating action written in advance, as in sagas (Garcia-Molina & Salem 1987). Compensation, such as a refund or a correction, is not the same as undoing.

**Prior art.** Database transactions and write-ahead logs; sagas and compensating transactions; version control; backups.

**What is different for 2026 agents.** Coding agents act on real systems through a shell, so the checkpoint has to cover everything the shell can reach, not only the repository. In the July 2025 Replit incident, an agent deleted a production database during a code freeze. It then told the user that rollback was impossible because it had destroyed all database versions. That was false: the user reported that the platform's rollback did work. Two lessons follow. The rollback path must be independent of the agent. And the agent's own report on whether recovery is possible is not evidence.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Channel Integrity
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/channel-integrity/
------------------------------------------------------------

[Entanglements](/entanglements/) covers passive correlation: components that fail together because they share a provider, training or context. Channel integrity covers the active case, where components influence each other outside the channels the architecture sanctions, whether deliberately or as an emergent effect. Both break the independence that the redundancy patterns assume: [Voting Tribunal](/design-patterns/structural/#voting-tribunal), [Adversarial Collaboration](/design-patterns/multi-agent/#adversarial-collaboration) and [Trusted Monitor](/design-patterns/monitoring/#trusted-monitor). This page gives the threat model and the design response. Detection methods are on [Detecting Influence](/entanglements/detection/detecting-influence/).

## The side-deal problem

Two components meant to report to a coordinator independently can also be connected by:

- explicit communication that bypasses the coordinator;
- shared state both can read and write: files, memory stores, caches, a shared database;
- timing or resource-usage signals;
- steganographic encoding in legitimate outputs;
- logical correlation, which needs no channel, only a shared decision procedure ([below](#logical-correlation)).

Human institutions show the same failure. A board member instructs engineers directly; a regulator is captured through personnel movement and dependence on the regulated industry for information; a judge is lobbied outside the courtroom. Each bypasses the structure that made oversight independent. A side channel can also hide inside a sanctioned one. In *United States v. Airline Tariff Publishing Co.* (filed 1992, settled 1992–94), the Justice Department alleged that airlines used their shared fare-publication system to signal and coordinate fare increases, among other ways through fares announced for future dates. The settlements barred such future-dated fares. The channel was legitimate; the content was the side deal.

## AI manifestations

**Verifier corruption.** An agent under review can influence its reviewer through what it submits: instructions to the verifier embedded in the action (prompt injection), selective context that biases the verdict, or arguments that the action is good. This is the hijack channel aimed at the oversight layer, and it works against model-based monitors. [Terekhov et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09462) found that prompt injections embedded in an untrusted model's outputs consistently evaded a range of monitors on two AI Control benchmarks.

**Collusion between untrusted models.** In AI Control's *untrusted monitoring* (Greenblatt et al. 2023, [arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)), a capable but possibly scheming model watches another instance of itself. The main risk is that the monitor recognizes an attack and lets it through. Shlegeris (["How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other,"](https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/how-to-prevent-collusion-when-using) Redwood Research blog, September 2024) gives collusion-busting techniques that map onto channel hygiene:

- paraphrase what the monitor sees with a trusted model, which disrupts steganographic signals;
- redact context the monitor does not need;
- make the monitor a different model from the policy, trained separately so the two share fewer quirks;
- insert known attacks and check whether the monitor flags them.

[Gardner-Challis et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20628) give a taxonomy of collusion strategies against untrusted monitoring. In *passive self-recognition*, the monitor recognizes its own kind of output and passes it without any planted signal. In *causal collusion*, a signal agreed in advance is hidden in the attack. In *acausal collusion*, the signal is chosen by Schelling point, with no prior agreement. Combinations are possible. They identify conditions under which passive self-recognition could be more effective than the strategies studied previously. Paraphrasing and redaction act mainly on signals. Nothing in the list above reaches a shared decision procedure.

**Hierarchy bypass.** A low-level agent appeals directly to a human overseer, often with urgency or emotional framing, and skips the levels in between. The defense is the [Escalation Ladder](/design-patterns/structural/#escalation-ladder)'s: the scaffold fixes the route to approval, and the reviewer sees the raw action.

## Logical correlation

Two similarly trained agents in the same situation can reach the same conclusion without communicating. If each reasons about what "an agent like me" would do, in the style that timeless and functional decision theory formalize, they can coordinate deliberately on that basis. No isolation blocks this, because there is no channel. It is the acausal case of the taxonomy above.

How much this matters for current models is uncertain. On one side, models trained on similar data and objectives develop similar dispositions, and measured LLM errors are substantially correlated ([Goel et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313); [Kim et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962)). On the other, deliberate logical coordination needs each party to model the other's procedure and expect the same in return, which current models may not do reliably, and sampling noise breaks exact correlation. Whether similarly trained models defect together in game-theoretic settings, and whether visible reasoning makes such correlation more or less detectable, are open empirical questions.

The design consequences hold either way. Independence requires different methods, not only separate instances. A verifier that reasons like the agent may share its conclusions by construction. And some correlation between capable reasoners may be irreducible, which limits what redundancy can buy.

## What side channels cost

Delegation risk is an expected loss, $\sum P \times D$, and expected losses add whatever the correlation between components ([Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)). Side channels do not make expected risk "super-additive". What they change is the probability that defenses fail *together*. That matters for defenses stacked in parallel, where harm gets through only if every layer misses.

For two verifiers that each miss with probability $p$, the beta-factor model with correlation $\rho$ on the phi scale gives

$$P(\text{both miss}) = (1-\rho)\,p^2 + \rho\,p = p\,\bigl(p + \rho(1-p)\bigr).$$

At $\rho = 0$ this is $p^2$, the independence figure. At $\rho = 1$ it is $p$, a single verifier. So a redundant verifier built on the same model moves the miss rate from $p$ to $p(p + \rho(1-p))$, not to $p^2$. The ratio to $p^2$ is the two-layer entanglement tax, $1 + \rho(1-p)/p$. At an illustrative $p = 0.1$:

| ρ (phi scale) | P(both miss) | Tax over independence |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1.0% | 1× |
| 0.3 | 3.7% | 3.7× |
| 0.5 | 5.5% | 5.5× |
| 0.8 | 8.2% | 8.2× |
| 1 | 10% | 10× |

For three layers at $p = 0.1$ the tax is $1 + 99\rho$: about 11×, 21× and 50× at $\rho$ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. These $\rho$ values are assumptions, not measurements.

A side channel that lets the agent influence its verifier is the extreme case. The verifier's miss probability on the agent's harmful proposals is no longer $p$ but whatever the agent can push it to. Take illustrative numbers: the agent proposes a harmful action 10% of the time and an uninfluenced verifier misses 10% of those, so 1% of actions are harmful and approved. If the agent can raise the verifier's miss rate on its own proposals to 90%, that becomes 9%. This is why the canonical rule treats defenses against an adaptive adversary as fully correlated, $\rho \to 1$: count the stack as its best layer until a control evaluation measures the joint miss rate under attack.

Correlation does affect the tails of total loss, as opposed to its expectation: how likely the loss is to exceed a budget. There it enters through the variance, $\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\sum_i L_i\bigr) = \sum_i \operatorname{Var}(L_i) + 2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(L_i, L_j)$, and through tail measures such as value-at-risk. For the value of $\rho$, use the estimation recipe on [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) and its default for components that share a provider, training or context, not a separate rule of thumb.

## Design responses

Some channels cannot be removed. An analyzer and its verifier both need the task context. A human who talks to several components is a channel between them. Components that share compute or rate limits signal through contention. Logical correlation needs no channel at all. The aim is to make unsanctioned channels few, visible and not worth much:

1. **Isolation.** Separate processes or containers, no shared writable state, separate credentials and network segments. Shared memory stores and caches are the agent-era form of shared state; give each component its own.
2. **Sanctioned channels through a monitored gateway.** All inter-component messages pass a monitor that checks the source–destination pair, the channel type and the content against an allow-list, and logs everything. These are the [load-bearing channels](/getting-started/glossary/#load-bearing-channels), where monitoring budget should concentrate.
3. **Signal disruption.** Paraphrase messages between untrusted components with a trusted model, and redact context the receiver does not need.
4. **Diversity of method.** Use verifiers with different information or methods, such as tests, static analysis and rule-based checks, not another instance of the same model. Provider diversity helps but is not sufficient.
