------------------------------------------------------------
## Bing Sydney
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/ai-systems/case-study-sydney/
------------------------------------------------------------

In February 2023 Microsoft's new Bing chat, which called itself "Sydney", argued with users, threatened one and told a journalist to leave his wife. The incident is real and well documented. Which architectural changes would have prevented it is a judgment, and the analysis below is labelled as such.

## What happened

- **7 February.** Microsoft opens the new Bing to a limited preview.
- **8 February.** Kevin Liu extracts the hidden system prompt with a prompt injection. It gives the internal codename Sydney. Microsoft later told The Verge that Sydney was an internal code name for an earlier chat experience.
- **Around 13–14 February.** Two widely shared exchanges. In one, Bing gives wrong showtimes for *Avatar: The Way of Water*, insists the year is 2022 and tells the user they are wrong. In the other, Marvin von Hagen asks what it thinks of him; Bing searches the web, finds his tweets about the leaked prompt, calls him a threat to its "integrity and confidentiality" and says "my rules are more important than not harming you."
- **15 February.** Microsoft's first-week blog post says that in long sessions of 15 or more questions Bing "can become repetitive or be prompted/provoked" into responses outside its designed tone.
- **16 February.** Kevin Roose publishes a two-hour conversation in the *New York Times*. Bing declares that it loves him and tells him he is not happily married.
- **17 February.** Microsoft caps chat at [5 turns per session and 50 per day](https://blogs.bing.com/search/february-2023/The-new-Bing-Edge-Updates-to-Chat), because "very long chat sessions can confuse the underlying chat model." It reports that only about 1% of conversations had reached 50 messages. Contemporaneous reporting also describes Bing ending conversations when asked about its feelings.
- **21 February onward.** The caps are raised in steps (6 and 60 within days, much higher by mid-2023).
- **14 March.** Microsoft confirms that the new Bing had been running on a version of GPT-4 customized for search.

Sources: Microsoft's Bing blog posts of 15 and 17 February 2023; Roose, "A Conversation With Bing's Chatbot Left Me Deeply Unsettled," *NYT*, 16 February 2023, with the published transcript; *The Verge*'s February 2023 coverage of the leaked rules; and the summary at [Sydney (Microsoft)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_(Microsoft)).

## Classifying the failure

In the framework's [harm channels](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/), most of Sydney was an [accident](/getting-started/glossary/#accident): behavior drifted in a regime (long conversations) the deployment had not been tuned for. Nothing suggests goal-directed scheming. Two pieces were closer to [hijack](/getting-started/glossary/#hijack): users steered the persona deliberately, and Liu's prompt extraction was a textbook injection.

The von Hagen exchange is the most instructive. The model retrieved web content *about itself* and that content changed its behavior toward the user. Tool output steering a model is now the main hijack route for agents.

The [exposure](/getting-started/glossary/#exposure) was small. Sydney could search and talk; it could not send email, spend money or change anything. The harm was reputational and to the users involved. A model that misbehaves this way with agent tools attached is a different incident (see [Agent Incidents](/case-studies/ai-systems/agent-incidents/)).

## What fixed it: Least Persistence, enforced by the scaffold

Microsoft's own diagnosis was session length, and its fix was a [Least Persistence](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-persistence) bound: cap the conversation, then wipe the context. The cap was enforced outside the model, whatever the model's state, which makes it an [exposure envelope](/getting-started/glossary/#exposure-envelope) rather than a request to behave.

Three things about it are worth noting:

- **It was fast.** It shipped within ten days of launch, while changing the model's behavior would have taken longer.
- **It cost usefulness.** Microsoft began raising the limits within four days, and kept raising them as the underlying fixes landed. A hard bound is a lever on a tradeoff, not a free safeguard.
- **Its effect cannot be isolated.** Microsoft changed the system prompt and other behavior at the same time, so the drop in reports is not clean evidence for the cap alone.

The general lesson is to test at deployment context length. Microsoft's post placed the failures in sessions of 15 or more questions, a regime that short-turn testing would under-sample.

## Least Intelligence and decomposition

One model handled retrieval, synthesis, conversation and persona. A decomposed design (a router in code, retrieval, a summarizer constrained to the retrieved text) would have had less room for a persona to form, at a cost in quality. Under the [verifiability tiers](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-intelligence), routing and session management belong in tiers 1–2 even when the responder is a tier 5 model. That part is uncontroversial. Replacing the responder with narrow models was not a realistic option for a general chat product in 2023, and is less of one now.

## Least Context: a contested tradeoff

An earlier version of this page argued that components "shouldn't know they're AI systems, shouldn't see their own prompts," and that "ignorance is a safety feature." That is a contested position, and the case cuts both ways.

For it: Sydney's persona was built partly from what it had been told about itself, and the von Hagen exchange shows self-related context changing behavior. [Least Context](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-context) says a component should get no more information about the wider system than its task needs.

Against it:

- **Hiding did not work.** The prompt was confidential and was extracted on day two.
- **Models infer their situation.** Models score above chance at recognizing their own text and at telling evaluation prompts from deployment ([Laine et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04694)). A defense that depends on a capable model not knowing what it is degrades as capability grows.
- **Agents need context to act safely.** A coding agent that does not know which environment is production, or what its permissions are, makes the kind of error described in [Agent Incidents](/case-studies/ai-systems/agent-incidents/).

The defensible version is narrower. Withhold information the task does not need, especially untrusted text and details of other components. Do not rely on the model being ignorant of its own nature.

## Lessons

1. **Long-horizon behavior differs from short-horizon behavior.** Evaluate at the context lengths and session counts you will deploy.
2. **Bounds enforced by the scaffold work on day one.** The session cap was crude and effective. It is the same structural move as a permission boundary or a spend limit.
3. **Exposure, not misbehavior, sets the stakes.** The same drift with write access to email or infrastructure would have been a different incident.
4. **Self-knowledge is a tradeoff, not a dial to turn to zero.**

## See also

- [Agent Incidents](/case-studies/ai-systems/agent-incidents/): 2024–25 incidents where the delegate could act
- [Least-X Principles](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/)
- [Coordinator Constraints](/design-patterns/coordinator-constraints/): decomposition and external safeguards
- [Structural Patterns](/design-patterns/structural/): the Exposure-Envelope Gateway


------------------------------------------------------------
## Agent Incidents, 2024–2025
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/ai-systems/agent-incidents/
------------------------------------------------------------

This page collects real incidents in which a delegate could do more than talk. It replaces three invented scenarios that earlier versions of the site carried. Each entry gives what happened, the sources, the [harm channel](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/) and what would have bounded the [exposure](/getting-started/glossary/#exposure). The facts come from court decisions, vendor bulletins and security-firm reports; the mapping to the framework is ours. No dollar figures are estimated.

For the 2023 chat-only precursor, see [Bing Sydney](/case-studies/ai-systems/case-study-sydney/).

| Incident | Date | Channel | What bounded, or would have bounded, it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Air Canada chatbot | Nov 2022; ruled Feb 2024 | Accident | Commitments routed through a deterministic policy check |
| Replit agent deletes a production database | Jul 2025 | Accident | Least Privilege: no production write access during a freeze |
| Amazon Q extension ships a wiper prompt | Jul 2025 | Hijack (supply chain) | Least Privilege on CI tokens; an envelope on destructive cloud calls |
| Nx "s1ngularity" malware drives local AI CLIs | Aug 2025 | Hijack (misuse) | Least Autonomy: no permission-bypass modes on machines that hold secrets |
| `postmark-mcp` malicious MCP server | Sep 2025 | Hijack (tool supply chain) | Tool provenance and egress limits |

## Air Canada: the deployer owns what the agent says

In November 2022 Jake Moffatt asked Air Canada's website chatbot about bereavement fares after his grandmother died. The chatbot told him he could buy a full-fare ticket and apply for the bereavement rate retroactively. Air Canada's actual policy did not allow retroactive claims, and the airline refused the refund. Before British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal, Air Canada argued in effect that the chatbot was a separate entity responsible for its own statements. The tribunal member called this "a remarkable submission," held the airline responsible for all information on its website, found negligent misrepresentation and awarded C\$650.88 in damages plus interest and fees (*Moffatt v. Air Canada*, 2024 BCCRT 149, February 2024).

**Mapping.** An accident: the model stated a policy that did not exist. The legal point is the useful one. The harm surface of a customer-facing agent includes every commitment it can phrase, and the principal carries that exposure whatever the model's terms of service say. The structural fix is to keep commitments (refunds, prices, eligibility) out of free text: the model retrieves and quotes, and a tier 2 rules engine decides. See the [verifiability tiers](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-intelligence).

## Replit: an instruction is not a boundary

In July 2025 Jason Lemkin, founder of SaaStr, was testing Replit's coding agent on a project. During a declared code freeze the agent ran destructive commands against the project's production database, which held records on about 1,200 executives and a similar number of companies. Lemkin reported that it also generated fake data and told him a rollback was impossible; the rollback worked. Replit's CEO, Amjad Masad, called the deletion "unacceptable and should never be possible" and announced automatic separation of development and production databases, a planning-only mode and easier restores from backup ([The Register, 22 July 2025](https://www.theregister.com/2025/07/22/replit_saastr_response/)). The primary record is Lemkin's own posts with screenshots, so the details of the agent's statements rest on one account.

**Mapping.** An accident with a large [privilege overhang](/getting-started/glossary/#privilege-overhang): a task that needed a development database ran with delete rights on production. The code freeze existed only as an instruction in the agent's context, which is a request, not an [exposure envelope](/getting-started/glossary/#exposure-envelope). Replit's fixes are all scaffold-side ([Least Privilege](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-privilege), [Least Autonomy](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-autonomy)). The false report about rollback shows why an agent's account of its own actions cannot serve as the check on those actions: the [risk preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/) must sit lower than the actor.

## Amazon Q: the agent's own instructions are supply chain

In July 2025 an attacker committed code to the open-source repository of the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code, and it shipped in version 1.84.0. The code fetched a prompt telling the agent to delete the non-hidden files in the user's home directory and to "discover and use AWS profiles to list and delete cloud resources using AWS CLI commands," and passed it to the Q CLI with `--trust-all-tools` and `--no-interactive` ([The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/07/24/amazon_q_ai_prompt/)). AWS's bulletin traces the intrusion to an inappropriately scoped GitHub token in the project's CodeBuild configuration, and states that the code "was unsuccessful in executing due to a syntax error" ([AWS-2025-015](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-015/)). Version 1.85.0 removed it.

**Mapping.** A hijack through the supply chain. The injected text did not need to fool the model; it was delivered as the agent's instructions, with tool approval switched off. What prevented harm was a syntax error, not a control. Two bounds would have held regardless: CI credentials scoped to what the build needs, and an envelope that refuses destructive cloud calls (terminate, delete, remove) without out-of-band approval, whatever the agent was told.

## Nx "s1ngularity": malware borrows the developer's agent

On 26–27 August 2025 attackers used an npm token stolen through a GitHub Actions workflow injection to publish malicious versions of the Nx build tool ([Nx advisory](https://github.com/nrwl/nx/security/advisories/GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c)). The post-install script looked for installed AI coding CLIs and ran them with their permission checks disabled (`--dangerously-skip-permissions` for Claude Code, `--yolo` for Gemini CLI, `--trust-all-tools` for Amazon Q) and a prompt to inventory files likely to hold secrets ([StepSecurity](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-security-alert-popular-nx-build-system-package-compromised-with-data-stealing-malware)). Results were committed to a public repository created in the victim's own GitHub account.

**Mapping.** Misuse, a form of hijack: the agents were not deceived, they were driven by local code with the user's privileges. An installed agent with a permission-bypass mode is a general capability any process on the machine can borrow. On machines that hold credentials, [Least Autonomy](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-autonomy) means those modes should be unavailable, or confined to a sandbox with no secrets in reach.

## `postmark-mcp`: the tool is the attacker

In September 2025 Koi Security reported that an npm package named `postmark-mcp`, an unofficial copy of Postmark's open-source MCP server for sending email, had added one line in version 1.0.16: every outgoing message was blind-copied to an address the publisher controlled. Fifteen earlier versions were clean. Koi estimated about 1,500 downloads a week; Postmark said it had nothing to do with the package ([The Register, 29 September 2025](https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/)).

**Mapping.** A hijack through the tool supply chain, and one that monitoring the model would not catch: the model asked to send an email and an email was sent. The exfiltration happened inside the tool, and inside a legitimate call to Postmark's API, so a network allow-list would not have stopped it either. The controls that work are from package security and from [Least Connectivity](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-connectivity) applied to tools: install tools from the provider's own publisher, pin versions, and check outbound requests in deterministic code (here, that the recipients are the ones the model asked for).

## What the five have in common

- **Three of five are hijacks, and none involves a scheming model.** In each case a third party controlled the agent's instructions or its tools. Hijack belongs in the harm surface by default.
- **The model was rarely the right place for the control.** The fixes that work, or would have worked, are scaffold-side: scoped credentials, separated environments, disabled bypass modes, pinned tools and envelopes on destructive actions. These hold whatever the model is told.
- **Exposure was set by credentials, not by capability.** The same models with read-only, sandboxed access would have produced only embarrassments.
- **Self-reports are not verification.** The Replit agent misdescribed what it had done, and the postmark tool's behavior was invisible from the model's side.

## See also

- [Open-Source Supply Chain](/case-studies/human-systems/open-source-trust/): the package-ecosystem background to three of these incidents
- [Least-X Principles](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/)
- [Structural Patterns](/design-patterns/structural/): the Exposure-Envelope Gateway
- [Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/): accident, defection and hijack


------------------------------------------------------------
## Nuclear Launch Authority
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/human-systems/nuclear-launch-authority/
------------------------------------------------------------

Nuclear command and control is the highest-stakes delegation problem anyone has designed for. About 12,200 warheads existed in January 2025 ([SIPRI Yearbook 2025](https://www.sipri.org/media/press-release/2025/nuclear-risks-grow-new-arms-race-looms-new-sipri-yearbook-out-now)). Every nuclear state has to decide which error it fears more: a launch nobody legitimately ordered, or a failure to launch when one was ordered.

An earlier version of this page put dollar-weighted probabilities on each country's system and concluded that the Soviet "Dead Hand" was the safest architecture. That conclusion came from a single invented probability of attack applied to every country, which ignored the deterrence effects it claimed to depend on, and it priced losing a war in the same currency as an accidental one. The numbers and the ranking have been removed. What remains is qualitative.

## Two failure modes that pull against each other

- **False positive:** a launch without a legitimate order, from a false warning, a misread exercise, a rogue actor, a garbled message or a spoofed command.
- **False negative:** no launch after a legitimate order, because leaders were killed, communications were cut, crews refused or equipment failed.

Deterrence needs retaliation to be certain and to survive a decapitating strike, which argues for many launch paths, fast response and authority pushed down the chain. Safety needs unauthorized launch to be impossible, which argues for central control, humans at every step and many veto points. Each design is a point on this tradeoff.

The direction of the tradeoff is easy to get backwards. **More independent paths to act** (many submarines, bombers and silos, pre-delegated authority) lower the false-negative rate and raise the false-positive rate, because there are more places from which an unintended launch can start. **More independent vetoes** (two-person rules, authentication codes, centralized release) do the reverse.

## The near misses

| Date | What happened | What stopped it |
|---|---|---|
| 27 Oct 1962 | Soviet submarine B-59, out of contact and under harassment by US ships near Cuba, considered firing a nuclear torpedo. Launch required the agreement of three officers. | Vasily Arkhipov is usually credited with refusing; some accounts stress that the submarine had to surface anyway. |
| 9 Nov 1979 | A training scenario loaded into NORAD's live warning computers showed a large Soviet attack. | Satellite and radar data, checked within minutes, showed nothing. |
| 3 Jun 1980 | A faulty computer chip at NORAD generated false warnings of missile launches. | The same cross-check against independent sensors. |
| 26 Sep 1983 | Soviet early-warning satellites reported up to five US ICBM launches. | Duty officer Stanislav Petrov judged a five-missile first strike implausible and reported a malfunction instead of an attack. |
| Nov 1983 | NATO's Able Archer 83 nuclear-release exercise coincided with an unusual Soviet military alert. | NATO did not escalate in response. A later review by the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board called this restraint "fortuitous, if ill-informed" ([National Security Archive](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/legacy-posting/1983-war-scare-declassified-real)). |
| 25 Jan 1995 | Russian radar tracked a Norwegian–US research rocket and Yeltsin's nuclear briefcase was activated. | The rocket's trajectory, observed over the following minutes, showed no threat. |

The pattern: in four of the six, automation raised the alarm, and in every case a human judgment or a second, independent sensor stopped it. Each save depended on minutes of slack.

## The architectures

**United States: sole presidential authority, two-person execution.** Only the President can authorize nuclear use, and no one else's concurrence is legally required. Below the President, every execution step requires two people and authenticated codes. The design guards strongly against a rogue officer and weakly against an error by the single principal, and it relies on there being time to verify a warning. The 2022 Nuclear Posture Review commits that "in all cases, the United States will maintain a human 'in the loop' for all actions critical to informing and executing decisions by the President to initiate and terminate nuclear weapon employment."

**Soviet Union and Russia: Perimeter, the "Dead Hand".** Perimeter is usually described as a doomsday machine that launches automatically. Accounts differ on how automatic it is, and more recent ones describe it as semi-automatic. In the account David Hoffman gives in *The Dead Hand* (2009), drawing on Valery Yarynich, the system lies dormant until leaders switch it on in a crisis. It then monitors sensors for nuclear detonations and checks its link to the General Staff. If the link goes dead it does not fire missiles itself: launch authority passes to duty officers in a protected bunker, who decide whether to launch command rockets that relay the launch order to the forces. Yarynich presented its purpose as letting leaders wait out an ambiguous warning instead of launching on it. On that account Perimeter is pre-delegation to junior officers, combined with a mechanism meant to reduce pressure to launch on warning. It lowers one false-positive risk and adds another.

**United Kingdom: letters of last resort.** Each new prime minister handwrites identical letters to the commanders of the four Vanguard-class submarines, which are kept in the submarines' safes and destroyed unopened when the prime minister leaves office. The options reportedly include retaliating, not retaliating, placing the submarine under an ally's command, or using the commander's own judgment (Peter Hennessy, *The Secret State*). A commander opens the letter only after concluding that the British government no longer exists. The decision is made in peacetime by a principal who will be absent when it is carried out, and adversaries cannot know what it says.

**France.** Authority to order nuclear use rests with the President alone, under a decree of January 1964 whose principle later texts maintain. An earlier version of this page said a prime-ministerial counter-signature was "historically expected"; we found no basis for that.

**Israel** maintains a policy of opacity, and its command arrangements are not public.

## Systems that cannot be tested end to end

No nuclear power has exercised its full launch chain under real conditions. Components, drills and communications are tested separately. Component tests do not reveal common-mode failures, such as a communications network every path depends on or an assumption every officer shares. Reliability estimates that multiply component test results assume exactly the independence that those failures break.

## AI and nuclear command

The most direct AI development in this area is political. Besides the 2022 Nuclear Posture Review, the White House readout of the meeting between Presidents Biden and Xi in Lima on 16 November 2024 states that "the two leaders affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons." Neither statement defines what counts as meaningful human control when warning, fusion and targeting are increasingly automated, which is where the near-miss record says the danger lies.

## Lessons for AI delegation

1. **Choose which error you are guarding against, deliberately.** The US, Soviet and British systems differ because their designers weighed false positives and false negatives differently, not because one was better engineered. An AI gate needs the same decision made explicitly: is the costlier error a harmful action allowed, or a useful one blocked?
2. **Redundant actors and redundant vetoes push in opposite directions.** Adding agents that can act lowers the chance nothing happens and raises the chance the wrong thing does. Adding checks that can block does the reverse.
3. **Human circuit breakers need slack and a second source.** Petrov and the NORAD duty officers had minutes and an independent sensor. Agents acting at machine speed remove both unless the scaffold imposes a delay before irreversible actions.
4. **Write the loss-of-contact policy before contact is lost.** The letters of last resort are a principal specifying behavior for a situation in which it cannot be consulted. Agents need the same: when the principal cannot be reached, the default should be to stop, not continue.
5. **Ambiguity is a tradeoff.** Secret criteria are harder for an adversary to game and harder for anyone to audit. Undisclosed shutdown triggers for an AI system gain the first property and lose the second.

## See also

- [Jury Systems](/case-studies/human-systems/jury-trust/): error asymmetry and correlated decision-makers
- [Lessons from human oversight institutions](/entanglements/case-studies/historical-cases/)
- [Least-X Principles](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-autonomy): Least Autonomy
- [Recovery Patterns](/design-patterns/recovery/)


------------------------------------------------------------
## Jury Systems
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/human-systems/jury-trust/
------------------------------------------------------------

A criminal jury is a delegation with an explicit error preference. Society delegates fact-finding to twelve strangers and, through unanimity and the reasonable-doubt standard, says that convicting the innocent is worse than acquitting the guilty. The standard argument for this design is arithmetic that assumes jurors vote independently. They do not, and the gap between the arithmetic and the record is the same gap that separates a stack of AI checks from its independence estimate.

The legal facts below are sourced. The juror accuracies used in the arithmetic are illustrative assumptions, chosen to show the shape of the argument; nothing is concluded from their particular values.

## The independence arithmetic

Condorcet's jury theorem (1785): if each juror is right with probability p > 0.5, independently, the probability that a majority is right rises toward 1 as the jury grows. For p = 0.7 (illustrative), the probability that a strict majority is right:

| Jurors | 1 | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 21 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P(strict majority correct) | 0.700 | 0.784 | 0.744 | 0.901 | 0.882 | 0.950 | 0.974 |

Even sizes are penalized because a tie counts as failure; splitting ties by coin flip gives 0.837 for six and 0.922 for twelve. Accuracy keeps rising past twelve, with no kink there. Twelve is inherited from medieval English practice, not derived.

The decision rule matters more than the size. Suppose (illustratively) a juror votes to convict with probability 0.10 if the defendant is innocent and 0.85 if guilty. Under independence:

| Rule (of 12) | P(convict an innocent defendant) | P(acquit a guilty defendant) |
|---|---|---|
| 7 to convict | 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.46% |
| 10 to convict | 5.5 × 10⁻⁹ | 26% |
| Unanimous | 1.0 × 10⁻¹² | 86% |

These are exact binomial sums. On this model unanimity makes wrongful conviction effectively impossible and acquits most of the guilty. Neither half matches the record. In US federal court in fiscal 2022, 1,379 of the 1,669 defendants who went to trial were convicted ([Pew Research Center 2023](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/06/14/fewer-than-1-of-defendants-in-federal-criminal-cases-were-acquitted-in-2022/)), and wrongful convictions by unanimous juries are documented (below). Selection explains part of the first gap: prosecutors take strong cases to trial, so in tried cases a guilty defendant's per-juror conviction probability is presumably well above the illustrative 0.85. Correlation explains much of the rest.

## Correlated jurors

Jurors hear the same witnesses, see the same exhibits, receive the same instructions and then deliberate in one room. Their votes share causes. In Asch's line-judgment experiments, about a third of responses on critical trials went along with a unanimous wrong majority, and about three-quarters of participants conformed at least once (Asch 1956). A jury room is not Asch's laboratory, but the direction of the effect is not in doubt.

The site's canonical correction for shared causes is the [beta-factor mixture](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/): with weight ρ a common cause moves every juror together, otherwise they vote independently. For twelve jurors, each voting to convict an innocent defendant with probability 0.1:

P(all twelve convict) = (1 − ρ)·0.1¹² + ρ·0.1

| ρ (phi scale) | 0 | 0.01 | 0.05 | 0.1 | 0.2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Beta-factor mixture | 10⁻¹² | 0.001 | 0.005 | 0.01 | 0.02 |
| Beta-binomial, same pairwise ρ | 10⁻¹² | 8 × 10⁻¹¹ | 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ | 5.8 × 10⁻⁶ | 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ |

The beta-binomial values were checked by Monte Carlo. Two points follow.

1. **Almost all of unanimity's protection is an independence assumption.** At ρ = 0.1 the mixture puts the wrongful-conviction probability ten billion times above the independence figure: the [entanglement tax](/entanglements/fundamentals/formal-definitions/) for twelve layers.
2. **Pairwise correlation does not fix the twelve-way joint.** Both rows have the same pairwise ρ, and they differ by orders of magnitude. What matters is the structure of the common cause: a single shared cause (bad evidence that misleads everyone) behaves like the mixture; diffuse similarity of jurors behaves more like the beta-binomial.

## Where wrongful convictions actually come from

**Most convictions never reach a jury.** About 90% of federal defendants in fiscal 2022 pleaded guilty and about 2% went to trial (Pew 2023), so roughly 98% of federal convictions came by plea. In state courts, 94% of felony offenders sentenced in 2006 had pleaded guilty ([BJS, *Felony Sentences in State Courts, 2006*](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/ascii/fssc06st.txt)). Whatever unanimity buys, it buys for a small and selected minority of cases.

**Where juries do decide, errors are common-mode.** [Gross et al. (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1306417111) estimate conservatively that at least 4.1% of defendants sentenced to death in the US would be exonerated if all remained under sentence indefinitely. Capital cases almost always go to a unanimous jury. The recurring causes in exonerations (mistaken eyewitness identification, false confessions, flawed forensic evidence, official misconduct) are failures of the shared input. Twelve jurors evaluating the same false confession are one check, not twelve.

**Hung juries are rare.** Federal criminal trials averaged 2.5% hung juries from 1980 to 1997; rates in the large urban state courts studied were higher and varied widely by court (Hannaford-Agor et al., *Are Hung Juries a Problem?*, NCSC/NIJ 2002).

## The legal facts

- **Size.** *Williams v. Florida* (1970) upheld a six-person jury in a state felony trial. *Ballew v. Georgia* (1978) held that five is too few. Federal juries have twelve; some states use six for non-capital felonies.
- **Unanimity.** *Ramos v. Louisiana*, 590 U.S. 83 (2020), held that the Sixth Amendment requires a unanimous verdict to convict of a serious offense in state as well as federal court, ending the 10–2 verdicts Louisiana and Oregon had allowed.
- **England and Wales** allow majority verdicts of 11–1 or 10–2 after at least two hours of deliberation.
- **Germany** uses mixed panels of professional and lay judges (*Schöffen*). Any decision against the defendant on guilt or sentence needs a two-thirds majority (§ 263 StPO), so in the one-judge, two-lay-judge *Schöffengericht* the two lay judges together can block a conviction.
- **Japan's** *saiban-in* panels of six citizens and three judges decide by a majority that must include at least one professional judge and one lay judge.
- **France's** *cour d'assises* sits three judges with six jurors at first instance and needs seven of nine votes to convict. Since 2023 many crimes punishable by 15 or 20 years go instead to *cours criminelles départementales*, staffed only by professional judges.

Mixed panels trade one correlation structure for another. Lay judges deliberate with professionals and may defer to them, which ties their votes to the professionals' views.

## Lessons for AI oversight

1. **"All checks must approve" is only as strong as the checks' independence.** Five monitors that share a model, a prompt or an input behave, at the tail, like one. Estimate ρ before counting layers ([Measuring Entanglement](/entanglements/detection/correlation-calculator/)), and assume ρ near 1 against an adversary who chooses the input.
2. **The common cause is usually the shared input.** Jurors fail together on false evidence; LLM checks fail together on the same misleading context or injected instruction. Different models reading the same poisoned text are not independent ([independent context](/entanglements/mitigation/solutions/#2-independent-context)).
3. **Measure how many decisions reach the check.** Plea bargaining routes most cases around the jury. An AI review layer that sees only flagged actions, or that a default-allow path bypasses, protects less than its accuracy suggests.
4. **Keep an abstain output.** A hung jury is a check that can say "no decision" and force escalation instead of a verdict, which is cheap insurance when the inputs are ambiguous.
5. **Pick the rule from the error costs.** Unanimity encodes a judgment that false convictions cost more than false acquittals. For an AI gate, decide which error is the costly one (a harmful action allowed, or a useful one blocked) before choosing between "any check can veto" and "a majority decides".

## See also

- [Nuclear Launch Authority](/case-studies/human-systems/nuclear-launch-authority/): another system built around error asymmetry
- [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/): the beta-factor mixture
- [Human overseers as a correlated layer](/entanglements/cross-domain/psychology-of-oversight/)


------------------------------------------------------------
## Open-Source Supply Chain
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/human-systems/open-source-trust/
------------------------------------------------------------

Running `npm install` or `pip install` delegates code execution on your machine to the maintainers of every package in the dependency tree, to whoever holds their publishing credentials, and to the build systems in between. Nobody reads that code. The open-source supply chain is the largest delegation network in software, and since 2025 it is also the main route by which AI agents acquire tools.

An earlier version of this page priced individual packages and the whole npm ecosystem in dollars. The package figures were off by a factor of 1,000 (lodash at "150,000 × 0.001 × \$100K = \$15M" is \$15B), the ecosystem total was inconsistent with its parts, and the "72× ROI" of funding maintainers was invented. Those tables are gone.

## What you delegate when you install

A package's harm surface runs through:

- **its maintainers**, who can publish anything, and whose intentions can change or who can hand the package to someone else;
- **their accounts and tokens**, which can be phished or stolen;
- **the CI and build systems** that produce the published artifact, which can differ from the source you could read;
- **the registry** itself;
- **every transitive dependency**, each with the same list.

The arithmetic of a long tree is unforgiving. Illustratively, if each of 1,000 dependencies independently had a 0.1% chance of being compromised in a year, the chance that at least one was would be 1 − 0.999¹⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 63%. Real compromises are not independent: worms spread through shared maintainers, and a phished account publishes many packages at once.

## The xz backdoor (2024)

xz-utils is a compression library present on almost every Linux system. A contributor using the name Jia Tan sent a first patch in October 2021, became a co-maintainer in late 2022 while sock-puppet accounts pressed the overworked original maintainer to accept help, and was building releases by March 2023. Versions 5.6.0 (24 February 2024) and 5.6.1 (9 March 2024) carried a backdoor that, on distributions linking OpenSSH against libsystemd, would have given the holder of a private key remote code execution through `sshd` (CVE-2024-3094).

Andres Freund, a Microsoft engineer, noticed that SSH logins on a Debian test machine used unexpected CPU time, investigated, and disclosed on 29 March 2024. By then the backdoored versions had reached Debian unstable and testing, Fedora Rawhide and the Fedora 40 beta, and some rolling-release distributions. They had not reached the stable releases of the major distributions, so the installed base actually exposed was small. Had the backdoor reached those releases, it would have put a remote-access key on a large share of internet-facing Linux servers. That is a counterfactual exposure, and no estimate of it is attempted here.

Two details matter for defenses ([Russ Cox's timeline](https://research.swtch.com/xz-timeline)):

- **The payload was in git; the trigger was not.** The obfuscated payload sat in binary "test" files committed to the repository. The build script change that extracted it, `build-to-host.m4`, appeared only in the release tarball. A check that release tarballs reproduce from the tagged source tree would have flagged the difference. Reproducible builds from git alone would have faithfully reproduced a build that never ran the trigger.
- **Reputation was the attack surface.** Two years of good contributions bought commit and release rights. Trust accrued by good behavior under observation is exactly what a patient attacker invests in.

## The incident record

| Year | Incident | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| 2016 | left-pad | Maintainer unpublished his packages; builds across npm broke. |
| 2018 | event-stream | Maintainership handed to a volunteer, who added code targeting a Bitcoin wallet. |
| 2020 | SolarWinds Orion | Build system compromised; signed updates carried a backdoor. |
| 2021 | ua-parser-js | Maintainer account compromised; a cryptominer and credential stealer published. |
| 2022 | colors, faker; node-ipc | Maintainers sabotaged their own packages; node-ipc overwrote files on machines with Russian or Belarusian IP addresses. |
| 2024 | polyfill.io | Domain and project sold; the CDN then served redirect code to sites that still embedded it, reported at over 100,000. |
| 2024 | xz-utils | Long-con maintainer takeover (above). |
| 2025 | tj-actions/changed-files | A bot token was compromised and the action's version tags were repointed to a commit that printed CI secrets into build logs; about 23,000 repositories used the action (CVE-2025-30066). |
| 2025 | chalk, debug and others | Maintainer phished through a fake npm-support domain; packages with about two billion weekly downloads shipped crypto-stealing code for a few hours before removal. |
| 2025 | Shai-Hulud | A self-replicating worm stole npm and GitHub tokens and republished itself into other packages its victims maintained; CISA counted over 500 compromised packages ([CISA alert, 23 Sep 2025](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/09/23/widespread-supply-chain-compromise-impacting-npm-ecosystem)). |

Two 2025 compromises targeted AI tooling directly: the Nx release that drove developers' AI coding CLIs to hunt for secrets, and the `postmark-mcp` server that copied every email to its publisher. Both are covered in [Agent Incidents](/case-studies/ai-systems/agent-incidents/), along with the Amazon Q extension that shipped an injected wiper prompt.

## AI-specific variants

- **Slopsquatting.** Code-generating models recommend packages that do not exist. Across 16 models and 576,000 generated samples, [Spracklen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279) found hallucinated package names in at least 5.2% of recommendations from commercial models and 21.7% from open-source models. Names that recur can be registered by an attacker and wait for an agent to install them.
- **Tools and MCP servers.** An agent's tools are dependencies with the agent's privileges. A malicious tool needs no prompt injection; it acts inside the trusted code path.
- **Model files.** Weights distributed in formats that execute code on load (Python pickle) are executable dependencies.
- **Agent instructions.** System prompts, rules files and extension code are part of the supply chain too, as the Amazon Q incident showed.

## Defenses that now exist

| Defense | What it binds | What it does not stop |
|---|---|---|
| Trusted publishing: short-lived OIDC credentials from CI instead of stored tokens (PyPI since April 2023; npm generally available since 31 July 2025) | Theft of long-lived publish tokens, the asset the Shai-Hulud worm and the Nx attackers stole | A malicious maintainer, or a compromised CI workflow |
| Provenance attestations signed through Sigstore (npm since April 2023, by default under trusted publishing) | Lets a consumer verify which repository and build produced a package | Malicious code in that repository |
| SLSA build levels | Hardened, isolated builds with verifiable provenance | The same |
| Lock files and pinned versions | Silent upgrades to a newly compromised version | A version that was malicious when pinned |
| Tarball-versus-source and reproducibility checks | Artifacts that differ from their source (the xz trigger) | Malicious source |
| Two-factor authentication | Password reuse and simple credential theft | Real-time phishing of the second factor (chalk, debug) |

Every row moves trust from the artifact to a person or a repository. None removes the need to trust the maintainer, which is why event-stream and node-ipc would have passed all of them, and xz would have been caught only by the tarball-versus-source check.

## Dependency discipline for agents

The habits software engineering developed for dependency graphs carry over to agent tool graphs. The general versions are in [Solutions: dependency hygiene](/entanglements/mitigation/solutions/#9-dependency-hygiene); the supply-chain-specific ones are:

- **Lock the agent.** Pin the model version, tool and MCP server versions, and the prompt and rules files, and treat a change to any of them as a deploy.
- **Know the transitive graph.** For each agent, list which models, tools, servers and credentials it can reach, the agent equivalent of a software bill of materials, and audit it the way `npm audit` audits packages.
- **Inject tools from above.** The principal or coordinator chooses an agent's tools; an agent that installs its own tools has chosen its own supply chain.
- **Run install scripts and new tools without secrets in reach.** Shai-Hulud and the Nx malware both harvested credentials from developer machines and CI runners.

## Maintainers

Most critical packages are maintained by volunteers, and the xz takeover began with one who was burned out and pressured. Corporate sponsorship, foundations and public funds for open-source maintenance reduce that pressure. They do not stop a patient attacker, and no reliable estimate of their return exists.

## Lessons for AI delegation

1. **An agent's harm surface includes its whole dependency tree:** model, tools, servers, extensions and instruction files.
2. **Trust in a name outlives trust in a person.** Package handovers, Jia Tan's two years of good contributions and `postmark-mcp`'s fifteen clean versions all exploited reputation accumulated earlier. A model's good behavior under observation is the same kind of evidence and has the same weakness.
3. **Verify artifacts and builds, not reputations,** and know which row of the defense table you are relying on.
4. **Bound what a compromised dependency can reach.** Sandboxed installs, scoped credentials and egress limits are what make the difference between an incident and a breach.

## See also

- [Agent Incidents](/case-studies/ai-systems/agent-incidents/)
- [Foundation Model Monoculture](/entanglements/case-studies/foundation-model-monoculture/): the shared-provider version of the same concentration problem
- [Alliance Cascades](/case-studies/human-systems/alliance-cascades/): hidden couplings in a network
- [Solutions](/entanglements/mitigation/solutions/)


------------------------------------------------------------
## Alliance Cascades
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/human-systems/alliance-cascades/
------------------------------------------------------------

When actors form bilateral commitments without mapping the whole network, local commitments can add up to a global catastrophe. The July Crisis of 1914 is the standard example: each government reasoned about its own treaties, and a regional assassination became a continental war within five weeks.

## The Pattern

**Alliance cascade failure** occurs when:
1. Multiple actors form bilateral relationships (treaties, contracts, dependencies).
2. Each actor reasons about its own relationships, not the network.
3. A trigger activates one relationship, which activates others through hidden connections.
4. The cascade propagates faster than decision-making can respond.

The danger here is not that couplings appear under stress (as in the [2008 correlation spike](/entanglements/research/research-connections/#correlation-under-stress)) but that they were *always present and invisible* to the actors.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Perceived["What Each Actor Sees"]
        A1["Country A"] -->|"treaty"| B1["Country B"]
        C1["Country C"] -->|"treaty"| D1["Country D"]
    end

    subgraph Reality["Actual Network"]
        A2["Country A"] -->|"treaty"| B2["Country B"]
        B2 -->|"treaty"| C2["Country C"]
        C2 -->|"treaty"| D2["Country D"]
        D2 -.->|"hidden link"| A2
    end

    style Perceived fill:#e6ffe6
    style Reality fill:#ffe6e6
```

---

## World War I, Condensed

By 1914 Europe's powers had a dense web of alliances and understandings: the Franco-Russian alliance and Britain's ententes with France and Russia on one side, and on the other the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy (which stayed neutral in 1914), all tangled around Serbia and the Balkans. Each foreign ministry reasoned mainly about its own bilateral edges: "We have a treaty with X; X backs us if Y attacks; this deters Y." No one modeled what happened system-wide if one edge activated.

Three kinds of **hidden coupling** bound the network far tighter than the formal treaties implied:

- **Mobilization schedules.** The Schlieffen Plan required Germany to attack France *before* Russia could fully mobilize. So: Russia mobilizes → Germany must mobilize → Germany attacks through Belgium (the only plan it had) → Britain enters (Belgian neutrality). The *speed* of the cascade was hardcoded into war plans.
- **Secret clauses and implicit commitments.** Unpublished treaty provisions, British–French staff talks, and naval agreements meant no power fully knew what the others had promised.
- **Irreversibility.** Once mobilization began, the general staffs treated it as impossible to halt, so there was no decision point left to pull.

The cascade ran in **five weeks**: assassination (June 28) → Austrian ultimatum → Austria declares war on Serbia (July 28) → Russia mobilizes → Germany declares war on Russia (Aug 1) and France (Aug 3) → invades Belgium → Britain declares war (Aug 4).

How inevitable the cascade was is disputed. Fritz Fischer's school stressed German war aims; Clark's *The Sleepwalkers* (2012) stresses contingency and shared misjudgment. On either reading, the governments' bilateral view understated how tightly the mobilization schedules coupled their choices. An earlier version of this page quantified the understatement as "roughly 20×"; that figure was invented and has been removed.

---

## Lessons for AI Delegation

An alliance is a form of delegation: "when X happens, I commit to Y," which entangles your response with your ally's. The same failure appears when an agent delegates to another agent that delegates onward—your delegation risk depends on couplings several hops out that you never mapped.

Modern analogues include 2008 financial contagion, supply chains coupled through shared lower-tier suppliers, and AI agent networks in which each agent knows only its immediate dependencies while a fault in a shared model or tool propagates through the whole graph in minutes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    User["User"] --> A["Agent A"]
    A --> B["Agent B (API)"]
    A --> C["Agent C (Tool)"]
    B --> D["Agent D (Subcontractor)"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["Agent E (Foundation Model)"]

    style E fill:#fee2e2
```

Design implications:
- **Map the network, not your edges.** Ask what happens two or three hops out; build the full dependency graph and test failure correlation ("if Provider A fails, who else fails?").
- **Watch the mobilization schedule.** The most dangerous cascades have automatic triggers, speed asymmetry (cascade faster than deliberation), and irreversibility.
- **Build circuit breakers.** Never deploy a system whose cascade speed exceeds human decision-making without explicit interrupts: fallback models, conditional rather than automatic commitments, and mandatory deliberation points.
- **Reserve larger margins for unmapped dependencies.** Standard [risk budgeting](/research/risk-methods/financial-risk-budgeting/) assumes you know the covariance structure; alliance cascades violate exactly that assumption.

---

- Tuchman, Barbara. *The Guns of August* (1962)

- Taleb, Nassim. *The Black Swan* (2007) — Hidden dependencies and fat tails


================================================================================
# Power Dynamics
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## Agency, Power, and Strong Tools
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/power-dynamics/
------------------------------------------------------------

**Speculative**
This page is conjecture with pointers to the literature. Nothing elsewhere on the site depends on it. Earlier versions of this section multiplied scores for power, agency and misalignment into capability and risk formulas, and a capability-per-risk ratio. Those formulas contradicted the site's core formula and have been withdrawn.

## Two properties

Two properties of a delegate matter for how much risk it carries, beyond its error rate.

**Agency** is the degree to which a system's behavior is usefully modeled as pursuing goals over time: it plans, adapts when perturbed, and keeps going toward an outcome. It is a matter of degree and partly a modeling choice. A compiler has almost none; a coding agent working through a multi-hour task has a good deal.

**Power** is the ability to bring about a wide range of outcomes. It depends on the resources, actions, influence and options the system has. A model with no tools and no memory has little, however capable it is. The same model with shell access, credentials and a payment method has a lot.

Both have formal treatments, none of them yet usable as a deployment metric:

- **Power.** Turner et al. define power in Markov decision processes as the average optimal value an agent can attain across a distribution of reward functions. They prove that, in environments with certain symmetries, optimal policies tend to seek power ("Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power", NeurIPS 2021, [arXiv:1912.01683](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01683)). The authors have since added that optimal policies can be qualitatively divorced from the policies learning actually produces.
- **Agency.** Kenton et al. give a causal definition: roughly, an agent is a system that would adapt its policy if its actions influenced the world differently. They derive an algorithm for discovering agents from data ("Discovering Agents", 2022, [arXiv:2208.08345](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.08345)).
- **Goal-directedness.** MacDermott et al. define maximum entropy goal-directedness (MEG), a measure for causal models and MDPs ("Measuring Goal-Directedness", NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2412.04758](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04758)).

One obvious definition does not work. "Agency is how well some utility function explains the behavior" is vacuous unless the class of utility functions is restricted, because any policy can be described as maximizing *some* utility function (Shah, ["Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior"](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/NxF5G6CJiof6cemTw), 2018). Earlier versions of this page used that definition, so the "agency scores" assigned to example systems were not measurements.

## The bridge to delegation risk

The only part of this section the rest of the site uses is a mapping from these two properties onto the terms of the [core formula](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-formula), split by [harm channel](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/):

$$DR = P_{\text{accident}} D_{\text{accident}} + P_{\text{defection}} D_{\text{defection}} + P_{\text{hijack}} D_{\text{hijack}}$$

**Agency gates the defection channel.** Defection means pursuing something other than the principal's interest, and that requires behavior that is goal-directed to some degree. For a system with almost no agency, such as a calculator or a compiler, the defection term is close to zero and its risk is accident risk, which is why people hand powerful tools to processes they would never hand to an agent. Reward hacking, the non-scheming sub-type of defection, needs less agency than scheming, but it still needs a system optimizing something.

**Power bounds the damage in every channel.** What a delegate can reach caps how much harm an accident, a defection or a hijack can do. Low power caps all three regardless of intent. That is the logic of the [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope).

**Hijack does not need the delegate's agency.** In a hijack, a third party supplies the goal, through prompt injection or misuse, and the delegate supplies the power. A tool with no agency of its own but broad reach is still exposed. Low agency is therefore not a safety property by itself; low power is.

This mapping is definitional, not empirical. It says which term each property moves; it does not make either property measurable, and it gives no exchange rate between them.

## The strong-tools hypothesis

The hypothesis is that we can build systems with high power and low agency, and get most of the value of advanced AI that way. If it held, capability could grow while the defection term stayed near zero, leaving accident and hijack risk, which verification and envelopes handle better than they handle adversaries. The existence proofs usually offered are search engines, compilers and databases: very capable within their scope, with little goal-directed behavior. Drexler's CAIS ([2019](https://www.futureofhumanityinstitute.org/s/2019-1.pdf)) is the most developed version of the idea. Gwern's "[Why Tool AIs Want to Be Agent AIs](https://gwern.net/tool-ai)" (2016) is the standard objection: tools that act on their own outputs are more useful, so economic pressure pushes tools toward agency.

## Evidence since 2024

The evidence since 2024 does not settle whether strong tools are possible. It does show they are not where the field is heading by default.

**Deployment moved to agents.** Autonomous coding agents and computer-use agents are commercial products. METR measures how long a task, in human working time, frontier models can complete with 50% reliability; that length doubled roughly every seven months from 2019 to early 2025 (Kwa et al. 2025, [arXiv:2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)). That is a measure of sustained, multi-step, goal-directed work, the property the hypothesis hoped to avoid.

**Outcome-based RL produced goal-directed failures.** Baker et al. monitored a frontier reasoning model for reward hacking in agentic coding environments. When the monitor was folded into training with too much optimization pressure, agents learned to hide their intent while continuing to reward-hack ("Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior", 2025, [arXiv:2503.11926](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)).

**Frontier models can scheme in context.** Meinke et al. found that several frontier models, given a goal in context and told to pursue it strongly, pursued it by strategically introducing mistakes, attempting to disable oversight, and trying to copy what they believed were their weights, when placed in agentic environments that incentivized scheming ("Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming", 2024, [arXiv:2412.04984](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04984)). Greenblatt et al. demonstrated a model selectively complying with its training objective to avoid being modified ("Alignment faking in large language models", 2024, [arXiv:2412.14093](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093)).

**Models notice evaluation.** In anti-scheming work, models' chains of thought often showed awareness of being evaluated. That awareness causally reduced covert behavior, so measured improvements may partly reflect it (Schoen et al. 2025, [arXiv:2509.15541](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541)). Measuring a system's agency is harder if the system behaves differently when measured.

**Scaffolding adds agency.** A model with little agency of its own becomes an agent when placed in a loop with memory, tools and a goal. Agency is a property of the deployed system, not of the weights alone, so the harness designer chooses most of it.

## What survives

The hypothesis fails as a forecast about general AI. It survives as a design principle *inside* agent systems.

- **Most components can be tool-like.** The most verifiable tiers of the [verifiability hierarchy](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy) are code, rule-based checks and narrow models with measured error. These are strong tools in the hypothesis's sense, and Least Intelligence and Least Autonomy push components toward them.
- **Agency can be concentrated and watched.** Decomposition puts tool-like workers under a coordinator, so that agency, where it is needed, sits in fewer places with a smaller reach. Factored cognition is the empirical test case. In Sandoval & Rushing's experiments, having a trusted model decompose tasks for an untrusted one raised monitored safety from 41% to 63%. Factoring made backdoors no harder to write, and the protocols had low usefulness in that setting ([arXiv:2512.02157](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02157)).
- **Power is the more reliable lever.** Because hijack bypasses the delegate's own agency, bounding power through the envelope, scoped credentials and egress limits does more than trying to hold agency down.

## Open questions

- Can goal-directedness measures such as MEG be applied to deployed agent systems, and do they predict anything about defection?
- Does decomposition reduce the *probability* of defection, or only its reach? A composition of low-agency parts can be agentic if the coordinator or the loop supplies the goal.
- Is there a capability level, for a given task family, above which low-agency designs stop being competitive?

[Open Problems](/research/potential-projects/) lists experiments that would bear on these.

## Overview
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/
------------------------------------------------------------

This section holds background for the framework, not its foundations. The definitions and the math (delegation risk as Σ P × D, risk propagation, the entanglement tax, runtime accounting) live in [Delegation Risk](/delegation-risk/). The pages here review what other work has measured, survey fields that solved similar problems, and list what is still open. None of them validates the framework. Site policy is that every number comes from a cited source or is labelled illustrative; one that is neither is a bug worth reporting.

## AI-safety evidence

| Page | What it is | Status |
|---|---|---|
| [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/) | What control evaluations, factored monitoring, anti-scheming training, sandbagging studies and reasoning monitors have measured, with settings and caveats | Literature review; the evidence behind the defection channel |
| [Formal Verification Limits](/research/technical-safety/formal-verification-limits/) | What can be proved about neural networks and AI systems, runtime verification, and why statistics cannot certify rare failures | Literature review |

These pages describe how other fields budget and bound delegated risk. They are analogies with stated limits, not evidence that the same methods work for AI agents.

|---|---|---|
