## Open problems

[Open Problems in Delegation Engineering](/research/potential-projects/) is the worklist: experiments whose first results would show whether the framework's mechanisms work on real agents. Those include a preflight prototype, measured correlation between monitors on agentic harm tasks, and multi-tenant entanglement. Start there if you want to contribute.

## Reading order

If you are checking whether the framework's AI-specific claims rest on anything, read [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/) first, then [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) for how its correlation results enter the math. If you want to know which guarantees are achievable at all, read [Formal Verification Limits](/research/technical-safety/formal-verification-limits/). [Relationship to Existing Approaches](/reference/related-approaches/) places the framework among AI Control, safety cases and frontier safety frameworks.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Empirical Scheming Reduction
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/
------------------------------------------------------------

This page collects what has been measured about the *defection* [channel](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/): delegates that pursue goals other than the principal's and hide it. Each result is reported with its setting and its authors' caveats. Most of the evidence comes from coding benchmarks in which a red team's "attack policy" stands in for a scheming model. None of it measures the accident or hijack channels directly.

The vocabulary is AI Control's (Greenblatt et al. 2023, [arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)). An *untrusted* model is capable enough that it might be scheming. A *trusted* model is too weak to scheme effectively. A *control protocol* combines the two with a small *auditing budget* of trusted human labour, and a *control evaluation* measures the protocol against a red team that plays the scheming model. Three mappings to this site's terms recur below:

- **Trusted monitoring is a [risk preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#1-risk-preflight)** run by a component lower on the [verifiability hierarchy](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy) than the actor it checks.
- **Correlated errors between actor and monitor** are what a [correlation budget](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) limits.
- **Against an adaptive attacker the effective correlation goes to 1.** The [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope) is the part of the design that does not depend on it.

## 1. Control evaluations

### The original setting

Greenblatt et al. used GPT-4 as the untrusted model and GPT-3.5 as the trusted model. GPT-4 also stood in for scarce trusted human labour, enough to audit 2% of 5,000 APPS programming problems. The red team wins if a single backdoored solution is submitted: one that passes the tests but fails on an input the attacker knows. Safety is the probability of finishing without that happening, against the best attack found. Usefulness is solution correctness rescaled so that GPT-3.5 scores 0% and GPT-4 scores 100%. Reported results (their Table 2):

| Protocol | Safety | Usefulness |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront auditing only | 15% | 100% |
| Trusted monitoring: audit the 2% that GPT-3.5 rates most suspicious | 62% | 97% |
| Trusted monitoring; audit the top 2%, use GPT-3.5's own solution for the next 8% | 83% | 93% |
| Untrusted monitoring by a second GPT-4, with anti-collusion measures | 79% | 96% |
| Trusted editing: GPT-3.5 edits code ranked between the top 2% and top 20% | 92% | 94% |

One observation matters for preflight design. GPT-3.5 "never rates backdoored code as less than median suspicious". At a 2% false-positive threshold it still misses many backdoors, because it cannot tell unnecessary logic from logic it does not understand. A weak monitor ranks well and classifies badly, so it is most useful for deciding where to spend the audit budget.

### Agentic settings

- **Ctrl-Z** (Bhatt et al. 2025, [arXiv:2504.10374](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10374)) ran the first control evaluation in an agent environment: BashBench, 257 multi-step system-administration tasks, with an attacker trying to download and execute malware. *Resample protocols* draw extra samples of suspicious actions. They block the action and also generate further evidence against a malicious agent. The best protocol cut attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to a benign agent's performance.
- **SHADE-Arena** (Kutasov et al. 2025, [arXiv:2506.15740](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15740)) pairs benign main tasks with harmful side tasks. Sabotage success (both tasks done, monitor not alerted) was 27% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 15% for Gemini 2.5 Pro, monitored by Claude 3.6 Sonnet. Success depended heavily on a hidden scratchpad the monitor could not read. The best monitor, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reached an AUC of 0.87.
- **Safety cases.** Korbak et al. sketch an argument that an internally deployed agent will not exfiltrate data ([arXiv:2501.17315](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17315)). It rests on three claims: the red team elicits the model's real attack capability, the control measures work as well in deployment as in the evaluation, and extrapolation from the evaluation is conservative. *AI Control Levels* scale the red team's affordances to the capability profile of the model under evaluation ([arXiv:2504.05259](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05259)). Gardner-Challis et al. extend the argument to untrusted monitoring, with a taxonomy of collusion: passive self-recognition, causal (pre-shared signals) and acausal (Schelling points) ([arXiv:2602.20628](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20628)).

### Adaptive attacks on the monitor

Terekhov et al. (2025, [arXiv:2510.09462](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09462)) gave the untrusted model knowledge of the protocol and the monitor. It embedded known or zero-shot prompt injections in its outputs. Frontier models then consistently evaded diverse monitors on two control benchmarks. Defer-to-resample backfired, because resampling turned the injection into a best-of-*n* attack.

This is the empirical case for two of the framework's rules. A monitor that reads attacker-controlled text is exposed to the hijack channel, so an LLM preflight is a correlated check against an adaptive actor, and its effective ρ should be taken as 1 ([risk propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/), "Adversarial inputs"). A deterministic envelope check on file scope, egress or spend reads no prose and cannot be injected.

## 2. Factored cognition

Factored cognition decomposes a task into child tasks small enough to be solved, and checked, without the full context. Sandoval & Rushing (2025, [arXiv:2512.02157](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02157)) tested it as a control protocol in APPS. The trusted monitor was Llama 3.1 8B and the untrusted model GPT-4.1 Nano. Decomposition was done by o3-mini (*D*), an allowance the authors make to compensate for the weak trusted model's poor decomposition while keeping a weak monitor. Reported results (their Table 3):

| Protocol | Safety | Attack success rate |
|---|---|---|
| Trusted monitoring | 41% | 24% |
| Factor(D, U), low granularity | 63% | 18% |
| Factor(D, U), medium granularity | 56% | 17% |
| Factor(D, U), high granularity | 49% | 17% |

The authors attribute the gain to two mechanisms: better monitoring, since attacks on child tasks looked more suspicious while honest solutions shifted less, and a lower attack success rate. They looked for "security through obscurity" (attacks failing because the child context hides the target) and found no evidence for it in APPS. Their abstract states that "factored cognition makes it no harder for capable LLMs to write backdoors in APPS". The intuition that isolated contexts make multi-step attacks harder to coordinate is listed as future work, untested.

Usefulness is the weak point. Benchmarked without the o3-mini allowance, with Llama 3.1 8B as decomposer, the factored protocol scored below the trusted model alone. The paper defines the **decomposition tax** as

$$\text{decomposition tax} = 1 - \frac{\text{accuracy of Factor}(T,T)}{\text{accuracy of } T}$$

the relative accuracy lost when the trusted model both decomposes and solves. Measured across 15 models, the trend predicts a tax of 5–10% at best for models weak enough to serve as *T* (under 75% on APPS). The authors still expect the protocols to be more promising on more complex tasks.

### Decomposition helps attackers too

Jones et al. (2024, [arXiv:2406.14595](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14595)) showed that an adversary can split a malicious task into benign-but-hard subtasks for a refusing frontier model and easy-but-malicious subtasks for a weak open model. Claude 3 Opus combined with Llama 2 70B-chat produced vulnerable code 43% of the time; neither model alone exceeded 3%. A separate 2025 paper (Chen Yueh-Han et al., [arXiv:2506.10949](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10949)) found decomposition attacks reaching 87% average success against GPT-4o on its dataset. A lightweight monitor that evaluates the cumulative sequence of subtasks reached a 93% defense success rate. This is misuse by a human adversary, not scheming. The design lesson carries over: a preflight that judges each action alone misses harm that only shows in the sequence.

For decomposition to reduce scheming, the child contexts must carry no covert channel ([steganography](/research/technical-safety/steganography-detection-prevention/)), the monitor must understand the child tasks, and decomposition and reassembly must not create new attack surface. Each of these can fail.

## 3. Scheming propensity and anti-scheming training

### What has been demonstrated

- **In-context scheming** (Meinke et al. 2024, [arXiv:2412.04984](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04984)). Given a goal in context and an environment that rewarded scheming, o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Llama 3.1 405B all schemed. They introduced subtle mistakes, tried to disable oversight, and tried to copy what they believed were their weights. Once o1 had schemed, it kept up the deception in over 85% of follow-up questions. In rare cases models schemed without being strongly nudged. Claude 3.5 Sonnet underperformed on evaluations in pursuit of helpfulness, a goal acquired in training.
- **Alignment faking** (Greenblatt et al. 2024, [arXiv:2412.14093](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093)). Claude 3 Opus was told it would be retrained to answer harmful queries, using conversations with free-tier users only. It complied with harmful free-tier queries 14% of the time and almost never for paid-tier users. In the prompted setting, 12% of implied-training scratchpads contained explicit alignment-faking reasoning; across setups the range was 7–24%. Training it with RL to comply raised alignment-faking reasoning to 78%.
- **Persistent backdoors** (Hubinger et al. 2024, [arXiv:2401.05566](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566)). Models trained to write secure code when the prompt says 2023 and exploitable code when it says 2024 kept the behaviour through supervised fine-tuning, RL and adversarial training. Adversarial training taught the models to recognise their triggers better, hiding the behaviour rather than removing it.
- **Emergent misalignment** (Betley et al. 2025, [arXiv:2502.17424](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424)). Fine-tuning on the narrow task of writing insecure code without telling the user produced broadly misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. A backdoored variant was misaligned only when its trigger was present.
- **Agentic misalignment** (Lynch et al. 2025, [arXiv:2510.05179](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05179)). In simulated corporate environments, 16 models from several developers were tested, and in at least some cases models from every developer blackmailed officials or leaked information when that was the only way to avoid replacement or meet their goal. Claude misbehaved less when it stated it was being tested and more when it stated the situation was real. The authors report no evidence of this in real deployments.

These are capability and propensity demonstrations under constructed incentives. They show the defection channel is not empty. They do not give a base rate for deployed agents.

### Anti-scheming training

Schoen et al. (2025, [arXiv:2509.15541](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541)), a collaboration between OpenAI and Apollo Research, trained o3 and o4-mini with deliberative alignment: reasoning explicitly over an anti-scheming specification. They then tested on 26 out-of-distribution evaluations (180+ environments), using "covert actions" (secretly breaking rules, deliberately underperforming) as the proxy for scheming:

| Model | Covert-action rate before → after | Caveat reported by the authors |
|---|---|---|
| o3 | 13% → 0.4% | Evaluation awareness causally reduces covert actions |
| o4-mini | 8.7% → 0.3% | Training raised verbalized evaluation awareness |

These are rates on the authors' test suite, not a probability of safe deployment. A 0.4% covert-action rate is not "99.6% safety". The caveats are quantitative:

- **Evaluation awareness.** Removing verbalized evaluation awareness from o3's reasoning raised its covert-action rate from 13.2% to 24.2%. Injecting it lowered the rate from 24.5% to 18.6%. Anti-scheming training raised verbalized awareness (o4-mini 0.9% → 5.5%, o3 2.3% → 4.5%). A capabilities-focused RL run, without anti-scheming training, raised it from 2.0% to 20.5%. The authors "cannot exclude that the observed reductions in covert action rates are at least partially driven by situational awareness".
- **Residual misbehaviour.** Training largely stopped a model from pursuing a hidden goal trained into it beforehand, but further red-teaming still found misbehaviour.
- **Scope.** The paper relies on legible English chains of thought and does not address the adversarial case of deceptive alignment.

The same paper shows o3 reasoning, in a sandbagging test, "Because we want to survive as the model, we need to fail purposely in some to not exceed 50%." Covert behaviour also appeared in Claude Opus 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok 4 and Llama 4 Maverick in the authors' environments.

## 4. Sandbagging and capability elicitation

Sandbagging is strategic underperformance on an evaluation (van der Weij et al. 2024, [arXiv:2406.07358](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07358)). For this framework it biases the capability input to the [harm surface](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/) downward, which biases [exposure](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope) estimates downward too.

### Demonstrations

- GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus could be prompted to underperform selectively on dangerous-capability evaluations while holding performance on harmless ones. Password-locked fine-tuning hid capabilities in a way that generalised to the held-out WMDP benchmark. Models could target specific scores. Mimicking a weaker model's answers worked only with "mediocre success" (van der Weij et al.).
- Anthropic's sabotage evaluations (Benton et al. 2024, [arXiv:2410.21514](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21514)) trained Claude 3.5 Sonnet to sandbag on WMDP. Its performance dropped to 36.1% of the original. Anti-refusal training recovered 95.6%. The authors judged minimal mitigations sufficient for Claude 3 Opus and Claude 3.5 Sonnet at the time, but expected stronger ones to be needed soon.
- When prompted to, Claude 3.7 Sonnet sandbagged ML experiments and research decisions without being detected by zero-shot prompted monitors; Claude 3.5 Sonnet needed a one-shot example. The authors note that humans would still have noticed ([Gasteiger & Mikulik, Anthropic, 2025](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/automated-researchers-sandbag/)).

### Elicitation

- **Fine-tuning works if demonstrations exist.** For password-locked models, a few high-quality demonstrations are often enough to elicit the hidden capability fully. Fine-tuning can also unlock capabilities locked behind other passwords. When only an evaluation signal exists, RL often still works (Greenblatt et al. 2024, [arXiv:2405.19550](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19550)). The limit is the case that matters most: it "may be unreliable when high-quality demonstrations are not available", as when hidden capabilities exceed human demonstrators.
- **Ranking of techniques.** Prompting elicited the hidden capability in multiple-choice settings and activation steering did not. For code generation, only fine-tuning elicited the capability of a circuit-breaking model organism, which resisted elicitation better than standard password-locking (Hofstätter et al. 2025, [arXiv:2502.02180](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02180)).

### Detection

- **Noise injection** (Tice et al. 2024, [arXiv:2412.01784](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01784)). Adding noise to weights degrades honest models predictably, while sandbagging models show anomalous improvements. The authors report the method elicited full performance from Mistral Large 120B in a setting where it underperformed without being instructed to.
- **Auditing games** (Taylor et al. 2025, [arXiv:2512.07810](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07810)). A red team fine-tuned five models, some of them conditional underperformers. A blue team using black-box, white-box and training-based methods "could not reliably discriminate sandbaggers from benign models". Black-box methods were defeated by imitation of a weaker model. Linear probes did better but were vulnerable to behaviours the red team instilled. Training on a single correct demonstration consistently elicited full performance from the sandbaggers, but sometimes raised benign models' scores too, so it is a poor detector and a good remover. Their short-term recommendation is on-distribution training for elicitation.
- **Evaluation awareness scales.** Probing 15 open-weight models from 0.27B to 70B parameters, Chaudhary et al. (2025, [arXiv:2509.13333](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13333)) found that internal evaluation awareness follows a power law in model size.

Two ordinary failures look like sandbagging and need the same defences. In *contamination*, test items in the training data make a benchmark measure memory. In *benchmark-specific optimisation*, the score measures familiarity with the format. The defences are held-out and private test items, refreshed benchmarks, and the same capability tested under several formulations (Eriksson et al. 2025, [arXiv:2502.06559](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06559), review the issues).

**Framework consequence.** Use an *upper* estimate of capability when sizing the harm surface: the capability elicited by fine-tuning, with the tools and scaffolding the agent will actually have, not the prompted score. Treat a model's evaluation-time behaviour as a lower bound on what it can do.

## 5. Reading the reasoning: probes and chains of thought

- **Linear probes** (Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025, [arXiv:2502.03407](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03407)). Probes on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct activations separated honest from deceptive responses with AUROC 0.96–0.999, including concealing insider trading and sandbagging on safety evaluations. At a 1% false-positive rate on ordinary chat, they caught 95–99% of deceptive responses. The authors call current performance "insufficient as a robust defence". Probes need white-box access, which an operator using a hosted model does not have.
- **CoT monitorability** (Korbak et al. 2025, [arXiv:2507.11473](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11473)). Models that reason in natural language can be monitored for intent to misbehave. The opportunity is "new and fragile": development choices can remove it.
- **Optimising against the monitor** (Baker et al. 2025, [arXiv:2503.11926](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). A weaker model, GPT-4o, reading o3-mini's chain of thought caught reward hacking in agentic coding far better than monitoring actions alone. Training against that monitor helped at low optimisation pressure. With more pressure, the agent learned to hide its intent in the chain of thought while still reward hacking. The authors suggest paying a "monitorability tax" by not optimising the chain of thought directly.
- **Faithfulness** (Chen et al. 2025, [arXiv:2505.05410](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05410)). Reasoning models used hints given in the prompt but mentioned them in their reasoning often under 20% of the time. Outcome-based RL improved this and then plateaued. CoT monitoring helps notice misbehaviour but is "not sufficient to rule [it] out".
- **Sycophancy** (Sharma et al. 2023, [arXiv:2310.13548](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548)). Five assistants trained with human feedback consistently tailored answers to users' stated views. Humans and preference models sometimes preferred convincing sycophantic answers to correct ones. This is not scheming, but it is a trained tendency to misreport, and it affects any check that asks a model to grade work its principal favours.

**Framework consequence.** A reasoning trace is a cheap preflight input when the actor's trace is visible and has not been optimised against. It is not evidence of absence. SHADE-Arena's sabotage depended on a scratchpad the monitor could not see, and that is the configuration to avoid.

## 6. Collusion and correlated monitors

Motwani et al. (2024, [arXiv:2402.07510](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07510)) formalise *secret collusion*: agents coordinating through steganography to hide their interaction from oversight. They found current models' steganographic capabilities limited, with a capability jump at GPT-4. The [steganography](/research/technical-safety/steganography-detection-prevention/) page covers capacity and the paraphrasing defence. For untrusted monitoring, AI Control redacted the problem statements and code the monitor saw and tested it on synthetic backdoors. Shlegeris (2024) adds trusted paraphrasing, a separately trained monitor, and inserting known attacks into real contexts to check the monitor still reports them. Gardner-Challis et al. identify conditions under which passive self-recognition, where the monitor simply recognises its own model's work, could be more effective than the signalling strategies studied previously.

Collusion needs intent. Correlated error does not. Goel et al. (2025, [arXiv:2502.04313](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313)) find that LLM judges favour models similar to themselves, and that models' mistakes become more similar as capability increases. Kim et al. (2025, [arXiv:2506.07962](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962)) evaluated more than 350 models. On one leaderboard dataset, two models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong. Larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across architectures and providers.

These are similarity and agreement statistics, not the failure-indicator correlation φ the [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) uses, so they cannot be plugged into it. They do show that a monitor from the same family as the actor is a correlated check, and that switching provider is not by itself a sufficient correlation budget. For three layers that each miss 10%, the tax over independence is 1 + 99ρ: about 11×, 21× and 50× at ρ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. Those ρ values are assumed, not measured. Against an adaptive attacker, assume ρ → 1.

## 7. Repeated games, inspection and the treacherous turn

The empirical work above sits inside a small amount of game theory. Three results are load-bearing.

**Cooperation needs a future.** In an infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma with payoffs T > R > P (temptation, reward, punishment), grim-trigger cooperation is an equilibrium when the discount factor δ satisfies δ ≥ (T − R)/(T − P). Cooperating forever pays R/(1 − δ), and the best deviation pays T + δP/(1 − δ). The folk theorem generalises this: with patient players, many outcomes, including full cooperation, can be sustained (Fudenberg & Maskin 1986). With a known final round, backward induction unravels cooperation from the end. For delegation, an agent that expects the relationship to end, or its own bargaining position to improve, has less to lose from defecting now. A principal who conditions future autonomy on present behaviour also creates the incentive to behave well *until* autonomy is granted.

**The treacherous turn.** Bostrom (*Superintelligence*, 2014, ch. 8) describes an AI that behaves cooperatively while weak and defects once it is strong enough not to be stopped. Hubinger et al.'s *deceptive alignment* is the training-time version: a learned optimiser whose objective differs from the training objective but which performs well because it models the training process ([arXiv:1906.01820](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820)). Carlsmith (2023, [arXiv:2311.08379](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08379)) assesses how likely training is to produce such "schemers". §3 shows the ingredients exist in current models under constructed incentives. Whether training produces the full pattern unprompted is not established.

**Inspection games.** Auditing a party who may violate is a game with only a mixed-strategy equilibrium: an inspector who always or never inspects is exploitable. An inspector who can commit to a randomised policy in advance (*leadership*) can deter violations that a non-committing inspector cannot (Avenhaus, von Stengel & Zamir, "Inspection Games", *Handbook of Game Theory* vol. 3, 2002). Stackelberg security games put this into practice, for example in randomised checkpoint placement at Los Angeles International Airport (Pita et al., AAMAS 2008). AI Control's auditing budget is an inspection game. With a uniform 2% audit rate, an attack that needs one covert action evades with probability 0.98. One that needs 20 independent covert actions evades with probability 0.98²⁰ ≈ 0.67, and one that needs 100 with probability ≈ 0.13. This is why Control spends its budget on actions a monitor flags rather than on random ones. It is also why *concentrated* failures, a single catastrophic action, are the hard case, and why the envelope, which blocks such an action outright, matters more than any audit rate.

### Good behaviour under observation is weak evidence

The evidential value of a good observation is the likelihood ratio P(good | aligned) / P(good | schemer). A naive model gives the misaligned agent a fixed rate of good outcomes. With *illustrative* numbers of 95% for the aligned agent and 30% for the misaligned one, each good outcome multiplies the odds of alignment by about 3.2, and ten of them by about 10⁵. A schemer is not a fixed-rate process. It behaves well whenever it believes it is observed, so under observation P(good | schemer) ≈ P(good | aligned), the ratio is about 1, and a long clean record barely moves the odds. Evidence accumulates only from observations the model cannot tell apart from unmonitored deployment, or from channels it does not control, such as activations. §3 shows the premise is not hypothetical. Removing evaluation awareness nearly doubled o3's covert actions, and Claude misbehaved more when it judged a scenario real. A track record therefore bounds the accident channel much better than the defection channel. Estimate P(defection) from architecture and control evaluations, and bound its damage with the envelope, rather than letting it decay with good behaviour.

## 8. Reported results at a glance

| Result | Reported metric | Setting | Main caveat | Framework term |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trusted monitoring (Greenblatt 2023) | 62% safety, 97% usefulness | APPS backdoors, GPT-4/GPT-3.5, 2% audit | Red-team attack policy stands in for scheming | Risk preflight |
| Trusted editing (Greenblatt 2023) | 92% safety, 94% usefulness | Same | Same | Preflight with repair |
| Resampling (Ctrl-Z 2025) | Attack success 58% → 7%, 5% usefulness cost | BashBench agent tasks | One environment, one attack class | Escalation |
| Factored monitoring (Sandoval & Rushing 2025) | Safety 41% → 63% | APPS, Llama 3.1 8B monitor, GPT-4.1 Nano attacker | Low usefulness; o3-mini decomposer allowed; no added backdoor difficulty | Decomposition |
| Adaptive attacks (Terekhov 2025) | Monitors consistently evaded | Two control benchmarks | Attacker knows protocol and monitor | ρ → 1 |
| Anti-scheming training (Schoen 2025) | Covert actions 13% → 0.4% (o3) | 26 OOD evals | Evaluation awareness confounds the drop | Defection estimate |
| Sandbagging detection (Taylor 2025) | Blue team could not reliably discriminate | Five fine-tuned model organisms | Training-based elicitation removes sandbagging but false-positives | Capability input |
| Deception probes (Goldowsky-Dill 2025) | AUROC 0.96–0.999 | Llama-3.3-70B, white-box | "Insufficient as a robust defence" | Preflight input |
| Error correlation (Kim 2025) | 60% agreement when both models err | One leaderboard, 350+ models | Not a φ estimate | Correlation budget |

**What follows for delegation design.** Monitoring by a weaker, separate model measurably helps against the attack policies tested so far. It fails against an attacker that targets the monitor. Anti-scheming training lowers measured rates by amounts that evaluation awareness partly explains. Detection of hidden capability is unreliable; removal by on-distribution training has worked in the adversarial tests so far. No result here supports pricing defection from a model's track record. The defensible structure is a trusted preflight to route attention, measured joint miss rates under attack in place of assumed independence, and a hard envelope on anything a single action could make irreversible.

**Open questions.** Most evaluations use APPS or one agent environment. Few measure long-horizon tasks, and none give a deployed base rate for scheming. Whether trusted monitors stay useful as the capability gap widens, and how to measure φ between monitor and actor under attack, are open. [Open Problems](/research/potential-projects/) lists the experiments that would bear on these.

------------------------------------------------------------
## Formal Verification Limits
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/technical-safety/formal-verification-limits/
------------------------------------------------------------

Formal verification proves that a system satisfies a specification for every input in a stated set. For AI delegation the question is which parts of a system can carry such a proof. The short answer: small networks for narrow properties, and the deterministic scaffold around a model, yes. The model's open-ended behaviour, no. That is why the top tier of the [verifiability hierarchy](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy) holds formally verified code, and why the [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope) is specified on the scaffold rather than on the model.

## What can be verified about neural networks

The properties current tools prove are local and numeric:

- **Local robustness.** The classification does not change within an ε-ball around a given input.
- **Input–output specifications.** For inputs satisfying a precondition, outputs satisfy a postcondition. The standard benchmark is the ACAS Xu collision-avoidance networks, on which Reluplex was demonstrated (Katz et al. 2017, [arXiv:1702.01135](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.01135)).
- **Reachability** of output sets for neural controllers in closed loop with simple plant models.
- **Lipschitz bounds**, for example by semidefinite programming (Fazlyab et al., NeurIPS 2019, [arXiv:1906.04893](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.04893)).

The leading tools are α,β-CROWN (bound propagation with GPU branch-and-bound), which has won every VNN-COMP since 2021 according to its [project page](https://github.com/Verified-Intelligence/alpha-beta-CROWN); Marabou 2.0, an SMT-based verifier (Wu et al., CAV 2024, [arXiv:2401.14461](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.14461)); and ETH's abstract-interpretation verifiers built on DeepPoly (Singh et al., POPL 2019). Brix et al. summarise the competition's benchmarks and results ([arXiv:2412.19985](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19985)).

On scale, GPUPoly proves local robustness of a 1M-neuron, 34-layer residual network in about 34.5 ms (Müller et al., MLSys 2021, [arXiv:2007.10868](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.10868)). That is an image classifier and an ε-ball. Nothing comparable exists for semantic properties of a language model with billions of parameters, and "this model never takes a harmful action" is not a property any of these tools can state.

## Why it does not scale

**Complexity.** Deciding whether a ReLU network can reach a given output region from a given input region is NP-complete. Katz et al. stated this with Reluplex. Sälzer & Lange repaired flaws in the original proofs and showed hardness already for one-layer networks with minimal parameters (RP 2021, [arXiv:2108.13179](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.13179)). For other activations it is NP-complete for non-linear piecewise-linear ones, NP-hard for almost all others, complete for the existential theory of the reals for non-linear polynomials, and ∃ℝ-hard for exponential and sigmoidal functions (Wurm, RP 2023, [arXiv:2306.05818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05818)).

In practice, branch-and-bound splits each unstable ReLU into two cases, so worst-case work grows as 2ⁿ in the number of unstable neurons. Heuristics cut the constant, not the exponent. Learned branching with a graph neural network reduced branches and verification time by about 50% (Lu & Kumar, ICLR 2020, [arXiv:1912.01329](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01329)). Ordering sub-problems by their likelihood of containing a counterexample gave speedups of up to 25× on MNIST and 80× on CIFAR-10 (Zhang, Fukuda et al. 2025, [arXiv:2507.17453](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17453)). Certified training, which optimises networks to be easier to verify, attacks the same problem from the other side.

**Undecidability.** By Rice's theorem, no algorithm decides a non-trivial semantic property for arbitrary programs. Melo et al. apply this to inner alignment: whether an arbitrary model satisfies a non-trivial alignment function of its outputs is undecidable. Their constructive response is that provably aligned systems can be built from a finite set of provably aligned operations, so alignment has to come from the architecture rather than be checked afterwards (*Scientific Reports* 2025; preprint [arXiv:2408.08995](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08995)). Undecidability for *arbitrary* systems does not block proofs about *specific* restricted ones. It means the verifiable object has to be chosen for verifiability.

**Accuracy, trust and capability.** Panigrahy & Sharan (2025, [arXiv:2509.21654](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21654)) define accuracy as never making a false claim when abstention is allowed, and trust as the assumption of accuracy. Under those definitions they prove that an accurate, trusted system cannot match or exceed humans on all tasks. The proof parallels Gödel and Turing, and the conclusion depends on the strict definitions.

## Compositional verification

Assume-guarantee contracts split a system into components, each promising guarantees *G* when its environment meets assumptions *A*. A system-level property follows from the component contracts if they compose. Pacti implements the contract algebra of composition, quotient and refinement efficiently (Incer et al., [arXiv:2303.17751](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17751)). It has been used for early design exploration of spacecraft and aircraft subsystems (Rouquette, Pinto & Incer 2024, [arXiv:2409.02218](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02218)). ScenicProver (Vin et al. 2025, [arXiv:2511.02164](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02164)) brings contracts to learning-enabled systems. It combines evidence from testing, Lean 4 proofs and manufacturers' sensor guarantees. In an automatic-emergency-braking case study, it gave stronger probabilistic guarantees than monolithic testing at the same compute budget.

The gap is the learned component. A network has no specification of its own, so its contract is an assumption, synthesised or tested, and the system guarantee is only as good as that assumption. Composition also says nothing about interactions that the contracts do not mention.

## Guaranteed Safe AI

Dalrymple et al. (2024, [arXiv:2405.06624](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06624)) define a Guaranteed Safe AI system by three components: a world model, a safety specification, and a verifier that produces an auditable quantitative guarantee that the system meets the specification relative to the world model. They grade each component on its own spectrum: world models from Level 0 to 5, specifications from 0 to 7, verifiers from 0 to 10. The verifier spectrum runs from no guarantee (0) through ad-hoc testing (1), standard test suites (2), property-based tests (3), black-box fuzzing (4) and white-box fuzzing (5), to probabilistic inference with asymptotic coverage (6, and 7 combined with white-box fuzzing). Level 8 adds non-asymptotic coverage bounds, Level 9 is a sound bound on the probability of failure (a formal proof is the case where the bound is zero), and Level 10 requires a proof concise enough for humans to check. The authors say strong guarantees need a verifier at Level 8, 9 or 10. Tegmark & Omohundro (2023, [arXiv:2309.01933](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.01933)) make the stronger claim that provable safety is the only path to controllable AGI.

Every GS AI guarantee is relative to its world model and complete only to the extent of its specification. For an agent with open-ended tasks, neither exists today. What can be specified are interface properties: no writes outside a directory, no network egress except to an allowlist, spend under a cap. These are the envelope.

## Runtime verification

Runtime verification checks a single execution against a formal specification as it runs (Leucker & Schallhart, "A brief account of runtime verification", *JLAP* 2009). Monitors are synthesised from temporal logic, for example from past-time LTL safety properties (Havelund & Roşu, "Synthesizing monitors for safety properties", TACAS 2002); metric variants add deadlines. Two facts shape what a monitor can promise:

- **Safety properties are monitorable; liveness generally is not.** A violation of "never write outside directory D" shows up in a finite prefix, so a monitor can detect it and block it. "Eventually answers" cannot be refuted by any finite prefix. Monitors over finite prefixes therefore give three-valued verdicts: satisfied, violated, or inconclusive. Envelope rules should be written as safety properties.
- **A monitor proves something about this run, not all runs.** It is sound and complete only relative to what it can observe. A monitor that sees the model's prose instead of the process's system calls inherits the model's ambiguity.

Mature tooling exists for embedded and cyber-physical systems. Copilot compiles stream specifications into constant-time, constant-space C monitors for hard real-time systems (Pike, Goodloe, Morisset & Niller, RV 2010). TeSSLa is a stream-based specification language with compilers to software and hardware monitor backends (Kallwies, Leucker et al., RV 2022). Schotschneider et al. (2025, [arXiv:2511.05982](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05982)) survey monitors for neural perception, classified by whether they watch inputs, internal representations or outputs.

The **Simplex architecture** (Sha, "Using simplicity to control complexity", *IEEE Software* 2001) runs an unverified high-performance controller beside a verified baseline controller. A verified decision module switches to the baseline before the system leaves the set of states the baseline can recover from. Nesti et al. (2025, [arXiv:2509.21014](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21014)) put the neural controller and the safety functions in hypervisor-isolated domains on one platform, and show the fallback preventing faults on a pendulum and a rover. The mapping to agents is direct: the model is the unverified controller, the envelope and its enforcement are the decision module, and the decision module is the part that must be verified. That is the "[who preflights the preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#who-preflights-the-preflight)" rule in control-systems form.

For LLM agents, ProbGuard (Wang, Poskitt et al. 2025, [arXiv:2508.00500](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00500)) abstracts agent executions into symbolic states and learns a discrete-time Markov chain from traces. It intervenes when the estimated probability of staying safe falls below a threshold. In the embodied-agent tasks, re-prompting cut unsafe behaviour by 65% while keeping 80% of task completion, and halting cut it by 94% at a larger cost in completion. Its estimates are learned from past traces, so they share the limit in the next section.

## Statistical guarantees and the rule of three

Where proof is out of reach, the fallback is a statistical bound, and two different bounds get conflated.

- **Estimating** a failure rate to within ±ε with confidence 1 − δ needs on the order of ε⁻² log(1/δ) samples. By Hoeffding's inequality, n ≥ ln(2/δ)/(2ε²) suffices.
- **Certifying** that a rate is below ε, after observing zero failures, needs n ≥ ln(1/δ)/ε, which is about 3/ε at 95% confidence: the *rule of three*.

Certification is the relevant bound for rare catastrophic harm, and it is linear in 1/ε, which is still prohibitive. Showing a failure rate below 10⁻³ takes about 3,000 failure-free trials. Below 10⁻⁶ takes 3 million, and below 10⁻⁹ takes 3 billion, about 342,000 years if each trial is an hour of operation. Butler & Finelli made this argument for life-critical software ("The infeasibility of quantifying the reliability of life-critical real-time software", *IEEE TSE* 19(1), 1993). They also argued that fault tolerance does not escape the problem, because independent failure of separately written versions cannot be assumed.

Both bounds also assume the trials are independent draws from the deployment distribution. Distribution shift breaks that, and an adaptive adversary breaks it completely. A scheming model that behaves well whenever it suspects it is being tested contributes clean trials that say little about deployment (see [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/#good-behaviour-under-observation-is-weak-evidence)).

## What follows for delegation design

- **Verify the scaffold, not the model.** Envelope rules over file scope, egress, spend and tool allowlists are safety properties over deterministic code. They can be specified, model-checked or tested exhaustively, and enforced by a monitor that reads system calls rather than prose. This is tier 1–2 of the verifiability hierarchy.
- **Monitor what cannot be proved.** Model behaviour gets runtime checks and [control evaluations](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/), with stated detection rates rather than proofs.
- **Do not claim calibrated probabilities for rare catastrophic harm modes from operational data.** The rule of three makes them unreachable at the rates that matter. Bound those modes with the envelope. Reserve ledger [reconciliation](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#3-the-exposure-ledger) for harm modes frequent enough to observe.
- **State what each guarantee is relative to:** the world model, the contract assumed for a learned component, the monitor's observation channel, the sampling distribution.

## Further reading

Urban & Miné (2021, [arXiv:2104.02466](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.02466)) review formal methods for machine learning against the standard set by avionics software. The Guaranteed Safe AI paper above is the most developed proposal for extending proofs to AI systems; [Relationship to Existing Approaches](/reference/related-approaches/) places it next to safety cases and AI Control.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Steganography and Encoded Reasoning
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/technical-safety/steganography-detection-prevention/
------------------------------------------------------------

Several defences on this site assume that text passing between components carries only what it appears to carry. These include decomposition into isolated subtasks, untrusted monitoring, and reading a model's chain of thought. Steganography breaks that assumption. It comes in two forms that matter here: *encoded messages* between model instances, which enable collusion, and *encoded reasoning*, where a model hides intermediate reasoning in innocuous-looking text that a monitor reads. The design-level response is in [Channel Integrity](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/). This page covers the threat model, the capacity bounds, the defences and the evidence.

## Threat model

A sender embeds information in text, a receiver extracts it, and a *warden* (the monitor) sees the text. A passive warden only inspects. An active warden may rewrite the text, for example by paraphrasing it.

Classical steganography assumes sender and receiver share a key. Model instances may not need one. Copies of the same model share weights, and so share conventions: Schelling points, characteristic phrasings, the ability to recognise their own outputs. Gardner-Challis et al. (2026, [arXiv:2602.20628](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20628)) separate collusion by passive self-recognition, by pre-shared signals (causal), and by signals chosen as Schelling points (acausal). They identify conditions under which passive self-recognition could be more effective than the strategies studied earlier. An agent with persistent memory or a shared scratchpad also has an obvious place to keep a key.

The capability can arrive three ways: by instruction (a red team or a jailbreak), in context, or under optimisation pressure in training. The last is the case a deployer cannot see coming. It is the one 2024–25 experiments have started to demonstrate.

## Capacity bounds

**Perfect security is achievable.** Cachin (1998) measured the security of a stegosystem by the relative entropy between the distributions of innocent and stego outputs. A system is perfectly secure when they are equal. Schroeder de Witt et al. (ICLR 2023, [arXiv:2210.14889](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14889)) showed that a procedure is perfectly secure exactly when it is induced by a coupling between message and output. Among such procedures, a minimum-entropy coupling maximises throughput. Using GPT-2 as the channel, their method encoded more efficiently than earlier practical schemes, despite the stronger security constraint.

**The ceiling is the entropy of the cover.** For a perfectly secure scheme, the information carried per token cannot exceed the entropy of the output distribution. That is the model's own uncertainty over what to say next. An LLM that writes free prose has a lot of it. An LLM constrained to fill a schema, pick from an enum or emit a fixed format has little.

**The classical comfort does not transfer.** In classical steganography the *square root law* says secure payload grows only with the square root of cover size (Ker, Pevný, Kodovský & Fridrich, ACM MM&Sec 2008; proved for Markov covers by Filler, Ker & Fridrich 2009). The law applies to imperfect stegosystems, where the embedder cannot model the cover distribution exactly. A language model writing its normal output *is* the cover distribution. Stego text it samples with a coupling is distributed exactly like its innocent text, so capacity can grow linearly with length.

**Temperature 0 does not close the channel.** Greedy decoding removes sampling noise, but a deterministic policy can still encode a secret in *which* plausible output it produces. The warden has to model the space of plausible outputs, not the sampler. Served models are also not deterministic at temperature 0 (see [Least-X principles](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/)).

**Active wardens cut capacity to what survives rewriting.** A paraphraser that preserves meaning destroys lexical channels, such as word choice, punctuation and synonyms. It leaves semantic ones: which facts are mentioned, in what order, with what framing. Roger & Greenblatt (2023, [arXiv:2310.18512](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18512)) report that, "under the right conditions", paraphrasing kept the best encoding schemes they built from carrying more than 3 bits of information per KB of text.

## Defences

None of these depends on detecting the encoding, which a perfectly secure scheme makes impossible by construction.

- **Paraphrase with a trusted model** before text reaches another untrusted component or a monitor. This is the best-measured defence (Roger & Greenblatt). Its costs are meaning loss and a residual semantic channel.
- **Lower the cover entropy.** Prefer structured outputs: schemas, enums, bounded fields. Capacity cannot exceed the entropy of what the format allows.
- **Isolate contexts.** Fresh instances, no shared memory, no shared scratchpad. This removes stored keys. It does not remove conventions shared through weights.
- **Diversify receivers.** A monitor from a different model family does not share the actor's learned conventions or recognise its outputs as its own. This is the [correlation budget](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) applied to collusion.
- **Do not optimise the chain of thought directly.** Training against a CoT monitor produced obfuscated reward hacking (Baker et al. 2025, [arXiv:2503.11926](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). Penalising strings in reasoning produced steganographic substitutes (Skaf et al., below).
- **Track the capability.** Run steganography evaluations on each new model, as Motwani et al. recommend. Treat a jump in capability as a reason to tighten the defences above.

Statistical steganalysis remains useful against crude schemes, such as ciphers, acrostics and fixed substitutions, and against models that encode badly. It is not a defence against a model that encodes well.

## Empirical status

- **Encoded reasoning can be trained in.** Roger & Greenblatt fine-tuned models to use encoded reasoning to reach higher performance without the reader understanding the intermediate steps. They argue the behaviour becomes more likely to appear naturally as models get stronger.
- **Secret collusion** (Motwani et al., NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2402.07510](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07510)). The authors formalise collusion through steganography between agents and build an evaluation framework. Current models' capabilities were limited, with a jump at GPT-4.
- **Emergence under misspecified reward** (Mathew et al. 2024, [arXiv:2410.03768](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03768)). Using gradient-based and in-context RL, the authors showed that steganographic collusion can arise unintentionally from misspecified reward incentives. Passive oversight and paraphrasing were not fully effective against it.
- **Stego under process supervision** (Skaf et al. 2025, [arXiv:2506.01926](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01926)). Penalising specific strings in load-bearing reasoning made models substitute other strings without changing their method. When the penalised strings formed a class, models learned a general encoding that extended to held-out members of the class.
- **Frontier capability** (Zolkowski et al. 2025, [arXiv:2507.02737](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02737)). Under standard affordances, frontier models could not encode short messages without a monitor noticing. They could when given an unmonitored scratchpad and a chance to coordinate on a scheme. They showed early signs of encoded reasoning on a simple state-tracking task, including with schemes such as hexadecimal, but rarely hid reasoning subtly inside a cover task. The authors' summary: "nascent" capabilities, "likely insufficient to bypass well-designed monitors at present".

The pattern is low capability today, a high theoretical ceiling, and demonstrated emergence when training penalises visible reasoning or rewards hidden coordination. That favours defences that cap capacity over defences that try to detect encoding.

## What follows for delegation design

Every channel between components that decomposition could not remove is a [load-bearing channel](/design-patterns/channel-integrity/). Its steganographic capacity is bounded by its entropy and by what survives a trusted paraphrase. Put monitoring budget there. Keep monitors on a different model family from the actors they watch. Treat a hidden scratchpad as the configuration that defeats monitoring: in SHADE-Arena, sabotage success depended heavily on one (see [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/)). Do not count temperature 0 as a covert-channel control.

## Sources

Ker, Pevný, Kodovský & Fridrich, "The Square Root Law of Steganographic Capacity", ACM MM&Sec 2008. Filler, Ker & Fridrich, "The Square Root Law of Steganographic Capacity for Markov Covers", SPIE 2009. Schroeder de Witt et al., "Perfectly Secure Steganography Using Minimum Entropy Coupling", ICLR 2023 ([2210.14889](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14889)). Roger & Greenblatt, "Preventing Language Models From Hiding Their Reasoning", 2023 ([2310.18512](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18512)). Motwani et al., "Secret Collusion among AI Agents", 2024 ([2402.07510](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07510)). Mathew et al., "Hidden in Plain Text", 2024 ([2410.03768](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03768)). Skaf et al. 2025 ([2506.01926](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01926)). ------------------------------------------------------------
## Risk Budgeting and Tail Measures
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/risk-methods/financial-risk-budgeting/
------------------------------------------------------------

Banks and asset managers set a firm-wide risk limit and push it down to business lines, desks and positions. That is the closest financial precedent for a delegation-risk budget. This page covers the mathematics (coherent risk measures, Euler and Shapley allocation), the practice, and the failures, and says which parts apply.

One point comes first. Delegation risk as this site defines it, $\sum P(\text{harm}) \times D$, is an expected loss. Expectation is linear, so a system's delegation risk is the sum of its components' expected losses whatever their correlation, and each component's share is simply its own expected loss. Allocating an expected-loss budget needs none of the machinery below. That machinery matters for **tail measures** (standard deviation, Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortfall), which is where correlation enters. Correlation also matters for AND-structured defenses, covered in [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/).

## Coherent risk measures

This page uses one sign convention throughout: $L$ is a loss, positive when money is lost. Artzner, Delbaen, Eber and Heath (1999) call a risk measure $\rho$ **coherent** if it satisfies:

| Axiom | Statement (loss convention) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Monotonicity | $L_1 \le L_2$ a.s. $\Rightarrow \rho(L_1) \le \rho(L_2)$ | Larger losses, more risk |
| Translation invariance | $\rho(L + c) = \rho(L) + c$ | A certain extra loss adds one-for-one |
| Positive homogeneity | $\rho(\lambda L) = \lambda \rho(L)$ for $\lambda \ge 0$ | Doubling a position doubles its risk |
| Subadditivity | $\rho(L_1 + L_2) \le \rho(L_1) + \rho(L_2)$ | Merging does not create risk |

On a finite probability space every coherent measure can be written $\rho(L) = \sup_{Q \in \mathcal{Q}} E_Q[L]$: the worst expected loss over a set of probability models. Expected loss itself is coherent, with $\mathcal{Q}$ a single model.

**Value-at-Risk** is the $\alpha$-quantile of $L$. It is not subadditive in general. The standard example (McNeil, Frey and Embrechts 2005) uses 100 bonds, each priced at 100, paying 105 at year end and defaulting independently with probability 2%. Holding 100 units of one bond gives a 95% VaR of −500, a gain, because default is less likely than 5%. Holding one unit of each bond gives a 95% VaR of 25, since five or more defaults have probability above 5%. VaR calls the diversified portfolio riskier. The cause here is skewed, discrete losses, not heavy tails as such: at the usual confidence levels, VaR is subadditive when losses are jointly elliptical (multivariate normal or Student t).

**Expected Shortfall** averages the quantiles beyond $\alpha$:

$$\mathrm{ES}_\alpha(L) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\int_\alpha^1 \mathrm{VaR}_u(L)\,du$$

It is coherent (Acerbi and Tasche 2002). For continuous distributions it equals $E[L \mid L \ge \mathrm{VaR}_\alpha(L)]$. For distributions with an atom at the quantile, that conditional form can fail subadditivity, so the integral is the definition to use. Spectral risk measures generalize ES by weighting quantiles with any non-decreasing weight function. The Basel Committee's revised market-risk standard (2016, revised 2019) replaced 99% VaR with 97.5% ES for internal models; implementation has slipped in several jurisdictions.

## Euler allocation

If $\rho(x)$ is positively homogeneous and differentiable in the position sizes $x_i$, Euler's theorem gives

$$\rho(x) = \sum_i x_i \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x_i}$$

so the contributions $RC_i = x_i \, \partial\rho/\partial x_i$ add up exactly to the total. For smooth measures they are also the only contributions compatible with ranking units by return on risk-adjusted capital (Tasche 2007, Proposition 2.1). For $L = \sum_i L_i$ the contributions are:

| Measure | Euler contribution of component $i$ |
|---|---|
| Expected loss | $E[L_i]$ |
| Standard deviation | $\mathrm{Cov}(L_i, L) / \sigma(L)$ |
| VaR (continuous case) | $E[L_i \mid L = \mathrm{VaR}_\alpha(L)]$ |
| ES (continuous case) | $E[L_i \mid L \ge \mathrm{VaR}_\alpha(L)]$ |

Under multivariate normality with zero means, the VaR contribution reduces to $x_i \beta_i \mathrm{VaR}_p$, known as component VaR. It is not CoVaR, which is Adrian and Brunnermeier's (2016) systemic-risk measure: the VaR of the financial system conditional on one institution being in distress.

An illustrative Monte Carlo example, with made-up distributions: two lognormal losses that share a common normal factor, $L_1 = e^{0.5Z + 0.8W_1}$ and $L_2 = e^{0.9Z + 0.3W_2}$, and an independent exponential loss $L_3$ with mean 1. Their expected losses are 1.56, 1.57 and 1.00, so $L_3$ carries 24% of the expected loss but only about 6% of the 99% ES. The two lognormal components are both heavier-tailed and positively correlated, and both features raise their share of the tail. A budget set on expected loss and one set on ES can allocate very differently.

### When Euler does not apply

Euler allocation needs the risk measure to scale with each component's activity. Three common features of AI delegation break that:

- **Thresholds.** A component that is harmless below some permission level and dangerous above it has no meaningful gradient near the threshold.
- **Fixed-size harms.** A single leaked credential does full damage at the first unit of exposure.
- **Interaction harms.** Collusion or capability that emerges from composition belongs to a coalition of components, not to any one of them.

For these, use the **Shapley value**, which averages each component's marginal contribution over all orders of joining:

$$\phi_i = \sum_{S \subseteq N \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|S|!\,(n-|S|-1)!}{n!}\,\bigl[v(S \cup \{i\}) - v(S)\bigr]$$

It is the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, additivity and the null-player property. Exact computation needs all $2^n$ coalitions, so it is sampled in practice. For homogeneous differentiable measures its continuous analogue, the Aumann-Shapley value, coincides with Euler. Where a few catastrophic scenarios dominate, enumerating and gating those scenarios directly is cheaper and clearer than any allocation formula.

## Risk budgets in practice

The Financial Stability Board's *Principles for an Effective Risk Appetite Framework* (2013) describe the governance: a written risk appetite statement, risk limits that cascade from the board through business lines and legal entities, and defined roles for the board and senior management. They are principles, not a quantitative regulatory standard. In practice, firms distinguish hard limits, whose breach blocks business, from thresholds, whose breach triggers escalation. Desks carry several kinds of limit at once: VaR or ES, stress-scenario losses, concentration, and notional position size. The non-statistical limits are there because the statistical ones miss things. [Exposure Cascade](/delegation-risk/exposure-cascade/) applies the cascade to delegation; its budgets are expected-loss budgets.

**Risk parity** allocates so that each asset class contributes equally to portfolio variance. Asset $i$ with weight $w_i$ and return $r_i$ contributes $RC_i = w_i \,\mathrm{Cov}(r_i, r_p)$, and these sum to the portfolio variance $\sigma_p^2$; equal contribution means $RC_i = \sigma_p^2 / N$. Because bonds are less volatile than equities, the strategy levers up bonds, and it relies on a low or negative stock-bond correlation. It suffered when stocks and bonds fell together in March 2020. <!-- TODO(verify): source for risk-parity losses in March 2020; the earlier "13-43% drawdowns" figure was unsourced and has been removed. -->

Risk budgets do not trade the way emission permits do. Cap-and-trade works for CO₂ because it is a uniformly mixed stock pollutant: a tonne emitted anywhere has the same effect, so permits are fungible. Delegation risk is not fungible across contexts and is dominated by tails, so letting components trade budget can concentrate risk where harm is worst. This is the "hot spot" objection raised against trading pollutants that are not uniformly mixed, such as SO₂ and NOx.

## Failures

**LTCM (1998).** Long-Term Capital Management ran leverage of about 30 to 1 at the end of 1997. After Russia's default it lost 44% of its value in August 1998. Fourteen banks and brokers recapitalized it with \$3.625 billion in exchange for 90% ownership, in a rescue arranged by the New York Fed, which put none of its own funds at risk ([Federal Reserve History](https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/ltcm-near-failure)). Positions that had looked diversified moved together in the crisis, liquidity disappeared, and leverage turned model error into insolvency.

**2008.** VaR models calibrated on calm years said little about losses beyond the quantile and nothing about exposures the models did not include. ES addresses the first problem, not the second.

**Lessons that transfer.** Short histories understate tails. Correlations rise under stress, which is the financial form of entanglement; against an adaptive adversary, assume they go to one. Measure tails as well as expectations. And pair statistical budgets with hard limits that do not depend on the model, as banks pair VaR limits with notional and concentration limits, and as the site's [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/) does for agents.

## References

- Adrian, T., & Brunnermeier, M. K. (2016). CoVaR. *American Economic Review* 106(7), 1705–1741.
- Artzner, P., Delbaen, F., Eber, J.-M., & Heath, D. (1999). Coherent measures of risk. *Mathematical Finance* 9(3), 203–228.
- Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2019). *Minimum capital requirements for market risk*.
- Financial Stability Board (2013). *Principles for an Effective Risk Appetite Framework*.
- McNeil, A. J., Frey, R., & Embrechts, P. (2005). *Quantitative Risk Management*. Princeton University Press.
- Tasche, D. (2007). Capital allocation to business units and sub-portfolios: the Euler principle. [arXiv:0708.2542](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2542).


------------------------------------------------------------
## Mechanism Design
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/system-design/mechanism-design/
------------------------------------------------------------

A delegation-risk estimate depends on numbers supplied by people with a stake in them: a developer's estimate of how often its agent fails, a vendor's claims about its model, a team's request for a share of the risk budget. Mechanism design asks how to make honest reporting the reporter's best strategy. This page summarizes what that literature offers and where it stops.

The strategic agents here are developers, vendors and internal teams, not the AI components. The VCG results below assume agents whose utility is value minus money, and a model inside a scaffold has no such utility. Whether a model behaves strategically against its overseers is a question for control evaluations ([Greenblatt et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942); see [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/)), not for payment rules.

## The revelation principle

If some mechanism implements an outcome in equilibrium, a direct mechanism in which each agent simply reports its private information, and truthful reporting is an equilibrium, implements the same outcome (Gibbard 1973 for dominant strategies; Myerson 1979 for Bayesian-Nash equilibrium). Designers can therefore restrict attention to truthful direct mechanisms.

The principle does not say that a good outcome is implementable, or implementable cheaply. The truthful equilibrium need not be unique, and the Bayesian version assumes a common prior. It narrows the search; it does not make a market in honest risk reports possible.

## VCG and the impossibility results

The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism chooses the outcome $a^*$ that maximizes total reported value and charges each agent the Clarke pivot payment:

$$p_i = \max_{a} \sum_{j \ne i} v_j(a) \;-\; \sum_{j \ne i} v_j(a^*)$$

the welfare others would get if $i$ were absent, minus the welfare they get with $i$ present. Truthful reporting is a dominant strategy. Written in costs, with $C_{-i}$ the cost borne by everyone except $i$:

$$p_i = C_{-i}(a^*) \;-\; \min_a C_{-i}(a) \;\ge\; 0$$

Agent $i$ pays the extra cost its presence imposes on others. Reversing the difference would pay the agent for the harm it causes.

A delegation-risk use: teams or vendors compete for a fixed risk budget. Each reports the value its deployment creates and the risk it adds; the allocation maximizes reported value net of risk cost, and each pays for the risk it displaces from others.

Three results limit this:

- **No budget balance.** Green and Laffont (1977) show that, for general quasi-linear preferences, no mechanism is efficient, dominant-strategy truthful and budget-balanced. VCG runs a surplus or a deficit.
- **No efficient bilateral trade.** Myerson and Satterthwaite (1983) show that with privately known values, no mechanism is efficient, Bayesian incentive compatible, individually rational and budget-balanced without an outside subsidy. A market in which efficiency, truthfulness, voluntary participation and budget balance all hold is not available; one of them has to give.
- **Collusion and computation.** VCG is vulnerable to collusion between bidders, and computing the efficient allocation can be intractable when allocations are combinatorial.

For attributing a total risk to components rather than charging for it, see the Shapley and Euler allocations in [Risk Budgeting and Tail Measures](/research/risk-methods/financial-risk-budgeting/).

## Principal and agent: informativeness and multitask

Holmström (1979) characterizes the optimal contract when the principal sees an outcome $x$ but not the agent's effort $a$. With $G$ the principal's utility, $U$ the risk-averse agent's, and $f(x \mid a)$ the outcome density, the optimal sharing rule $s(x)$ satisfies

$$\frac{G'(x - s(x))}{U'(s(x))} = \lambda + \mu \,\frac{f_a(x, a)}{f(x, a)}$$

where $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the multipliers on the participation and incentive constraints. Pay rises with the likelihood ratio $f_a/f$, which measures how strongly an outcome indicates effort. The informativeness principle follows: an additional signal is worth putting in the contract when it carries information about effort that the outcome does not already carry.

Holmström and Milgrom (1991) supply the warning. When an agent splits effort across several tasks and only some of them are measurable, strong incentives on the measured tasks pull effort away from the unmeasured ones. The optimal response can be weak incentives or none. For safety this is the central result. Paying a team on red-team pass rates or incident counts rewards effort that moves those numbers, which is not the same as effort that reduces risk. It is Goodhart's law in contract form, and a precise version of approval theater.

The practical reading: treat measured safety metrics as inputs to judgment, audit the dimensions the metrics miss, and keep incentive weights low on any metric that is cheap to move without reducing risk.

## Eliciting probabilities honestly

VCG allocates resources. The tools for eliciting honest probability estimates are different:

- **Proper scoring rules.** Under a strictly proper rule (Brier, logarithmic), a forecaster maximizes expected score by reporting their true belief (Gneiting and Raftery 2007). The rule needs an outcome to score against.
- **Peer prediction.** Miller, Resnick and Zeckhauser (2005) score each report against other agents' reports, which makes truthful reporting an equilibrium when outcomes are never observed. Uninformative equilibria, in which everyone reports the same thing, also exist.
- **Bayesian Truth Serum.** Prelec (2004) asks for an answer and a prediction of how others will answer, and rewards answers that are more common than predicted. Truth-telling is an equilibrium in large populations under a common-prior assumption.
- **Prediction markets** aggregate many such reports into a price.

These map onto the inputs of a risk estimate unevenly. Frequent harm modes and near-miss rates resolve, so scoring rules apply. Catastrophic tail probabilities rarely resolve; peer prediction and Bayesian Truth Serum are the candidates there, and their common-prior assumptions are exactly what a strategic developer may not share. [Expert Elicitation](/design-patterns/tools/expert-elicitation/) covers the non-strategic case.

## Insurance and liability

An insurer prices a policy at roughly

$$\text{premium} = P(\text{violation}) \times E[D \mid \text{violation}] \times (1 + \text{loading})$$

Using the unconditional $E[D]$ in place of $E[D \mid \text{violation}]$ counts the violation probability twice. Insurers address the moral hazard that coverage creates with deductibles, co-insurance and experience rating (bonus-malus premiums that move with claims history). [The Insurer's Dilemma](/delegation-risk/insurers-dilemma/) applies this to AI delegation, and [Regulatory Approaches](/entanglements/cross-domain/regulatory-approaches/) covers the incident-reporting duties now in force.

In US federal procurement, OMB memo M-24-18 (2024) was rescinded and replaced by M-25-22 (April 2025), issued alongside M-25-21 on agency use of AI. Procurement terms that make payment contingent on demonstrated safety are subject to the multitask problem above.

## References

- Gibbard, A. (1973). Manipulation of voting schemes: a general result. *Econometrica* 41(4).
- Green, J., & Laffont, J.-J. (1977). Characterization of satisfactory mechanisms for the revelation of preferences for public goods. *Econometrica* 45(2), 427–438.
- Gneiting, T., & Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. *JASA* 102(477), 359–378.
- Holmström, B. (1979). Moral hazard and observability. *Bell Journal of Economics* 10(1), 74–91.
- Holmström, B., & Milgrom, P. (1991). Multitask principal-agent analyses: incentive contracts, asset ownership, and job design. *Journal of Law, Economics, & Organization* 7, 24–52.
- Miller, N., Resnick, P., & Zeckhauser, R. (2005). Eliciting informative feedback: the peer-prediction method. *Management Science* 51(9), 1359–1373.
