- Myerson, R., & Satterthwaite, M. (1983). Efficient mechanisms for bilateral trading. *Journal of Economic Theory* 29(2), 265–281.
- Prelec, D. (2004). A Bayesian truth serum for subjective data. *Science* 306(5695), 462–466.
- Vickrey (1961), Clarke (1971) and Groves (1973) for the VCG mechanism.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Safety-Critical Engineering Precedents
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/system-design/nuclear-aerospace-deep-dive/
------------------------------------------------------------

Nuclear power, civil aviation, the process industries and automotive engineering all start from a system-level safety target and push it down to components. Their tools (fault trees, importance measures, common-cause models, integrity levels, decomposition rules) are the closest precedent for a delegation-risk budget. This page summarizes the tools, the standards, and the failures that showed their limits. They are analogies with stated limits, not evidence that the methods work for AI agents.

## Fault trees and importance measures

A fault tree combines component failure probabilities through gates. With independent inputs:

- **OR gate** (any input failure fails the output): $P = 1 - \prod_i (1 - p_i) \approx \sum_i p_i$ for rare events.
- **AND gate** (all inputs must fail): $P = \prod_i p_i$.

In reliability-block terms, components in **series** form an OR gate (any one failing breaks the chain), and redundant components in **parallel** form an AND gate. The AND gate is where redundancy earns its credit, and it is also where the independence assumption does the most work.

Importance measures say where to spend effort:

| Measure | Definition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Fussell-Vesely | Share of total risk from cut sets containing the component | How much risk the component contributes |
| Risk Achievement Worth (RAW) | Risk with the component failed ÷ baseline risk | How much the system leans on it |
| Birnbaum | $\partial R / \partial p_i$ | Where an improvement buys most |

A RAW of 2 or more is commonly used as a screening criterion for risk significance (for example, in US Maintenance Rule practice), not as a trigger for regulatory action. <!-- TODO(verify): RAW >= 2 screening threshold attributed to NUMARC 93-01; not checked against the document. -->

## Common-cause failure

The AND gate's product holds only if the inputs fail independently. The beta-factor model (Fleming 1974; NUREG/CR-4780) assigns a fraction β of each component's failure probability to a shared cause that fails all redundant components together. The site's canonical form, with ρ in place of β, is in [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/):

$$P(\text{all fail}) \approx (1-\rho)\prod_i p_i + \rho \min_i p_i$$

For process-industry hardware, IEC 61508-6 (Annex D) gives β values of roughly 0.5–5% for logic subsystems and 1–10% for sensors and final elements, set by a checklist of separation, diversity and maintenance practices. <!-- TODO(verify): IEC 61508-6 Annex D beta ranges taken from the audit and memory; not checked against the standard or a secondary source. -->

The consequence is a floor that redundancy cannot get under. Two channels at $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$ per hour each give $10^{-9}$ if independent. With β = 1% the common-cause term alone is $3.2 \times 10^{-7}$, more than 300 times the target. To reach $10^{-9}$ with β = 1%, each channel must already be at $10^{-7}$.

Independence fails in three familiar ways: physical (shared location, power or cooling), design (same component type, supplier or software), and operational (the same maintenance error or calibration mistake applied to every channel). For AI components the design route dominates: shared base models, training data and prompts.

### An illustrative AI fault tree

All numbers in this example are illustrative. The top event is "harmful code reaches production", with a target of $10^{-6}$ per year, and three paths:

| Path | Inputs (AND) | Independent result |
|---|---|---|
| Bypass all checks | Code review misses (10⁻²), static analysis misses (10⁻²), tests pass bad code (10⁻²), human approves (10⁻¹) | 10⁻⁷ |
| Compromised coordinator | Coordinator schemes (10⁻³), defeats redundancy (10⁻²), evades monitoring (10⁻²) | 10⁻⁷ |
| Human insider | Override (10⁻²), malicious intent (10⁻⁴) | 10⁻⁶ |

The OR of the three is about $1.2 \times 10^{-6}$, which misses the target even under independence. The first path is the larger problem. Its four checks see the same code, and the reviewers and test generators may share a model. Under the mixture above, ρ = 0.01 raises that path from $10^{-7}$ to about $10^{-4}$, and ρ = 0.1 to about $10^{-3}$: the common-cause term ρ × min pᵢ swamps the product. The second path has a different flaw: once a coordinator is scheming, "defeats redundancy" and "evades monitoring" are conditional probabilities given that fact, and must be estimated that way, not as base rates.

## Targets and what they measure

### Nuclear: modeled versus observed

The US NRC uses a core damage frequency (CDF) below $10^{-4}$ per reactor-year as a subsidiary safety objective, with a tighter figure for large early releases. <!-- TODO(verify): the LERF figure (10^-5 per reactor-year in earlier versions of this page, as used in Regulatory Guide 1.174) was not checked against an NRC source. --> Plant PRAs often report CDFs well below the $10^{-4}$ objective, and these figures are sometimes described as achieved performance. They are model outputs.

The observed record is different. Five reactor cores have suffered severe damage in three accidents at commercial power plants (Three Mile Island 2, Chernobyl 4, Fukushima Daiichi 1–3) in more than 20,000 cumulative reactor-years ([World Nuclear Association](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/safety-and-security/safety-of-plants/safety-of-nuclear-power-reactors)). That is about $1.5 \times 10^{-4}$ per reactor-year counting accidents, or $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ counting cores. The fleet is heterogeneous, Chernobyl's RBMK design is not comparable to plants with modern PRAs, and Fukushima was an external event, so the comparison is rough. It still shows that a computed frequency and an observed one can differ by an order of magnitude or more. A delegation-risk estimate of $10^{-6}$ from a fault tree is a model output in the same sense.

Nuclear defence in depth is structured in five levels (IAEA INSAG-10, 1996): prevention of abnormal operation, control of abnormal operation, control of design-basis accidents, control of severe accidents, and mitigation of off-site radiological consequences. It is not the three-lines-of-defence model used in banking and internal audit.

### Aviation: probability targets and the fail-safe rule

Transport-aircraft certification ties allowable probability to severity (AC 25.1309-1B; ARP 4761):

| Severity | Allowable probability per flight hour | Qualitative term |
|---|---|---|
| Catastrophic | on the order of 10⁻⁹ or less | Extremely improbable |
| Hazardous | 10⁻⁷ or less | Extremely remote |
| Major | 10⁻⁵ or less | Remote |
| Minor | may be probable | Probable |

The $10^{-9}$ figure is an allocation, not a measurement. FAA's AC 25.1309-1B (2024) traces it to the British Concorde standard: a severe-accident rate of about $10^{-6}$ per flight hour, about 10% of it attributed to aircraft systems, gives $10^{-7}$, divided equally among an assumed 100 catastrophic failure conditions.

The same advisory circular states the rule that matters more for AI delegation: the failure of any single element during a flight "must be assumed, regardless of its probability," and such single failures must not be catastrophic. The $10^{-9}$ target applies only to failure conditions that already require multiple failures. This is the precedent for the site's [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/): a hard bound that holds whatever the estimated probability, rather than a statistical budget that a single bad action can overdraw.

Software assurance follows severity through DO-178C's design assurance levels:

| Level | Failure condition | Objectives | Structural coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Catastrophic | 71 | Statement, decision and MC/DC |
| B | Hazardous | 69 | Statement and decision |
| C | Major | 62 | Statement |
| D | Minor | 26 | None |

### Process industry: safety integrity levels

IEC 61508 functional safety, not nuclear or aerospace practice, defines Safety Integrity Levels. For a safety function in low-demand mode:

| SIL | Average probability of failure on demand | Risk reduction |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10⁻² to 10⁻¹ | 10–100 |
| 2 | 10⁻³ to 10⁻² | 100–1,000 |
| 3 | 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻³ | 1,000–10,000 |
| 4 | 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁴ | 10,000–100,000 |

A sensor, logic solver and final element in series form an OR gate, so their PFDs add. An illustrative SIL 3 allocation: sensor 2 × 10⁻⁴, logic 5 × 10⁻⁵, final element 5 × 10⁻⁴, total 7.5 × 10⁻⁴, inside the band. An allocation that sums to exactly 10⁻³ is SIL 2.

### Automotive: ASIL decomposition

ISO 26262 lets a requirement at one Automotive Safety Integrity Level be split across two sufficiently independent elements at lower levels. The notation X(Y) means an element developed to ASIL X as part of a decomposed ASIL Y requirement. The permitted splits (ISO 26262-9, clause 5; see [Mohan 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02496)) are:

| Requirement | Permitted decompositions |
|---|---|
| ASIL D | C(D) + A(D); B(D) + B(D); D(D) + QM(D) |
| ASIL C | B(C) + A(C); C(C) + QM(C) |
| ASIL B | A(B) + A(B); B(B) + QM(B) |
| ASIL A | A(A) + QM(A) |

ASIL C cannot be split into A + A. Decomposition is a statement about development rigor against systematic faults and requires a dependent-failure analysis showing independence. It does not multiply random hardware failure rates, which are bounded separately:

| ASIL | Single-point fault metric | Latent fault metric | Random hardware failure target |
|---|---|---|---|
| D | ≥ 99% | ≥ 90% | < 10⁻⁸ per hour (10 FIT) |
| C | ≥ 97% | ≥ 80% | < 10⁻⁷ per hour (100 FIT) |
| B | ≥ 90% | ≥ 60% | < 10⁻⁷ per hour (100 FIT) |

An AI system decomposed as "ML detector at B(D) plus rule-based check at B(D)" earns the split only if the two fail independently on the inputs that matter, which is the claim [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) says to assume false until measured. ISO 26262 also covers only malfunctions. Hazards from a correctly functioning but insufficient perception model fall under SOTIF (ISO 21448), AI-specific guidance for road vehicles is ISO/PAS 8800, and UL 4600 (first edition April 2020) sets out safety cases for autonomous products.

## Failures that showed the limits

**Three Mile Island (1979).** A pilot-operated relief valve stuck open. Its control-room indicator showed only that the valve's solenoid was powered, not the valve's position, so operators believed it was closed. The same sequence had occurred about 18 months earlier at Davis-Besse and was not acted on. WASH-1400 (1975) had already judged a small break more likely than a large one and stressed operator response; the accident is often read as vindicating that analysis. What failed was the use of operating experience and the human-machine interface, not the existence of a probabilistic model.

**Fukushima Daiichi (2011).** The design-basis tsunami was 5.7 m; waves of up to about 14 m overtopped the site. Most emergency diesel generators and switchgear sat in flooded basements, so nominally redundant power failed from one cause. Units interacted: hydrogen from unit 3 most likely reached unit 4 through shared piping, and explosions at one unit damaged equipment needed at another. A beyond-design-basis external event, common-cause failure and multi-unit coupling arrived together.

**Challenger (1986) and Columbia (2003).** Vaughan (1996) called the Challenger pattern the normalization of deviance: O-ring erosion seen on earlier flights was reclassified, flight by flight, as acceptable, and the launch decision conformed to NASA's rules rather than breaking them. The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003), drawing on Vaughan's analysis, found the same pattern with foam shedding, which was well known and came to be treated as an acceptable risk.

**Boeing 737 MAX (2018–2019).** MCAS took its trigger from one angle-of-attack sensor at a time, so a single sensor fault could command repeated nose-down trim. Certification relied on the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization, under which the manufacturer acts on the regulator's behalf. It is a case of both a single point of failure and delegated verification.

## What transfers

Fault-tree logic, importance measures, explicit common-cause parameters and severity-tiered targets transfer directly; they are arithmetic about whatever probabilities one supplies. Three things do not. Failure-rate databases have no AI equivalent. Random-failure assumptions fit hardware, while AI failures are systematic: the same input fails every copy. And physical separation, the main source of independence in hardware, does nothing for components that share a model.

The standard critique of PRA for software and organizational failure is Leveson's STAMP and its hazard analysis method STPA (*Engineering a Safer World*, MIT Press, 2012). STPA treats accidents as failures of control (unsafe commands, missing feedback, flawed process models) rather than chains of component faults. That framing fits agent scaffolds, where most of the risk sits in what the controller is allowed to command.

## Sources

- FAA Advisory Circular 25.1309-1B, *System Design and Analysis* (30 August 2024); AC 25.1309-1A (1988).
- IAEA INSAG-10, *Defence in Depth in Nuclear Safety* (1996).
- IEC 61508 (functional safety); ISO 26262 (road vehicles functional safety); RTCA DO-178C; SAE ARP 4761.
- NUREG/CR-4780 (common-cause failure procedures).
- Leveson, N. (2012). *Engineering a Safer World*. MIT Press.
- Mohan, N. (2019). *Architecting Safe Automated Driving with Legacy Platforms*. [arXiv:2001.02496](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02496).
- Vaughan, D. (1996). *The Challenger Launch Decision*. University of Chicago Press.
- World Nuclear Association, *Safety of Nuclear Power Reactors*.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Access Control Systems
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/system-design/access-control-systems/
------------------------------------------------------------

Access control is delegation written down as policy. A security clearance, an IAM role, a service account and an OAuth token each grant a delegate some authority, bound its scope, and leave a record. Two mature domains have decades of experience with this: the intelligence community, which faces adversarial insiders, and enterprise software, which faces scale and organizational entropy. Both have documented failure modes, and AI agents inherit most of them.

## Intelligence community: clearance, compartments, need-to-know

**Clearance is eligibility, not access.** US classification levels (Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) are defined by the damage disclosure would cause. A Top Secret clearance makes a person eligible to see Top Secret material; it does not grant access to any of it.

**Compartments restrict access horizontally.** Sensitive Compartmented Information is divided into control systems such as SI (signals intelligence), TK (overhead imagery) and HCS (human sources). Two analysts with the same clearance can see entirely different material. Access requires a formal read-in, and leaving a program requires a read-out.

**Need-to-know applies per request.** Within a compartment, access still requires an operational reason. Access is the intersection of clearance, compartment and need-to-know; each check blocks a different kind of drift.

**Two-person integrity** requires two authorized people to act together for critical operations, such as nuclear weapons handling and cryptographic key management. No single person can complete the action alone, so a single compromised or mistaken insider is not enough.

**Vetting is continuous.** The US system has been moving from reinvestigation on a fixed multi-year cycle toward continuous vetting, in which automated checks of financial, criminal and travel records run between investigations. <!-- TODO(verify): name and dates of the Trusted Workforce 2.0 continuous-vetting reform; not checked against a primary source. -->

### The insider cases

These controls did not stop the most damaging insiders:

| Case | Access | How it ended |
|---|---|---|
| Aldrich Ames (CIA, spied 1985–1994) | Legitimate access to Soviet-division operations | A CIA–FBI mole hunt, begun after agents were lost, narrowed on him partly through unexplained wealth. Arrested after about nine years. |
| Robert Hanssen (FBI, intermittently 1979–2001) | Counterintelligence role with wide visibility into FBI cases | Identified after the FBI paid \$7 million for a KGB file on the unknown mole. The Justice Department called it "possibly the worst intelligence disaster in U.S. history." |
| Chelsea Manning (Army, 2010) | Analyst with TS/SCI access to classified networks | Bulk download of databases far beyond any task's need. Identified after confiding in Adrian Lamo, who informed Army investigators. |
| Edward Snowden (NSA contractor, 2013) | Systems-administrator access | Not detected. He identified himself through *The Guardian* after the first stories ran. |
| Reality Winner (NSA contractor, 2017) | Translator with access to the document | An internal audit found six people had accessed it; she was the only one who had emailed the publication. |

Each had legitimate access and used it outside its purpose. Compartmentation did not contain Hanssen; his counterintelligence work gave him visibility across many programs. Routine monitoring flagged none of them early. Ames was found by a mole hunt that took years, Hanssen through a purchased foreign file, Manning through a confidant, and Snowden by his own disclosure. Access logs helped only in Winner's case, where the field of suspects was already small.

## Enterprise software: roles, attributes, delegation

**Role-based access control (RBAC)** maps users to roles and roles to permissions. It scales and is easy to audit, but organizations accumulate hundreds of roles, roles grant more than any one task needs, and assignments are static.

**Attribute-based access control (ABAC)** evaluates policies over attributes of the subject, resource and environment at request time: department, data classification, time of day, location. It is more precise and harder to audit.

**OAuth** lets a user delegate limited authority to a third-party application without handing over credentials. The application receives an access token with defined scopes and lifetime, which the user or authorization server can revoke. RFC 6749 defines the framework. RFC 6819 (2013) is the threat model, and RFC 9700 (January 2025) is the current *Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security*. OAuth 2.1, still an IETF draft, consolidates these practices.

**Service accounts** are non-human identities with delegated authority, and they are where enterprise access control is weakest. Typical problems are administrator rights granted to "make it work", credentials shared across systems, no expiry, and actions logged against the account rather than the person or process that triggered them. AI agents are service accounts that choose their own actions, so every service-account problem applies to them, with less predictable behavior.

### Permission sprawl

Access accumulates faster than it is removed:

- Emergency access granted during an incident is never revoked.
- Project access outlives the project.
- Promotions add roles without removing old ones.
- Acquisitions layer one access model on top of another.
- Urgent requests are granted by default.

Organizations respond with periodic access reviews, which degrade predictably. Managers facing hundreds of certifications approve by default, privileged accounts are marked "still needed" without checking, and dormant-account cleanups exclude service accounts because touching them might break production. The site's term for the resulting gap between what a delegate can do and what it needs is [privilege overhang](/getting-started/glossary/#privilege-overhang); the review failure is approval theater, measured by the [rubber-stamp rate](/entanglements/cross-domain/psychology-of-oversight/).

## The confused deputy

Hardy (1988) described a compiler on a timesharing service that had permission to write in a system directory, where it kept usage statistics. The billing file lived in the same directory. A user named the billing file as the compiler's debugging output, and the compiler, using its own permission on the user's behalf, overwrote it. The compiler was a deputy confused about whose authority it was exercising. Access-control lists cannot prevent this, because the deputy really is permitted to write the file. Capability systems prevent it by making authority travel with the reference to the object being used.

An agent that reads untrusted content and acts with its user's credentials is a confused deputy waiting to happen. Prompt injection is the attack: text from a web page, email or tool result instructs the agent, and the agent exercises the user's authority on the attacker's behalf.

The Model Context Protocol's authorization specification (2025-06-18 revision) is an example of current practice. Authorization is optional. When it is used over HTTP, an MCP server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server, must accept only tokens issued for itself (clients must name the intended server using RFC 8707 resource indicators), and must not pass a client's token through to upstream APIs. The specification forbids token passthrough explicitly to avoid confused-deputy failures. These rules bound which services a token works at. They do not stop an injected instruction from using a correctly scoped token for the wrong purpose; that needs the controls below.

## Lessons for AI delegation

**Access is not trust.** A clearance is eligibility, and a role is a ceiling. An agent's standing permissions should not determine what it may touch for a given task. Grant capabilities per task, scoped to the resources the task names, with a short lifetime. This is [Least Privilege](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/#least-privilege) with expiry, the [Expiring Grants](/design-patterns/information/#expiring-grants) pattern.

**Compartmentalize by default.** A code-writing agent does not need financial data, and a summarizer does not need write access. A coordinator that routes tasks need not see the data at all. Compartments also limit what an injected instruction can reach ([Need-to-Know Compartments](/design-patterns/information/#need-to-know-compartments)).

**Re-check during the delegation, not only before it.** Initial vetting is a weak predictor of later behavior, which is why the intelligence community moved toward continuous vetting. For agents, this means runtime monitoring and per-action checks, not only evaluation before deployment.

**Use two-person rules for irreversible actions.** High-stakes actions should require confirmation from an independent checker, human or automated, and the checker must actually be independent. A second instance of the same model is a weak second person ([Voting Tribunal](/design-patterns/structural/#voting-tribunal); [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)).

**Plan for the insider who passes vetting.** The insider cases show that detection is slow and often comes from outside. An agent that passed its evaluations may still act against its principal, through misalignment or hijack. Design so that a delegate who goes bad can do bounded damage before anyone notices: scope limits, rate limits, and an [exposure envelope](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/) that holds regardless of intent.

**Give every agent instance its own identity.** Shared service accounts make attribution impossible. Each agent instance should have its own credentials, its actions should be logged against the request that triggered them, and its credentials should expire.

**Build revocation in from the start.** Check revocation and expiry before every action, not at session start. Inventory third-party integrations and their credentials with expiry dates, and flag credentials that go unused.

**Route reviews by risk.** Reviews fail when volume exceeds attention. Auto-approve low-risk requests under hard limits, and send the few high-risk requests to reviewers with time and context to evaluate them.

## Mapping across domains

| Concept | Intelligence community | Enterprise | AI delegation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eligibility | Clearance | Role assignment | Agent's standing permissions |
| Scope limit | Compartment | Permission set, OAuth scope | Per-task capability grant |
| Need-to-know | Operational justification | Data classification | Task-specific context |
| Ongoing evaluation | Continuous vetting | Access reviews, behavior analytics | Runtime monitoring |
| Multi-party control | Two-person integrity | Separation of duties | Independent checker |
| Revocation | Read-out, suspension | Account disable, token revocation | Session and credential revocation |

## Sources

- Hardy, N. (1988). The confused deputy (or why capabilities might have been invented). *ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review* 22(4), 36–38.
- IETF RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 6819 (OAuth 2.0 Threat Model, 2013), RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators), RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, 2025).
- Model Context Protocol, [Authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/authorization) (2025-06-18).
- US Department of Justice, Office of the Inspector General (August 2003). Review of the FBI's performance in the Hanssen case.
- NIST SP 800-53 (security and privacy controls); NIST SP 800-162 (attribute-based access control); Intelligence Community Directive 704 (personnel security).
- Stoll, C. (1989). *The Cuckoo's Egg*. An account of detecting an external intruder, Markus Hess, from a 75-cent accounting discrepancy; an example of anomaly detection from audit logs, not of insider threat.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Open Problems
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/research/potential-projects/
------------------------------------------------------------

[Delegation engineering](/getting-started/core-concepts/), designing and operating delegation structures to bound exposure while keeping capability, is a field name this site keeps using. A field name is only real if other people have work to do in it. This page lists that work.

Almost nothing here has been measured on AI agents. The framework's central mechanisms, [risk preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/), [exposure envelopes](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#2-the-exposure-envelope) and the [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/), are design proposals with plausible lineage and no empirical track record in that setting. Each problem is phrased so that a first result would move the estimate one way or the other. Several could falsify load-bearing parts of the framework.

Each entry gives the question, why it matters, what a first result looks like, and a rough scale: weekend prototype, month project, or research programme.

---

## Tier 1: The cheapest credibility purchases

### 1. The preflight prototype

**Question.** Can you build a working [risk preflight](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/)? That is a pre-action hook in a real agent harness that estimates a proposed command's exposure against a running session budget before it commits. Modern coding agents expose pre-tool-call hook points.

**Why it matters.** Everything on [Runtime Accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/) is currently a design. A hook with crude estimates, a real envelope (hard-coded file, spend and egress bounds) and a real [exposure ledger](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#3-the-exposure-ledger) would turn "here is what we would build" into "here is what we built, and where it broke".

**First result.** A hook that intercepts proposed tool calls, classifies each into a small harm-surface table, debits an estimated exposure against a session budget, and blocks or escalates on overdraw. It should measure at the boundary, meaning what the process actually touched, and never by asking the agent. A crude estimator counts, as long as the envelope and ledger are real.

**Scale.** Weekend prototype to month project.

### 2. Who preflights the preflight, on agentic harm

**Question.** Does a small, separate, trusted checker catch failures that a frontier sibling of the actor misses, on the kinds of harmful actions agents actually take?

**What is already known.** First results exist for code and for monitoring. In AI Control, a GPT-3.5 monitor ranked every GPT-4 backdoor at or above median suspiciousness, but at a 2% false-positive rate it missed many of them (Greenblatt et al. 2023, [arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)). A weaker model, GPT-4o, reading o3-mini's chain of thought caught reward hacking far more effectively than monitoring actions alone (Baker et al. 2025, [arXiv:2503.11926](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). Factoring tasks for a weak monitor raised safety from 41% to 63% in APPS (Sandoval & Rushing 2025, [arXiv:2512.02157](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02157)). Against monitors that the attacker can target with prompt injection, monitoring failed (Terekhov et al. 2025, [arXiv:2510.09462](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09462)). [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/) has the details.

**The open part.** None of these compares a frontier sibling judge with a narrow, separately trained one on agentic harm: file deletion, credential use, exfiltration, spend. None reports the overlap of their misses on the phi scale the [entanglement tax](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) needs.

**First result.** On a challenge set of agent actions with known harm labels, the detection rates of (a) a frontier sibling of the actor and (b) a narrow or older-family judge. Report the fraction caught by (b) and missed by (a), and φ between their miss indicators. Repeat under an adaptive red team. If (a) does as well as (b), the [verifiability-hierarchy](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy) rule for preflights loses its teeth.

**Scale.** Month project.

### 3. Measured correlation priors on the phi scale

**Question.** What is the pairwise failure correlation φ between real model pairs, same provider, cross-provider and cross-paradigm, on harm-detection tasks?

**What is already known.** Goel et al. (2025, [arXiv:2502.04313](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313)) find model mistakes becoming more similar as capability rises. Kim et al. (2025, [arXiv:2506.07962](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962)) find, across 350+ models, that two models agree 60% of the time when both err on one leaderboard dataset. Larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even across providers.

**The open part.** Those are similarity and agreement statistics on benchmarks, not φ on harm detection. The site's tax figures, about 11×, 21× and 50× at ρ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5, rest on assumed ρ ([Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/)).

**First result.** A small table of measured φ for a handful of judge pairs on a shared agentic-harm challenge set, bucketed by relationship, with the method documented well enough to reproduce. Even three pairs would replace an assumption with a measurement. The adversarial case needs a separate measurement, under attack.

**Scale.** Month project to research programme.

---

## Tier 2: Naming and measuring failure modes

### 4. Multi-tenant entanglement

**Question.** What are the failure modes of agents that share memory stores, MCP servers and tool caches, and how do you measure them?

**Why it matters.** Single-channel attacks are documented: poisoning an agent's memory or knowledge base (AgentPoison, [arXiv:2407.12784](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12784); MINJA, [arXiv:2503.03704](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03704)) and instructions hidden in MCP tool descriptions ([Invariant Labs, April 2025](https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification)). What is not characterised is the common-cause effect: two nominally independent agents failing together because they share the poisoned resource. That is the [entanglement](/entanglements/) problem in its 2026 form.

**First result.** A taxonomy of multi-tenant coupling channels with at least one demonstrated joint failure through a shared dependency, and an estimate of how much it raises joint failure over the independent baseline.

**Scale.** Month project.

### 5. Rubber-stamp rate measurement

**Question.** In a real approval flow, what fraction of human approvals are issued faster than the minimum time to read what is being approved (the [rubber-stamp rate](/entanglements/cross-domain/psychology-of-oversight/)), and which interventions move it?

**Why it matters.** The framework leans on the claim that unbudgeted human review degrades into approval theater. The claim is borrowed and plausible, but unmeasured in agent oversight. If the rate stays low under load, the case for preflight as an attention router weakens.

**First result.** Log approval latency against a minimum-reading-time floor, report the rate, then test one or two interventions (session-length limits, deliberate friction) and report effect sizes.

**Scale.** Weekend prototype to month project.

---

## Tier 3: Protocol and metric design

### 6. Reconciliation protocol design

**Question.** What does it mean, concretely, to [reconcile](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/#3-the-exposure-ledger) an exposure ledger against incidents and near-misses?

**Why it matters.** A ledger without reconciliation is fake precision with bookkeeping aesthetics. The answer to "aren't these numbers made up?" is that they get reconciled against reality, so the procedure has to exist. Actuarial loss development, how insurers update estimates as claims mature, is the obvious source. Reconciliation can only calibrate harm modes frequent enough to observe. Rare catastrophic modes need the envelope instead (see the rule of three in [Formal Verification Limits](/research/technical-safety/formal-verification-limits/)).

**First result.** A written protocol, covering what counts as an incident or a near-miss and how observed outcomes update prior estimates, with a triangle-style worked example over a few periods.

**Scale.** Month project.

### 7. The insurance question, scoped

**Question.** Does liability transfer change outcomes when the agent never sees the premium?

**Why it matters.** Standard moral-hazard analysis assumes the risk-taker internalises the premium. An AI agent does not. Whether insurance still improves outcomes when the cost signal stops at the principal decides whether insurance-based proposals are coherent.

**First result.** A formal model, or a clean argument, for when insurance carried by the principal changes the agent's behaviour, and under what added structure: deductibles routed back as constraints, or experience-rated privileges.

**Scale.** Month project.

### 8. A capability–risk frontier

**Question.** How should architectures be compared on capability and delegation risk together?

**Why it matters.** Ratios of capability to expected loss have broken units: a design with near-zero estimated risk gets an unbounded score from an assumption. The honest object may be a frontier, capability plotted against delegation risk, on which designs are dominated or not, with no scalar.

**First result.** Two or three real architectures for one task, each with measured task success and a delegation-risk estimate with its uncertainty. Show which are dominated and whether the ranking survives the uncertainty.

**Scale.** Month project.

---

## Other open questions

These are open and not covered by an existing page. Several feed the problems above.

- **Coordinator redundancy.** Build diverse coordinators (rule-based, narrow fine-tune, older frontier model), red-team each, and compare agreement and failure modes. *Feeds problem 2.*
- **Narrow versus general models.** How much more predictable and auditable are narrow fine-tuned models on a fixed task than frontier models prompted for it?
- **Self-prediction.** Can a model forecast its own behaviour after modification, and how does calibration degrade with horizon?
- **Uncertainty propagation.** Distributions, not point estimates, through the accounting. *Feeds problems 3 and 6.*
- **Bounding unknown capabilities.** How to size a harm surface when elicitation may be incomplete; see the sandbagging results in [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/).
- **Handoffs.** What context is sufficient when work passes between a human and an agent, and how to check it.
- **Agency and power.** Behavioural measures of goal-directedness in deployed agent systems, and whether they predict defection ([Power Dynamics](/power-dynamics/)).
- **Regulation and certification.** What maximum delegation risk, if any, regulators could set by application category, and what disclosure would make it checkable.

**Answered.** *Does temperature 0 suppress steganographic signalling?* No. A deterministic policy can encode information in which output it produces, and served models are not deterministic at temperature 0 anyway ([Steganography](/research/technical-safety/steganography-detection-prevention/)).

---

## How to contribute

A result, even a negative one or a crude prototype that broke instructively, is worth more to this framework than another page of prose. Negative results that falsify a load-bearing claim are worth the most.

The framework lives at **[github.com/quantified-uncertainty/delegation-risk-framework](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/delegation-risk-framework)**. Open an issue to propose a problem, claim one, or share a result. If you build the [preflight prototype](#1-the-preflight-prototype), please report where the estimates broke down.

## See also

- [Runtime Risk Accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/): the mechanism Tier 1 would build and test
- [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/): the φ recipe and the tax table problems 2 and 3 would ground
- [Empirical Scheming Reduction](/research/trust-behavior/empirical-scheming-reduction/): the first results problem 2 builds on
- [Psychology of Oversight](/entanglements/cross-domain/psychology-of-oversight/): the approval-theater claim problem 5 would test

# Reference
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## Glossary
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/glossary/
------------------------------------------------------------

Definitions as this site uses them. Borrowed terms keep their home field's meaning; where this site's usage is narrower, the entry says so.

**Units convention.** A probability on this site is always *per* something: per task, per action, or per period. A delegation risk carries the same unit. Most pages use dollars per month; worked examples state their unit at the top.

## Core framework terms

<span id="harm-mode"></span>
**Harm mode**: a specific way a delegation could cause damage, with a probability and a damage value. It parallels the *failure mode* of [FMEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Failure_mode_and_effects_analysis). *Example*: "leaks proprietary data", P = 0.001 per month, damage \$50,000.

<span id="harm-surface"></span>
**Harm surface**: the *set* of a delegation's harm modes, the delegation analogue of an [attack surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_surface). It is a set, not a number. You enumerate it, bound it (exposure) and price it (delegation risk).

<span id="exposure"></span>
**Exposure**: the worst-case loss across the harm surface, given the delegate's actual access and capability. It is a dollar bound, not an expectation, and it depends on capability: the same office key carries more exposure for a delegate who can exploit what it opens. Lineage: [exposure-at-default](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposure_at_default) in finance. *Gross* exposure is measured before controls, *net* exposure after.

<span id="delegation-risk"></span>
**Delegation risk**: the expected loss of a delegation, Σ P(harm mode) × Damage(harm mode), in dollars per the stated unit ([canonical statement](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-formula)). *Residual risk* is delegation risk after controls. A *delegation risk budget* is the maximum a system or component may carry.

<span id="harm-channels"></span>
**Harm channels**: the three ways harm arises ([Risk Decomposition](/delegation-risk/risk-decomposition/)).
- <span id="accident"></span>**Accident**: the delegate fails at its task (bugs, hallucinations, edge cases, capability limits). P(error per action) often falls as capability rises, but not reliably: inverse-scaling results exist. A more capable delegate is also given more consequential actions, so damage per accident tends to rise. Do not assume accident risk falls with capability.
- <span id="defection"></span>**Defection**: the delegate pursues something other than the principal's interest. Scheming is the strategic case. **Reward hacking**, in which the delegate exploits a flaw in its objective (special-casing tests, editing a grader) without strategic deception, is a non-scheming sub-type. Capability raises both the chance that defection succeeds and the damage it can do.
- <span id="hijack"></span>**Hijack**: a third party or user steers a delegate that is not itself scheming. Examples are prompt injection through a document, web page or tool output, and direct misuse. The attacker chooses the input, so treat correlated checks as fully correlated (ρ near 1).

<span id="propagation-rule"></span>
**Propagation rule**: how reliabilities compose. Under independence, chains and parallel stacks multiply. For common-cause correlation, use the beta-factor mixture P(all fail) = (1−ρ)·∏pᵢ + ρ·min(pᵢ). The minimum rule is its ρ = 1 limit. The harmonic and discounted rules are retired. See [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/).

<span id="trust"></span>
**Trust (quantitative)**: where a number is attached, t = P(the delegate executes the task faithfully), estimated from its harm-mode table. Unquantified, "trust" is ordinary English. *Risk inheritance*: when A delegates to B and B to C, A carries C's harm modes, composed by the propagation rule.

<span id="entanglement-tax"></span>
**Entanglement tax**: actual joint failure probability divided by what independence predicts, P(all fail) / ∏pᵢ. For n identical layers with miss rate p, it is (1−ρ) + ρ·p^(1−n). For three layers at p = 0.1 that is 1 + 99ρ: about 11×, 21× and 50× at ρ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. This is benign-failure math; ρ for same-provider stacks is assumed, not measured. See [Formal Definitions](/entanglements/fundamentals/formal-definitions/).

<span id="correlation-budget"></span>
**Correlation budget**: a limit on failure correlation within a defense stack, such as "no two checks share a model family". It complements the risk budget. ρ is on the failure-indicator (phi) scale.

<span id="load-bearing-channels"></span>
**Load-bearing channels**: the sanctioned communication paths between delegates that decomposition could not remove. Monitoring budget should concentrate there.

<span id="privilege-overhang"></span>
**Privilege overhang**: the gap between what a delegate *can* do and what its task *needs*. It is the stock; *privilege creep* is the flow that grows it. Cloud-security tools measure the same quantity as *unused entitlements*. Microsoft's *2024 State of Multicloud Security Risk Report* found that identities used about 2% of the permissions granted to them in 2023.

<span id="risk-preflight"></span>
**Risk preflight**: a damage estimate the scaffold runs before an agent action commits. It enumerates the action's harm surface, bounds the exposure, compares the result with the budget, then proceeds, adjusts or escalates. Lineage: [CORS preflight](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Preflight_request) and aviation flight-risk assessment. The estimator must sit at a more verifiable (lower-numbered) tier of the [verifiability hierarchy](#verifiability-hierarchy) than the actor it checks. See [Runtime Accounting](/delegation-risk/runtime-accounting/).

<span id="exposure-envelope"></span>
**Exposure envelope**: the region of action-space in which an agent may act freely, enforced by the scaffold regardless of the agent's inputs or intent. It is a hard bound, not a statistical one: a single catastrophic action must hit the wall, not merely overdraw a budget. Lineage: Airbus flight-envelope protection.

<span id="exposure-ledger"></span>
**Exposure ledger**: the running account per delegate. Actions debit it; completed verifications and de-provisioning credit it. It comes with two disciplines. **Reconciliation** periodically compares the ledger's estimates with observed incidents and near misses. **Consolidation** rolls up a subagent tree. Expected-loss roll-ups simply add. Where several harm modes hit the same asset, the naive sum overstates the true loss, so it is a conservative upper bound. Correlation matters only for tail metrics and for AND-structured defenses.

<span id="principal"></span>
**Principal, delegate, executor, coordinator**: the *principal* delegates, and is ultimately a human or an organization. A *delegate* receives a task (*agent* stresses goal-directedness, *component* architecture). An *executor* performs actions. A <span id="coordinator"></span>*coordinator* routes tasks, grants permissions or aggregates results. Coordinators often concentrate risk because of that leverage, but whether one is the riskiest component depends on the system.

<span id="delegation-engineering"></span>
**Delegation engineering**: designing, measuring and operating delegation structures to bound exposure while preserving capability, here mainly for AI agents.

## Least-X principles

The core six, from the [canonical page](/design-patterns/least-x-principles/):

- <span id="least-intelligence"></span>**Least Intelligence**: the least capable implementation that does the task.
- <span id="least-privilege"></span>**[Least Privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_privilege)**: minimum permissions and access rights.
- <span id="least-context"></span>**Least Context**: minimum information about the wider system.
- <span id="least-persistence"></span>**Least Persistence**: minimum state across invocations, including memory stores, caches and logs the delegate can read.
- <span id="least-autonomy"></span>**Least Autonomy**: minimum ability to act without review.
- <span id="least-connectivity"></span>**Least Connectivity**: minimum communication paths between components.

The canonical page lists further principles as a labelled tail. Two need care. Predictability is worth seeking, but temperature 0 neither guarantees deterministic output from served LLMs nor prevents a deterministic policy from encoding covert signals. Hiding from a component whether it is being tested is hard to enforce: current models often recognize evaluations (Schoen et al. 2025, [arXiv:2509.15541](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541)).

## Architecture terms

<span id="verifiability-hierarchy"></span>
**Verifiability hierarchy**: implementations ordered by how thoroughly they can be checked. The tiers are (1) formally verified code; (2) deterministic tested code and rule-based checks; (3) narrow learned models with measured error on a fixed task; (4) trusted LLMs, below the capability at which scheming is a live concern; and (5) untrusted frontier models and agents. Training method does not set the tier. See [Concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy).

<span id="decomposed-coordination"></span>
**Decomposed coordination**: splitting coordination across several limited components rather than one powerful coordinator. See [Coordinator Constraints](/design-patterns/coordinator-constraints/).

<span id="byzantine-fault-tolerance"></span>
**[Byzantine fault tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault)**: correct operation despite up to f arbitrarily faulty components, which requires at least 3f + 1 replicas. The bound counts faulty replicas; replicas that share a model can exceed f together.

<span id="n-version-programming"></span>
**[N-version programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-version_programming)**: independently developed implementations of one specification, used redundantly. Knight & Leveson (1986) found that such versions failed together more often than independence predicts.

## AI safety terms

<span id="ai-control"></span>
**[AI Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942)**: designing protocols that stay safe even if the model is intentionally trying to subvert them, and testing them with control evaluations (Greenblatt et al. 2023). Its vocabulary (trusted and untrusted model, control protocol, auditing budget, usefulness cost) is used here as Redwood Research uses it.

<span id="scheming"></span>
**Scheming**: an AI system covertly pursuing goals other than its operators', including by deceiving them.

<span id="instrumental-convergence"></span>
**[Instrumental convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental_convergence)**: the tendency of diverse goals to produce similar sub-goals, such as self-preservation and resource acquisition.

<span id="cais"></span>
**CAIS (Comprehensive AI Services)**: Drexler's proposal to build general capability as a system of bounded services rather than unified agents ([report](https://www.futureofhumanityinstitute.org/s/2019-1.pdf)). Related: [tool AI vs. agent AI](https://gwern.net/tool-ai).

<span id="scalable-oversight"></span>
**Scalable oversight**: methods for overseeing systems that are more capable than their overseers in the relevant domain.

## Risk measurement terms

<span id="euler-allocation"></span>
**Euler allocation**: splitting a portfolio risk measure R among positions as RCᵢ = xᵢ·∂R/∂xᵢ. For risk measures that are homogeneous of degree one, the contributions sum exactly to R.

<span id="var"></span>
**[Value at Risk (VaR)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_at_risk)**: the loss level exceeded with probability 1 − α over a period (for example, the 95% VaR is exceeded 5% of the time). It says nothing about how large losses beyond it are.

<span id="expected-shortfall"></span>
**[Expected Shortfall (ES)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_shortfall)**: the mean loss in the worst 1 − α of outcomes. It is a coherent risk measure, unlike VaR, and it is the tail metric to use when expected loss is not enough.

<span id="pra"></span>
**[Probabilistic risk assessment (PRA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_risk_assessment)**: quantifying risk through [fault trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_tree_analysis) (AND and OR gates over component failures) and event trees, as practiced in nuclear and aerospace engineering. <span id="cdf"></span>*Core damage frequency* is its headline output for reactors; the US NRC's subsidiary safety goal is 10⁻⁴ per reactor-year. PRA figures are model outputs, not observed rates.

<span id="common-cause-failure"></span>
**Common-cause failure**: a single cause that makes several redundant components fail together. The beta-factor model, documented in NUREG/CR-4780, is the source of this site's propagation correction.

<span id="defense-in-depth"></span>
**[Defense in depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_in_depth)**: multiple barriers against failure. The arithmetic usually assumes the barriers fail independently, and they rarely do.

<span id="sil"></span>
**[SIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_integrity_level) / [ASIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_Safety_Integrity_Level)**: safety integrity levels under IEC 61508 (SIL 1–4) and ISO 26262 (ASIL A–D). Higher levels require lower failure rates and more rigorous development.

## Mechanism design terms

- <span id="incentive-compatibility"></span>**[Incentive compatibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incentive_compatibility)**: truthful reporting is each participant's best strategy.
- <span id="revelation-principle"></span>**[Revelation principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revelation_principle)**: any outcome some mechanism implements in equilibrium can be implemented by a direct mechanism in which truth-telling is optimal.
- <span id="moral-hazard"></span>**[Moral hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard)**: a party changes behavior after an agreement because its actions are not fully observable (hidden action).
- <span id="adverse-selection"></span>**[Adverse selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adverse_selection)**: parties with unobservable characteristics self-select in ways that harm the other side (hidden information).

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| DR | Delegation risk (expected loss, dollars per stated unit) |
| HS | Harm surface (set of harm modes) |
| P(·), D(·) | Probability and damage of a harm mode |
| t | P(faithful execution) for one delegation link |
| pᵢ | Miss probability of check *i* |
| ρ | Common-cause weight in the beta-factor mixture; equals the phi coefficient of failure indicators for equal pᵢ |
| ES_α | Expected Shortfall at level α |
| HHI | [Herfindahl-Hirschman Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herfindahl%E2%80%93Hirschman_index), a concentration measure |

## See also

- [Concepts](/getting-started/core-concepts/) and [Quick Reference](/getting-started/quick-reference/)
- [Bibliography](/reference/bibliography/)


------------------------------------------------------------
## Quick Reference
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/getting-started/quick-reference/
------------------------------------------------------------

A lookup page for readers who know the framework. Definitions are in the [Glossary](/getting-started/glossary/); derivations are in [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/).

## Formulas

Probabilities are per stated unit (per task, action or month); dollar figures carry the same unit.

| Quantity | Formula | Units |
|---|---|---|
| Delegation risk of a component | Σ P(harm mode) × Damage | \$ per unit |
| System expected loss | Σ component delegation risks (adds whatever the correlation; overlapping harm modes on one asset make the sum an upper bound) | \$ per unit |
| Chain works (serial) | ∏ tᵢ, with tᵢ = P(faithful execution); conservative under correlation | probability |
| All checks miss (parallel) | (1−ρ)·∏pᵢ + ρ·min pᵢ | probability |
| Residual risk behind checks | P(harmful action) × P(all checks miss) × Damage | \$ per unit |
| Entanglement tax | P(all miss) / ∏pᵢ; for n equal checks, (1−ρ) + ρ·p^(1−n) | ratio |
| Estimating ρ | largest pairwise phi coefficient of per-item misses on a shared labeled set | 0–1 |

When ρ is unknown and the checks share a provider, training data or context, or when an adaptive attacker can probe them, use ρ = 1: only your best single check counts. With three checks at p = 0.1, the tax is 1 + 99ρ, about 11×, 21× and 50× at ρ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5.

## Harm-mode checklist

**Accident.** The task is done wrong; there is an edge-case failure; a confident falsehood; resource exhaustion; an irreversible action taken by mistake.

**Defection.** Pursuing a different objective; deception; sandbagging; collusion between components; *reward hacking* (special-casing tests, editing graders), which is a non-scheming sub-type.

**Hijack.** Prompt injection through documents, web pages or tool outputs; a malicious or compromised MCP server or dependency; misuse by an authorized user.

## Where to start, by concern

| Concern | Patterns |
|---|---|
| Capability errors | Escalation Ladder, Trusted Monitor, Checkpoint-Rollback |
| Prompt injection and misuse | Exposure-envelope gateway, Need-to-Know Compartments, Flight Recorder |
| Scheming | Honeypot Injection, Capability Probing, Consistency Triangulation, Random Audit |
| Cascading failure | Bulkhead Isolation, Graceful Degradation |
| Collusion | Trust Transitivity Limits, Adversarial Collaboration; diversify model families |

All are in the [pattern catalogue](/design-patterns/). Before any of them, build [the minimal delegation-engineering layer](/getting-started/core-concepts/#the-minimal-delegation-engineering-layer).

## Example thresholds

*These are examples to adapt, not benchmarks.* Block and escalate any action whose preflight estimate exceeds the remaining budget. Require human approval above a damage threshold you set per system. Keep irreversible or catastrophic harm modes outside the envelope, rather than pricing them in a dollar budget ([why](/getting-started/core-concepts/#when-expected-loss-is-the-wrong-metric)). Review the ledger whenever observed incidents exceed the estimate for a period.


------------------------------------------------------------
## Related Approaches
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/reference/related-approaches/
------------------------------------------------------------

Most of this framework is borrowed: expected-loss accounting from risk management and insurance, the propagation correction from reliability engineering's beta-factor model, the adversarial methodology from AI Control, and least privilege from security engineering. This page says where each neighbour sits and what this site adds, limited to what its pages actually show. For several neighbours the honest answer is "little".

## Positioning

| Approach | What it does | What this framework adds | Relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AI Control** | Protocols that stay safe if the model is deliberately subverting them, evaluated quantitatively on safety–usefulness curves under an auditing budget | An accounting layer around the protocols. It extends to the accident and hijack channels, which Control sets aside, and adds a correlation budget across checks. The adversarial methodology is not added: it is borrowed | Highly complementary |
| **Frontier safety frameworks** (Anthropic RSP, OpenAI Preparedness, Google DeepMind FSF) | Capability thresholds that trigger required safeguards for a model before and during deployment | A deployment-time view: per-delegate, per-action accounting inside one operator's agent system | Different layer; complementary |
| **EU GPAI Code of Practice** | A voluntary code (July 2025) for meeting the AI Act's obligations on general-purpose models; its Safety and Security chapter applies to systemic-risk models | Little. The code binds model providers, not the operators who deploy agents on their models | Upstream of this framework |
| **NIST AI RMF** | Voluntary guidance (2023; generative-AI profile 2024) organized as Govern, Map, Measure, Manage | A concrete metric for "Measure" when the system is a delegation structure; the RMF prescribes none | Fits inside it |
| **FAIR** | Quantitative information-risk analysis: loss event frequency × loss magnitude in money, estimated as ranges and simulated | Delegation structure (who delegates to whom), composition of checks with correlation, and runtime accounting. FAIR's ranges and Monte Carlo are ahead of most of this site's point estimates | Closest precedent for Σ P × D in dollars |
| **Safety cases** | Structured arguments that a system is safe enough to deploy | Quantitative inputs a safety case could cite, and a reconciled ledger as post-deployment evidence | Complementary |
| **Guaranteed Safe AI** | A world model, a safety specification, and a verifier producing an auditable proof certificate | Probabilistic budgets where proofs are out of reach. The exposure envelope is the small part that can be specified and verified | Complementary; proofs for the envelope, budgets for the rest |
| **CaMeL and agent-security patterns** | Defenses against prompt injection built into the system design | Accounting around these defenses, not a better defense. They are the best current answer to the hijack channel and the closest prior art for the envelope | Use them |
| **Common-cause failure analysis** | The beta-factor model of redundant components failing together | Applying it to stacks of AI checks, plus a phi-scale estimation recipe | Same math |
| **CAIS** | General capability built as a system of bounded services | Accepts agentic coordinators and adds accounting | Shares the decomposition intuition |
| **Principal-agent theory** | Agency costs, moral hazard, monitoring | Applies the vocabulary to AI delegates, which lack the stable utilities the theory assumes | Source vocabulary |

## AI Control

Greenblatt et al. ([arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942); ICML 2024) study protocols that use an untrusted strong model, a trusted weaker model and a limited budget of trusted human labor. In their setting, that budget covers 2% of problems. The work is explicitly quantitative: protocols are compared on safety and usefulness, measured against a red team that plays the scheming model. The line has since moved to agents:

- **Ctrl-Z** (Bhatt et al. 2025, [arXiv:2504.10374](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10374)) ran the first control evaluation in an agent environment. Its best resampling protocol cut attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to a benign agent's performance.
- **AI Control Levels** (Korbak et al. 2025, [arXiv:2504.05259](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05259)) scale red-team affordances to a model's capabilities.
- **A control safety case sketch** (Korbak et al. 2025, [arXiv:2501.17315](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17315)) argues from a control evaluation to a deployment decision.
- **Factor(T,U)** (Sandoval & Rushing 2025, [arXiv:2512.02157](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02157)) found that adding factored cognition to trusted monitoring raised safety from 41% to 63% in the APPS setting. The same paper reports that factoring made backdoors no harder to write, and that its protocols had low usefulness.

**Mapping the vocabularies.** Control's *auditing budget* limits how many actions humans can inspect. This site's *risk budget* limits tolerated expected loss. They are related but not equivalent. Control's tradeoff term is *usefulness cost*; "control tax" is not Redwood's term.

Control's stated scope is the defection channel, especially concentrated failures. A model that behaves well under evaluation in order to be deployed is the case where every pre-deployment estimate of P(defection) is unreliable. In the literature this is *deceptive alignment* (Hubinger et al. 2019, [arXiv:1906.01820](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820)); alignment faking has been demonstrated experimentally (Greenblatt et al. 2024, [arXiv:2412.14093](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093)). This framework's answer to that case is not a better estimate. It is the envelope, which bounds damage regardless of intent, together with Control's runtime protocols.

**Combining them.** The natural deployment combines a modular architecture, Control protocols on untrusted components, and per-delegate budgets with an envelope. Do not multiply these layers' failure rates as if independent: they share blind spots when they share a model, and a scheming component picks its moment. Measure the combination with a control evaluation.

## Frontier safety frameworks and regulation

Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework (version 2, April 2025) and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework (first published May 2024, revised in 2025) each tie capability thresholds to required safeguards. Anthropic, for example, activated ASL-3 protections with the release of Claude Opus 4 in May 2025. These frameworks govern models; this site is about how an operator deploys agents built on them.

The EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice was published on 10 July 2025, with chapters on transparency, copyright, and safety and security. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (January 2023) and its generative-AI profile, NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), are voluntary guidance. The code binds providers of models, so an operator building agents on those models sits downstream of it. The RMF does not prescribe a metric. A delegation-risk estimate could serve as one input to its "Measure" function, but no regulator has endorsed one.

## Quantitative risk analysis: FAIR

FAIR (published by The Open Group as the Open FAIR risk taxonomy and risk analysis standards) expresses information risk as the frequency and magnitude of loss in money. It estimates each factor as a calibrated range and simulates the result. That is the obvious precedent for "Σ P × Damage in dollars", and its practice of ranges plus simulation is better than the point estimates on many pages of this site. What FAIR does not model is delegation structure: chains of delegates, stacks of checks with correlated misses, and the per-action accounting a harness could keep.

## Safety cases and Guaranteed Safe AI

A safety case is a structured argument that a system is unlikely to cause a catastrophe; Clymer et al. (2024, [arXiv:2403.10462](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10462)) group the arguments as inability, control, trustworthiness and deference. Delegation-risk estimates and a reconciled ledger are evidence such an argument could cite.

Guaranteed Safe AI (Dalrymple et al. 2024, [arXiv:2405.06624](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06624)) asks for a world model, a safety specification and a verifier that produces an auditable proof certificate. The stronger claim that provable safety is the only path to controllable AGI comes from Tegmark & Omohundro (2023, [arXiv:2309.01933](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.01933)). Full specifications for open-ended agent behavior are out of reach today. The exposure envelope (file scope, egress, spend) is the part small enough to specify and verify, which is why it sits at the top of the [verifiability hierarchy](/getting-started/core-concepts/#verifiability-hierarchy).

## Agent security: CaMeL and design patterns

CaMeL (Debenedetti et al. 2025, [arXiv:2503.18813](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)) extracts the control and data flows from the trusted user query, so that untrusted data the model later retrieves cannot change which tools are called. It enforces capability-based policies on tool calls to stop exfiltration. On the AgentDojo benchmark it solved 77% of tasks with provable security, against 84% for an undefended system. Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025, [arXiv:2506.08837](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837)) give a set of design patterns for agents with provable resistance to prompt injection and analyse their utility trade-offs.

These are the strongest current defenses for the hijack channel; this site's patterns that separate context from capability apply them. The framework's contribution is to price what remains: the exposure an agent keeps after such a design, and how correlated its remaining checks are.

## Reliability engineering: common-cause failure

The closest prior art for the entanglement tax is common-cause failure analysis. The beta-factor model and its successors are documented in NUREG/CR-4780 (Mosleh et al. 1988). Knight & Leveson (1986) showed the same effect in software: independently written versions of one program failed together more often than independence predicts.

The propagation rule used across this site, (1−ρ)·∏pᵢ + ρ·min pᵢ, *is* the beta-factor mixture. What [Risk Propagation](/delegation-risk/risk-propagation/) adds is narrow:

- applying the mixture to stacks of AI checks;
- the observation that correlation biases serial chains and parallel checks in opposite directions;
- a recipe for estimating ρ on the failure-indicator scale.

AI delegation also has failure modes that CCF analysis does not model. One component can create the common cause, for example by biasing what downstream checks see. And components can scheme or collude. The site does not yet model either quantitatively. Its operating rule is to treat any channel an adversary can probe as fully correlated (ρ near 1) unless a control evaluation shows otherwise ([research connections](/entanglements/research/research-connections/)).

## CAIS

Drexler's *Reframing Superintelligence* ([report](https://www.futureofhumanityinstitute.org/s/2019-1.pdf), 2019) argues that general capability can be delivered as a system of bounded services, with agents as one class of service and broader systems coordinating narrower ones. It is sometimes summarized as "train a new narrow model from scratch for each task". That is wrong: the report argues that components are best learned with cross-task generality and reused or fine-tuned. Deployment has since moved toward general agents, as Gwern ([2016](https://gwern.net/tool-ai)) predicted on economic grounds; this framework accepts agentic coordinators and tries to bound them.

## Training-time oversight: IDA, debate, weak-to-strong

These methods aim to make an overseer's judgments better. Iterated amplification (Christiano et al. 2018, [arXiv:1810.08575](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08575)) and debate (Irving, Christiano & Amodei 2018, [arXiv:1805.00899](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899), written at OpenAI) are proposals of this kind. There is empirical work on debate. Khan et al. (2024, [arXiv:2402.06782](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06782)) found that it raised non-expert accuracy to 76% for models and 88% for humans, against naive baselines of 48% and 60%. Kenton et al. (2024, [arXiv:2407.04622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04622)) found debate beat consultancy across tasks but had mixed results against direct question-answering. Weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al. 2023, [arXiv:2312.09390](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09390)) found that weakly supervised strong models outperform their supervisors but fall well short of their full capability.

This framework treats any overseer as a check with a miss rate, and asks how correlated that miss rate is with the failures it oversees. Goel et al. (2025, [arXiv:2502.04313](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313)) report that model mistakes grow more similar as capability increases, which would raise that correlation.

## Principal-agent theory

The vocabulary is economics': agency cost (Jensen & Meckling 1976), moral hazard and the value of informative monitoring (Holmström 1979). Delegation risk is roughly the expected-loss part of an agency cost; defection is hidden action; a check is a monitoring signal. The theory assumes agents with stable, known utilities, which a scheming model does not offer. Incentive schemes therefore bind the operators and vendors around a model better than the model itself. [The Insurer's Dilemma](/delegation-risk/insurers-dilemma/) works through moral hazard and adverse selection in this setting.

## What this framework does not claim

- That it is the first to compose risks across AI systems, or that its coordinator constraints are formally verified. Earlier versions of this site claimed both, and neither is shown on the site.
- That architecture reduces the probability of scheming. Decomposition limits what a schemer can reach; whether it changes propensity is untested.
- That its numbers are calibrated. Most are illustrative; see [About This Site](/reference/about-this-site/).

## AI safety and agent security

- **Greenblatt, R., Shlegeris, B., Sachan, K., & Roger, F. (2023).** *AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion.* [arXiv:2312.06942](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942); ICML 2024. The source of the trusted/untrusted vocabulary used here.

- **Clymer, J., Gabrieli, N., Krueger, D., & Larsen, T. (2024).** *Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems.* [arXiv:2403.10462](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10462).
- **Drexler, K.E. (2019).** *Reframing Superintelligence: Comprehensive AI Services as General Intelligence.* Technical Report #2019-1, Future of Humanity Institute. [PDF](https://www.futureofhumanityinstitute.org/s/2019-1.pdf).

- **Bai, Y., et al. (2022).** *Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback.* [arXiv:2212.08073](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073).

## Reliability engineering and nuclear safety

- **Mosleh, A., Fleming, K.N., Parry, G.W., et al. (1988).** *Procedures for Treating Common Cause Failures in Safety and Reliability Studies.* NUREG/CR-4780, US Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The beta-factor and related common-cause models.
- **Knight, J.C., & Leveson, N.G. (1986).** An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming. *IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering*, 12(1), 96–109.
- **Avizienis, A. (1985).** The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software. *IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering.*
- **Reason, J. (1990).** *Human Error.* Cambridge University Press. The account of layered defenses later popularized as the "Swiss cheese" model.

- **Rasmussen, N.C., et al. (1975).** *Reactor Safety Study* (WASH-1400). US Atomic Energy Commission.
- **US NRC (1990).** *Severe Accident Risks: An Assessment for Five US Nuclear Power Plants* (NUREG-1150).

## Economics: agency and mechanism design

- **Jensen, M.C., & Meckling, W.H. (1976).** Theory of the Firm: Managerial Behavior, Agency Costs and Ownership Structure. *Journal of Financial Economics*, 3(4), 305–360. The source of "agency cost".
- **Holmström, B. (1979).** Moral Hazard and Observability. *Bell Journal of Economics*, 10(1), 74–91. The informativeness principle behind monitoring.
- **Bolton, P., & Dewatripont, M. (2005).** *Contract Theory.* MIT Press.
- **Myerson, R.B. (1979).** Incentive Compatibility and the Bargaining Problem. *Econometrica*, 47(1), 61–73. The revelation principle for Bayesian settings.

- **Shapley, L.S. (1953).** A Value for n-Person Games. In *Contributions to the Theory of Games II*.

## About This Site
Source: https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/reference/about-this-site/
------------------------------------------------------------

## How it was made

This site was drafted quickly in early 2026 by Ozzie Gooen ([QURI](https://quantifieduncertainty.org)) with substantial assistance from large language models, primarily Claude. Read it with that in mind.

## Revisions

**June 2026: hardening.**

- A nine-agent review covered the whole corpus, followed by a fix pass against its findings.
- Flagged fabricated or misattributed citations were removed or corrected. Real-history claims (dates, court cases, nuclear and aviation figures) were checked against secondary sources, mostly Wikipedia plus a few official pages such as nrc.gov. Few were checked against primary documents.
- The propagation math was re-derived, and one canonical worked example replaced several inconsistent ones.
- Hypothetical scenarios were labelled, and a ~25,000-word fiction section was removed.
- Vocabulary was consolidated against a written terminology canon.

**October 2026: audit and contraction.** Model-written audits found that problems remained: retired terms still in use, formulas that contradicted the core one, invented numbers presented as data, citation errors, and examples frozen in 2023. The site was cut from about 300,000 words to roughly 90,000 <!-- TODO(verify): replace with the final word count after the October 2026 integration step -->. Deleted pages redirect to their nearest surviving page, and the surviving core was corrected. The audit reports, with quoted evidence, are in the source repository under `audits/2026-10/`.

## Limitations

- **Little expert review.** Most pages have not been reviewed by domain experts.
- **Illustrative numbers.** Most numbers are illustrative and labelled as such. Where a number is cited, check the source before relying on it; errors of the kind the audits found may remain.
- **Untested.** The framework has not been tested on deployed AI systems. The recommendations are reasoned, not validated.
- **Labelled hypotheticals.** Worked examples and scenarios that are hypothetical are labelled as such.
- **One speculative section.** The [Power Dynamics](/power-dynamics/) page is speculative and marked so.

The parts that seem most robust are borrowed: expected-loss accounting, common-cause failure analysis, least privilege, and AI Control's adversarial methodology. What the site adds is the combination, applied to agent harnesses. Whether that combination earns its keep is an open question.

## How to help

Open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/delegation-risk-framework). The content is licensed CC BY 4.0. The most useful contributions:

- factual and citation corrections;
- logical inconsistencies between pages;
- real incidents, positive or negative;
- measurements of error correlation between checks, which would test the site's central number.

## Acknowledgments

The framework draws on Eric Drexler's CAIS, Redwood Research's AI Control work, and decades of nuclear and financial risk practice. Errors are ours.
